note:
Survey (Bouwmans, El Baf, Vachon) of Mixture-of-Gaussians (MOG) background modeling for foreground detection with static cameras. It sorts improvements to Stauffer & Grimson [1] into two groups. Intrinsic improvements change the model itself: adaptive number of Gaussians K (Zivkovic [94], Cheng [95], Shimada [96], Tan [97], Carminati [98]), initialization (EM [99], approximated EM [84], training sequences that contain foreground [60, 82, 83]), maintenance rules and mechanisms (Kalman [38], counters [60, 70], CUSUM [85]), learning-rate adaptation (PSO tuning of alpha/T [138], variable rates [87, 136, 139, 140]), foreground detection (likelihood/MAP, Jeffreys divergence, PPM, explicit foreground model [57, 85, 109]), and features (block-wise [145, 146], cluster-wise [147]). Extrinsic improvements add spatial or temporal post-processing such as MRF [153], S-TAPPMOG [43] and ASTNA [92].

Section 7 ('7. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION') gathers published Wallflower results as FP, FN and Total Error (TE). The per-sequence Table 5 values are not in the supplied passages. The only qualitative claims are: PSO roughly halves TE; IHLS brings TE 'just under 10 0000' (the digit grouping is ambiguous: 10000 or 100000?); Wang et al. [70] is the best intrinsic method; MRF [153] is the best overall, followed by S-TAPPMOG and ASTNA; Light Switch gives the most false positives. S-TAPPMOG and ASTNA do not report results for MO, TOD or LS, so their totals are not comparable to the others.

Critical points:
- All numbers come from other papers, not from the authors' own runs. No common implementation, parameters or post-processing were used.
- TE is a raw pixel count. It has no normalization, precision/recall or F-measure.
- The survey does not report hardware, FPS, latency or power. Real-time and computation-time constraints are only discussed qualitatively, and those sections are not supplied.
- Metadata conflict: the record says 2010, Recent Advances in Computer Science and Communications. The HAL preamble cites Recent Patents on Computer Science, 2008, 1(3), pp. 219-237 (hal-00338206). This needs manual checking.

No benchmark rows were produced. The passages contain no measured hardware result, and no exact accuracy value can be copied because Table 5's contents are missing.

note:
Scope: this paper is about prognostics, not FPGAs. It trains a convolutional selective autoencoder (CSAE, 416,779 parameters) in Theano/Lasagne/NoLearn. Frames from a lab-combustor flame video are resized from 100×237 to 16×16. The network learns to mask stable-flame frames and pass unstable ones. It is compared with a selective CRF (SCRF, Matlab, 8064 cliques). FPGAs are only proposed as future work ("dedicated FPGAs … can enable on-line real-time instability detection"). The paper reports no FPGA design, resources, power or throughput, so the LUT, DSP, BRAM, power and GOPS fields are n/r. The 'autoencoder-fpga' axis tag is weak and should be checked by hand.

Measured results: Table 2 gives CSAE inference at about 4.7 ms/frame on CPU and about 1 µs/frame on GPU. SCRF takes about 0.24 s/frame on CPU. Model size is O(MB) for CSAE and O(KB) for SCRF. The CPU and GPU models, batch sizes and whether preprocessing is included are not stated. Only the training GPU is named: a Titan Black with "16MB video RAM", which is probably a typo. The GPU figure of about 1 µs/frame is not in ms, so latency_ms is n/r for that row rather than a converted value.

Accuracy: there is no classification accuracy. The quality measure is the ratio Σ(z)/µ(z) of the instability metric, and a transition frame number. For protocol 50040to30 with 10 code units, the ratio is 1.045 for CSAE and 0.2139 for SCRF (Table 3). Thresholds come from the 95% CI of stable validation frames: 0.003901 for CSAE-10 and 0.03636 for SCRF. The column alignment in Table 1 is garbled in the extraction. The DOI (ijphm.2016.v7i4) suggests the paper is from 2016, not 2020 as the metadata says.

Pynq-YOLO-Net is a single-class face-mask detector built on YOLO. Its lightweight backbone has one 3x3 stride-2 convolution, 3 inverted residual bottlenecks and 3 linear bottlenecks. Input is 128x128 and the output grid is 8x8. The class-probability branch is dropped and the confidence score is used as the mask/no-mask decision. The model is pruned and quantized to 1-bit weights and 2-bit activations, with 8-bit input and output, then retrained. On a Pynq Z1, feature extraction runs in the programmable logic (PL) and the fully connected and output layers run on the ARM processor.

Reported results:
- FP32 model: precision 94.6 and recall 95.8.
- Compressed model: precision 90.7 and recall 92.3.
- On the board: 16 FPS, with board power that "does not exceed 5 watts".

Critical issues:
1. **Accuracy numbers conflict.** The abstract claims 97% detection accuracy, but no 97 appears in the results. The text also says "90.7% of Accuracy", while Table I labels 90.7 as precision.
2. **The FPS may not be tied to the compressed model.** The paper implies 16 FPS was measured with the compressed model but never says so explicitly. Latency is not reported.
3. **The power figure is weak.** 5 W is an upper bound for the whole board, not a measured value, and the measurement method is not described.
4. **Hardware details are missing.** There are no LUT, DSP or BRAM counts, no clock frequency, no GOPS, and no toolflow is named (e.g. FINN or HLS), even though the 1-bit weights/2-bit activations suggest FINN/BNN-PYNQ.
5. **The quantization method is mislabeled.** It is called "post-training quantization", but it includes retraining, which makes it closer to quantization-aware fine-tuning.
6. **The evaluation setup is weak.** The test set is 30% of a merged dataset (RMFD, MFDD, SMFRD, MAFA). These sources overlap, since SMFRD is merged into MFDD, and many images are synthetic, so train/test leakage is possible.
7. **The comparison is unfair.** The Table I baselines (RetinaFaceMask; the SSD row is empty) were evaluated on different data. The paper gives no IoU threshold or mAP, and there is no ablation of the pruning and quantization steps.

rows.model: YOLOv3 with dynamic discarding (single output layer)
rows.baseline: Standard YOLOv3 (all 3 output layers) on same device: 22% speed improvement with one output layer, at least 5.5% with two
Standard Tiny-YOLOv3 (3l) without discarding; FPS improved for all individual outputs (input sizes 416/608/832/1056), values in Table 8 not supplied

note:
Critical reading: The paper proposes a "dynamic discarding" technique for YOLOv3 and Tiny-YOLOv3 (3l). It skips YOLO output heads that are not needed at run time. A proximity sensor gives the object's distance, and only the matching scale head runs: layer 0 for near, 1 for medium, 2 for far. Accuracy is claimed to be preserved because only unused operations are removed.

Hardware: this is NOT an FPGA paper, despite the auto-inferred 'yolo-fpga' axis. Everything runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier GPU through PyTorch. TensorRT, OpenCV (CPU-only here), TF Lite and Snapdragon could not run the technique. This means TensorRT optimisation was not used, so the absolute speed is likely far from what this device can reach. FPGAs appear only in Related Work (Moussawi et al., SSD on Arria 10; Hemmati et al., HOG+SVM on Zynq).

Measured results in the supplied passages are only relative: at least 5.5% speed-up with two output heads and 22% with one, against standard YOLOv3 in MAXN (30 W) mode. The actual FPS, latency and BFLOPS values are in Tables 7 and 8, which are not in the supplied text. For Tiny-YOLOv3 (3l), the passages only say FPS improved for every single-head output across input sizes 416, 608, 832 and 1056.

Accuracy: the 55.3 mAP on COCO is the original YOLOv3 author's figure, not re-measured. It is probably AP50 at 608. The per-distance accuracy (Tables 9 and 10) comes from the authors' own driving tests. They say far-range accuracy drops when only head 2 runs, so heads 1 and 2 need to run together.

Caveats: 30 W is the power-mode cap, not measured power, so power is recorded as n/r. Precision is not stated (probably FP32 PyTorch). No LUT, DSP or BRAM figures apply. Metadata extraction was flagged 'ok: false'.

note: Critical reading: The paper runs YOLOv3 on a PYNQ-Z1 (Zynq) board to find hazardous objects (gun, blade, knife) in X-ray baggage images. Only one step is fully described: pre-processing, 3x3 kernel operations and YOLOv3 classification are split between the PS and PL. The reported results are per-class mAP from Table 1: gun 98.5, blade 98.0, knife 98.9. The abstract's claim of '98.9% accuracy' is the single best class (knife), not an overall figure. There are several serious weaknesses. (1) Training used Darknet in Google Colab with only 500 samples. The dataset is not named, and no train/test split or IoU threshold is given. The confidence threshold was picked to give '98% accuracy', which suggests it was tuned on the evaluation data. (2) The text does not say whether the mAP was measured on the FPGA or in software. (3) No throughput, latency, power, clock frequency or quantization/data format is reported, even though the paper names data representation as a key issue. (4) Table 2 (resources) did not survive extraction. The only value left is '130 k', near the classification row, and its column is unknown. A PYNQ-Z1 (XC7Z020) has about 53.2k LUTs and 106.4k FFs, so 130k cannot be a LUT count; it may be FFs, a different unit, or a mistake. I left LUT/FF/BRAM/DSP as n/r; check them against the original PDF. (5) There is no baseline comparison to other FPGA YOLO designs or to CPU/GPU. The sections on CNN vs handcrafted features and transfer learning are claimed but not backed by numbers. Overall, treat this as weak evidence that YOLOv3 can run on an FPGA for this task; it gives no usable performance figures.

rows.model: Sparse (90%) Robust Deep Autoencoder, weight sharing k=16, CRS format

rows.model: Sparse (90%) Robust Deep Autoencoder, CRS format, no weight sharing
rows.baseline: 32-bit float FPGA version (2.9x slower; BRAM 21.5, DSP 10, LUT 6037)

note:
Soga et al. (IEICE 2021) build an ECG outlier detector: an unsupervised Robust Deep Autoencoder (RDA) trained on MIT-BIH Arrhythmia data. Weights are pruned to 90% sparsity, converted to 10-bit fixed point, and weight-shared (K-means, k=16, no retraining). They are stored in CRS sparse format and run on a Xilinx ZedBoard (Zynq-7000) at 100 MHz, built with SDSoC 2018.2.

Reported results against an ARM Cortex-M3 (Arduino Due): 11.7x faster ('12x' in the abstract), 11% of the CPU power, and 0.94% of the energy (106x better). Energy is power times execution time over 1282 ECG waves. Power is for the FPGA or CPU only, not the whole board.

Table 5 resources for the weight-sharing design: BRAM 13.5 (9.64%), DSP 7 (3.18%), LUT 5381 (10.11%), FF 8476. For the fixed-point design without weight sharing: BRAM 14.5, DSP 7, LUT 6285. The fixed-point design is 2.9x faster than float, and weight sharing keeps roughly the same speed. Parameter volume falls to 4.13% of the dense float model.

Critical issues:
(1) The supplied passages do not give the absolute throughput (waves/s), power (W), execution time (ms) or energy (J); only ratios are given. So fps, latency and power are n/r.
(2) The F1 values contradict each other. Dense = 0.967 and 90% sparse = 0.968, but the text also says the 10/11-bit fixed-point F1 of 0.989 is 'identical to the 90% sparse model'. It also says 9-bit = 0.957 is '1% lower' than dense.
(3) The accuracy degradation is given as 0.83 points in some places and 0.84 in others.
(4) The F1 score of the final k=16 weight-sharing design is not stated in the passages.
(5) The baseline is a very low-end microcontroller, which inflates the speedup and energy gains. There is no comparison with other FPGA or ASIC ECG detectors.
(6) Power seems to be tool-estimated or chip-level (FPGA only), but the method is not stated.
(7) Metadata extraction failed, so every passage is labelled '(préambule)'.

YOLOv4 on Jetson Nano (1.6 FPS, 94.2 mean confidence)

note:
What the paper does: it benchmarks Darknet YOLO models on three edge boards: Jetson Nano, Jetson Xavier NX (6-core 15 W mode) and Raspberry Pi 4B with an Intel NCS2 (OpenVINO FP16 IR). The models are YOLOv3/v3-tiny at S=416 on all boards, YOLOv3/v3-tiny at S=320/608 on the Nano, and YOLOv4/v4-tiny at S=416 on the Nano. The test data is two videos from gitee: Video1 (1596 frames, 768×436) and Video2 (960 frames, 1920×1080). Weights are COCO-pretrained. Results are averaged over 10 runs. It is not an FPGA paper, so there are no LUT, DSP or BRAM figures and no GOPS.

Critical issues:
(1) Accuracy is reported only as 'mean confidence' (average score of correctly detected objects). There is no mAP and no ground truth is described, so these numbers are not comparable to standard detection accuracy.
(2) The text and tables disagree. The text and conclusion say YOLOv3-tiny scores 57.9 on Jetson, but Table 3 shows 59.7. The text also says Video1 has 960 frames, while the table note says 1596. The abstract claims NCS2 YOLOv3-tiny FPS is 7.6× YOLOv3; Table 3 gives 18.8/2.5 = 7.5.
(3) NCS2 YOLOv3-tiny runs at 18.8 FPS on Video1 but scores 0 mean confidence because the OpenVINO Model Optimizer broke the Region layer conversion. That FPS therefore does not represent a working detector.
(4) The toolflow on Jetson is unclear: Darknet is compiled on the device, but the paper also says 'GPU to compile TensorFlow'. TensorRT was deliberately not used, so the Jetson results understate what the hardware can do.
(5) The FP16 claim rests on a questionable rationale ('Nano only supports FP16'). How precision was enforced in Darknet is not described.
(6) Power scope is mixed. Table 3 'Power' comes from JTOP on the Jetsons and a USB meter on the RPi, so it is probably board-level but this is not stated. Tables 5–6 report GPU-rail power only. Idle power is not subtracted.
(7) Latency is not reported; only FPS and total time are given.
(8) The Table 3 extraction merges rows; the values below were separated by position, so they carry some risk of misreading.

These passages contain no FPGA or other hardware measurements. The only compute platform mentioned is a GPU-enabled Google Colaboratory instance with 12 GB RAM, used for the software implementation in TensorFlow/Keras. Throughput, latency, power and resource figures are therefore all n/r. The 'autoencoder-fpga' axis looks like an automatic mis-tag and should be removed or confirmed.

Method: a VAE with a class-wise focal loss (CFLVAE, 87-40-20-10-20-40-87) generates extra samples for the rare attack classes. A lightweight DNN (87-40-20-10-5) is then trained on the balanced NSL-KDD data, using the 20% training subset of 25,192 samples.

Results:
- **KDDTest+:** accuracy 88.08, recall 88.02, precision 88.25, F1 87.69, FPR 3.77.
- **KDDTest-21:** accuracy 76.22, F1 76.66, FPR 6.51.

Critical issues:
1. **R2L and U2R rates are swapped in the abstract.** It gives U2R 79.25 and R2L 67.5, but the body and Table 2 give R2L 79.26 and U2R 67.5.
2. **Hyperparameters were tuned on the test set.** Gamma and alpha were chosen by trial and error on KDDTest-21, which is also a reported test set, so the Test-21 results are optimistically biased.
3. **The SOTA comparison uses other papers' published numbers** under different protocols. The claims of best F1 and best minority-class rates rest on that table. SCDNN has higher accuracy (91.97) and ICVAE-DNN has lower FPR (2.74).
4. **The 'lightweight, suitable for IoT' claim is not measured.** No inference cost, model size, or on-device deployment is reported.
5. **Naming and metadata are inconsistent.** The text uses both CFVAE and CFLVAE and has an 'NSK-KDD' typo. The metadata gives the first author's given name as 'Salma', but the preamble says 'Shapla'.

rows.model: LSTM-based VAE + NRMSE image + Otsu thresholding (RADIS)
rows.dataset: Tanker ship Diesel GenSet sensor data (14 parameters, >66,000 instances each, 1-min sampling)

note:
RADIS is an offline-trained LSTM-based VAE that reconstructs 14 sensor parameters from a tanker ship's diesel generator. The data has more than 66,000 one-minute instances per parameter. Pre-processing finds steady states using a first-order Markov transition-matrix image and connected component analysis, then normalises values to [-1, 1] and applies sliding windows. Per-parameter NRMSE between observed and reconstructed subsequences forms an image. Multi-level Otsu thresholding labels anomalies, with the number of classes chosen by GMM/EM and BIC. In practice this was reduced to two-level thresholding because the multi-level version was too slow for real-time use. Hyperparameters were chosen by grid search with k-fold cross-validation. The reported result is an average accuracy of 92.5 on anomalies simulated by injecting Gaussian/random noise, not on real faults.

Critical points:
(1) The passages contain no FPGA or other hardware implementation and no measured hardware result: no latency, throughput, power or resource figures. FPGA appears only in the literature review (Cheng et al. 2019 denoising filter), so the 'autoencoder-fpga' axis tag looks wrong.
(2) The real-time claim is only simulated. The authors say a real-world deployment and inference acceleration remain future work.
(3) The evaluation uses synthetic noise anomalies, reports only accuracy (no precision, recall or F1), and has no baseline comparison.
(4) The authors acknowledge that the Markov states and VAE hyperparameters were chosen heuristically and that the model may miss long dependencies.
(5) The paper's metadata still needs manual checking.

rows.task: object detection (intrusion/human monitoring in smart mirror)

note: Critical reading: This is an IoT smart-mirror prototype. A Raspberry Pi with a camera, PIR sensor and touch sensor runs YOLOv5 object detection for intrusion and human monitoring, emails captured images to the owner, and shows weather, time, news and calendar text on the mirror. Reported numbers: none. The Results section (3 Results and Discussion) describes hardware tests only in qualitative terms (Fig. 11 detection output, Fig. 12 email notification). It gives no accuracy, mAP, FPS, latency, power or resource figures, no dataset and no baseline comparison. The claims of "more accuracy", faster detection and "highest level of accuracy and precision" have no supporting evidence. Inconsistencies: the title and Results say Raspberry Pi 4, but the Abstract says Raspberry Pi 3. The Introduction describes intrusion detection by background subtraction or frame differencing, while the Results credit YOLOv5. The Methodology describes a face-recognition pipeline (alignment, anti-spoofing, Euclidean/angular loss) that is never evaluated. The Conclusion mentions "experimental results for several approaches", but no such results appear in the supplied passages. Relevance: there is no FPGA or accelerator content, so the automatically assigned 'yolo-fpga' axis looks wrong. This paper should be reclassified as embedded CPU/IoT. One row is recorded only to log the qualitative hardware demonstration. Every metric is n/r.

rows.baseline: FP32 YOLOv3-Tiny (accuracy); Yu et al. [27] etc. on 7Z020 (hardware)

note:
HFOD (Zhang et al., IEICE ELEX 2022) quantizes YOLOv3-Tiny channel-wise and uniformly, with 2-bit weights and 8-bit activations. It also fuses batch-norm (BN) layers into the quantized conv layers. The model runs on a Vivado HLS accelerator on PYNQ-Z2 (XC7Z020, 150 MHz, tiles Tm,Tn,Tr,Tc = 10,4,26,26). Its convolution unit uses line and window buffers with the K×K loops fully unrolled, which is meant to save BRAM and get more work out of each DSP.

Points to read critically:
(1) The headline 90.6 GOPS is the peak of a single layer (conv layer 12, a 3×3 layer). It is not the average throughput over the whole network. The supplied text reports no end-to-end FPS or latency.
(2) The passages give accuracy only as a drop of about 5.3 mAP from FP32 on VOC2007 test. They do not give the absolute mAP values from Table I.
(3) The numbers in Tables II and III (LUT, DSP, BRAM, power, GOPS/W) were not in the extracted text, so resources and power are n/r here. The abstract says 1.4× faster and 2× better power efficiency than a peer on the same board, but that cannot be checked from these passages.
(4) The comparisons mix different models (YOLO, YOLO-tiny, YOLOv3-Tiny), precisions and FPGAs. The paper says the design has the best throughput among RTL designs, while admitting that Afzal et al. [32] has higher throughput.
(5) Results on an infrared aerial dataset are described only in words, with no numbers.

The metadata extraction was flagged as unreliable, and no section headings were detected apart from the Abstract.

Baker & Xiang (2023, IEEE COMST) is a survey of the Artificial Intelligence of Things for healthcare (AIoMT), not an experimental paper. What it contributes: (1) a three-layer computing hierarchy (device/embedded, edge, cloud) plus an application layer; (2) a proposed cross-layer AI approach, where lightweight models on the device or edge handle data quality checks, preprocessing and offloading decisions, and heavier models run in the cloud; (3) overviews of sensors (PPG, ECG, EEG, rPPG, sweat and interstitial-fluid sensors), communications (LoRaWAN, Sigfox, NFC, NB-IoT, 5G, RedCap, 6G, LEO satellite) and ML model families (CNN, RNN/LSTM, RF, autoencoders, transformers/BERT/ViT); (4) a review across monitoring, diagnosis, prognosis and explainability, plus use cases (dementia, stroke, breast cancer, COVID-19). Critical points: FPGA and CMOS embedded AI get only a one-line mention with citations [24], [25]. No accelerator design, resource use, latency, throughput or power is reported, so the paper adds nothing to hardware benchmarking. The accuracy figures it quotes come from other papers, with datasets and protocols that aren't comparable: 96.7% of heat-stroke cases detected with kNN [180]; 80% for RF on 12 patients [181]; 83.33% kNN and about 79% RF/SVM for Wi-Fi CSI respiratory rate [145]; 95.30% CNN for CSI activity recognition [185]; 65.3% RF for depression/anxiety [144]. Some quoted numbers use very small cohorts (for example 12 patients). The comparison with other surveys (Table I) is a simple checkmark matrix defined by the authors themselves. Some claims, such as vision transformers 'routinely outperform' CNNs, are stated without quantitative support in these passages. Metadata extraction was flagged as needing manual checking. No benchmark rows were produced: none of the supplied passages reports a measured hardware result, and the accuracy numbers belong to the cited primary works, not to this paper.

Survey (IEEE Access 2023) of unsupervised visual anomaly detection for industrial images. It groups methods into five families: reconstruction-based (AE/VAE/GAN, student-teacher STPM/RSTPM/reverse distillation), normalizing-flow (CFLOW-style, CS-Flow, FastFlow), representation-based (SPADE, PaDiM, PatchCore, FYD), data-augmentation/synthetic-anomaly (DRAEM, NSA, CutPaste, SSPCAB, AnoSeg) and algorithm enhancement (IGD, FCDD, mean-shifted contrastive loss). It also covers datasets (BTAD, ELPV, AITEX, MTD, KolektorSDD, DAGM, MVTec AD, edible oil). Critical points: (1) The supplied passages include only captions for the comparison tables (AUROC on BTAD, AITEX/ELPV, MTD, KolektorSDD, DAGM, MVTec AD, edible oil). No numbers were supplied, so no accuracy values can be extracted. (2) The results appear to be collected from other papers and are not a controlled re-benchmark, apart from Table 12 (edible oil), which may be the authors' own run but is not described. (3) The complexity discussion is qualitative only (e.g., SPADE's KNN makes inference slow; NF methods avoid KNN search). It reports no hardware platform, latency, FPS, power or resource figures. (4) There is no FPGA or accelerator content, so the paper is not relevant to hardware benchmarking. (5) The claims about limitations (threshold uncertainty, ImageNet bias of backbones) are asserted without supporting experiments in these passages. No benchmark rows are included because the passages contain no measured hardware result and no extractable numbers.

rows.dataset: MOT20 (plus authors' own dataset per abstract)

note: Critical reading (from the supplied passages only): The paper swaps YOLOv3's Darknet-53 backbone for MobileNet (depthwise plus pointwise convolutions, 416x416 input per Table 1). It adds a Kalman-filter denoising step and binary cross-entropy for class prediction. Evaluation uses frame sequences described as MOT20. The paper calls MOT20 a "real-time video dataset acquired on this work", but it is a public benchmark. Reported headline numbers: accuracy 99 (Abstract and Fig 5), precision 98, recall 95, TP 95, FP "94" and detection rate 93. It gives baseline precision of 95/93/91/82/81 for SSD/RCNN/F-RCNN/YOLOv2/YOLOv3. There are serious methodological red flags. (1) Metric definitions are confused: FP is described as both false alarms and frames per second, a high FP rate is called "most excellent", MAP is defined as "mean absolute position" rather than mean average precision, and precision is defined as measurement repeatability. (2) Reporting per-frame-sequence maxima suggests best-case reporting. (3) There is an internal inconsistency in Table 1 (a 7x7 average pool applied to a 13x13 map). (4) No hardware platform, FPGA device, quantization, toolflow, resource usage or throughput is given. Table 11 (power and latency) appears only as a caption, with no values in the passages. The automatic 'yolo-fpga' axis is not supported by this text, so no measured hardware result is present. The rows below record only the algorithmic accuracy and precision claims, with low confidence.

Survey (ACM Computing Surveys 2023) on building AI-based safety-critical systems in industrial and transportation domains, covering systems from traditional functional safety (FuSa) to autonomous ones. It proposes a taxonomy with five parts: types of AI (connectionists, Bayesians, symbolists, analogizers, optimization); levels of automation (automatic, heteronomous, autonomous); safety standards (FuSa: IEC 61508 and ISO 26262; heteronomous/SOTIF: ISO/PAS 21448; autonomous: UL 4600 and VDE-AR-E2842-61; AI and safety: ISO 5469 and ISO/AWI PAS 8800); where AI is applied (product, runtime, process); and compliance classes I, II and III. The main technical point is how products reach FuSa compliance. Class I relies on offline formal verification. Class II relies on runtime compensation such as a safety bag or diverse monitor (IEC 61508-7 C.3.4), which makes the monitor the safety function. One example is a SIL4 railway interlocking system. Uncertainty management runs through the survey: the 'semantic gap' between intended and specified functionality, data quality and train/test split requirements, and the fact that formal verification is limited to moderate-size NNs. The section on the inference execution platform (GPU, FPGA, multicore, specialized DNN accelerators; hypervisors, ROS, AUTOSAR, TensorRT/cuDNN; Vulkan SC and OpenGL SC) is a qualitative literature map of random-error diagnostics and fault tolerance. Limitations: this is a survey with no experiments of its own. None of the supplied passages report a measured hardware result (no FPS, GOPS, latency, power or FPGA resource figures) or an accuracy number, so I produced no benchmark rows. FPGA-related claims only point to cited works [34, 101], which would have to be read separately. PDF extraction found no section headings, so every passage is under '(préambule)'. Several tables (Tables 1–6) came through fragmented or as captions only, so the classification mappings between studies and techniques should be checked against the original PDF. The metadata is flagged for manual checking.

rows.source_section: IV. C L A S S I C A L M A C H I N E L E A R N I N G O N E D G E

note: Survey article (Proc. IEEE 2023) about deep learning inference on edge devices. It covers edge-AI elements (caching, training, inference, offloading), classical ML on the edge, DL basics, compression, lightweight models, codesign software, and hardware platforms (FPGA, ASIC/SoC, MCU, VPU). The supplied passages contain no measurements made by the authors. NILM load classification (17 classes, 64x64 current images)

note:
Tapiador et al. (DCIS 2023) take a small NILM load-classification CNN (from their earlier ref. [7]: 64x64 current-window images, 17 classes, BLUED data at 4 kHz). They quantize it with Brevitas quantization-aware training and build a streaming IP with FINN for a Zybo Z7-20 (XC7Z020). The weights are 3-bit, except the first fully-connected layer (8192-256), which is 2-bit. The passages give no activation bit width. To fit FINN, padding was added to the convolutions, which grows the first FC layer from 6272 to 8192 inputs. The FC1 weights are stored in BRAM and the other layers in LUTRAM. The IP sits in a Zynq SoC with ARM and DMA, and an extra FINN transform was needed to add TLAST.

Measured results: post-implementation resources, CNN IP / whole system: LUT 16911/20937, FF 32920/38518, RAMB36E1 118 (84.29%)/120, DSP 75/75. On-board accuracy on the test set was 96.96, against 98.19 for the float CNN and 96.94 for the software QCNN. Precision, recall and F1 were 97.26, 96.72 and 96.95.

Caveats:
- Throughput is only FINN's estimate (21 FPS at 100 MHz), not a measurement. The design deliberately trades latency for fewer resources.
- No power, energy or measured latency is reported.
- No comparison with other FPGA or CPU implementations.
- BRAM use (about 85%) is the binding constraint.
- Test-set size and class balance are not given in the passages. The drop is also uneven across classes (class 00 is hit harder).
- Metadata was flagged for manual check.

note:
Critical reading: Valente et al. (ISGC 2023) train a convolutional JointVAE (continuous Gaussian plus Gumbel-Softmax discrete latents). It does unsupervised anomaly detection on 40x40 jet images: 200K QCD jets are the background and top jets are the signal, with a 75/25 split. Only the encoder is meant to go on the FPGA. For that reason, only KL-based anomaly scores are used (KL continuous, discrete and total); reconstruction-based scores are not available. To fit the Vivado HLS 2020.1 limit of 2048 parameters per layer, the encoder was reduced (fewer and shorter filters, plus a linear conv_fin layer). It was then trained quantization-aware in QKeras at <16,6> fixed point and converted with hls4ml. The reduction lowered KL-total performance, while quantization raised KL-discrete. The quantized KL-total AUC is about 81.2. Other values from Tables 1–3 (TPR@FPR=0.1 and the energy in µJ) are not in the supplied passages. The only energy figure given is a relative drop of 39.2%, estimated with QTOOLS for a 45 nm process; it is not an FPGA power measurement.

The hardware evidence consists only of per-layer Vivado HLS resource estimates at a 5 ns target clock (200 MHz) on an Alveo U250. Nothing was synthesized, placed and routed, or run on the board. No throughput or power figures are reported. The table caption mentions latency, but the supplied table has no latency values. The first layer, conv2_b0_0, could not be simulated in HLS. Its resources were extrapolated linearly from computational complexity to 6189696 LUTs (358% of the device), so the authors conclude the design cannot fit on a single FPGA. Overall this is a negative feasibility result, not a working accelerator.

Caveats: resource percentages are per layer and are not a full-design total. Blocks are repeated in the real model, so the true totals would be higher. The metadata still needs manual checking.

note:
Zhai et al. (Sensors 2023) build a Zynq-7000 accelerator that runs pruned YOLOv3 and YOLOv3-tiny for vehicle detection, with DeepSORT tracking on the host CPU. The models are compressed with binary-search dynamic-threshold structured pruning plus knowledge distillation. They are then quantised to dynamic 16-bit fixed point, choosing Q per layer for weights, activations and intermediate results. Memory is reused between layers, weights are reordered in advance, and transfers use ping-pong double buffering. Software can switch between the two models depending on traffic.

Headline result (Table 8, Fixed-16 at 230 MHz): YOLOv3-tiny reaches 91.65 fps and 67.91 GOP/s at 12.51 W full power (1.31 W dynamic), with mAP 0.599 on UA-DETRAC. YOLOv3 reaches 3.23 fps and 63.51 GOP/s at 0.711 mAP.

(1) Table 8 gives only two resource columns for 'This Work'. I matched them to the Float-32 and Fixed-16 designs because they line up with the dual-core figures in Table 9 (DSPs 602 ≈ 2×301; BRAM 263 ≈ 2×132.5). Each design appears to be shared by both models, so both rows use the same resource values. This alignment is my inference, not stated in the paper.
(2) mAP is identical for Float-32 and Fixed-16 (0.711 / 0.599). Either quantisation caused no loss, or accuracy was not measured separately for each precision.

(4) The exact Zynq part is not named. Full-power measurement is not described, so its scope may be board or SoC. The fps figures probably leave out host-side preprocessing, NMS and DeepSORT.
(5) Table 7 gives no power for Baseline3 (ZCU9EG) yet reports an efficiency of 3.71 GOPS/W.

note:
Critical reading note — Hozhabr & Giorgi, "A Survey on Real-Time Object Detection on FPGAs" (IEEE Access 2025).

What the paper is: A survey of FPGA implementations of real-time object detection, mostly one-stage CNN detectors (YOLO, SSD). It covers the algorithms, datasets and metrics used, how FPGA accelerators are built (single computation engine vs. streaming designs), acceleration techniques (quantization, pruning, Winograd, pipelined NMS) and optimization strategies. Its main claimed contribution is comparing designs by pixel throughput, meaning FPS weighted by input resolution, so that systems running different image sizes can be compared fairly (Tables 9 and 10, Figure 18). It also compares power efficiency (Figure 19).

Strengths:
- It is the first survey framed around the real-time requirement specifically, including the hard vs. soft real-time distinction.
- Pixel throughput is a reasonable way to compare speed across different input resolutions.
- The case studies are reviewed in chronological order and pair architecture details with results, e.g. Chang et al.'s mixed-precision pipelined multicore design.

Limitations and caveats:
- Every hardware number is second-hand, summarized from the cited works, and often without key context: dataset, input resolution, clock frequency, and whether power was measured for the chip or the whole board. For example, Fan et al. [47] report 9.9 W with no scope stated; Nguyen et al. [15] report 51.68 mAP with no dataset named in the passage.
- Accuracy is sometimes given only as a drop (Fan: 1.8% loss after pruning; Suh: 0.24% mAP drop) rather than an absolute value.
- Some claims are hard to check or look inconsistent. "Pruning up to 10% of the channels" is said to give a model 3× smaller. "More than sixfold" improvement over a TITAN X Pascal GPU is stated without the GPU's own figures.
- The supplied passages list Tables 9 and 10 by caption only, so their values could not be extracted.
- The claim that streaming architectures suit real-time work better is argued qualitatively, not quantified.
- The extraction warned that section I headings were not detected, so introduction text appears under the "FIGURE 1." heading.

About the rows: both are secondary rows, taken from cited primary works (Fan et al. [47] and Nguyen et al. [15]) as the survey reports them. Confidence is set to medium because the values should be checked against the original papers. Other results mentioned in the passages but not tabulated:
- Chang et al. [82]: YOLOv3 on ZCU102, 22 FPS, 49.7 mAP.
- Suh et al. [69]: SSD with UniPOT 8-bit on ZU3EG, 158 GOPS, 79 GOPS/W, 88.42 mAP on a custom drone dataset.
- Anupreetham et al. [67]: SSD on Stratix 10, 2.13 ms end-to-end latency, 22.8 mAP on MS COCO.

note:
FINN (FPGA'17) presents a Vivado HLS framework that generates heterogeneous streaming dataflow accelerators for fully binarized NNs. Each layer gets its own compute engine (an MVTU with P PEs × S SIMD lanes), and folding factors are sized to meet a target FPS. Three hardware tricks make the mapping cheap: popcount instead of signed accumulation (376 vs 759 LUTs for 128-bit), batchnorm+sign folded into an unsigned threshold (6 LUTs vs 2 DSPs + 40 LUTs), and max-pool implemented as a Boolean OR after thresholding. All results are measured on a ZC706 (Zynq-7045) at 200 MHz.

Headline results:
- SFC-max: 12361 kFPS, 0.31 µs latency, 8265.45 GOPS, 7.3 W chip / 21.2 W wall power, 4.17% error on MNIST.
- CNV-max: 21.9 kFPS (the abstract gives 21906 FPS), 283 µs latency, 2465.5 GOPS, 3.6 W chip / 11.7 W wall power, 19.90% error on CIFAR-10 and 5.10% on SVHN.

Critical points:
1. The accuracy gap is large. SFC's 4.17% MNIST error is far behind float networks (Table 1). The accuracy-for-speed trade-off rests on a roofline argument (16× binary vs 8-bit), not on a matched-accuracy hardware comparison.
2. The prior-work comparison mixes chip and wall power, and different precisions and platforms. Several GOPS figures are the authors' estimates (marked ~).
3. Table 3 is garbled in extraction. It lists 4.5 BRAM for SFC-max, but Sec. 5 says 130.5, so the BRAM value was left as n/r. The LUT columns may also be misaligned.
4. The max designs are bottlenecked differently: SFC is memory-bound, LFC is BRAM/resource-bound (46% of roofline), and CNV is limited by the SWU unit. Reported runtime efficiency is about 70–90%.
5. The board's idle power is about 7 W, which dominates the wall-power efficiency figures.
6. DSP usage is not reported.

Unit handling: the paper reports throughput in kFPS and latency in µs. These do not match the fps and latency_ms columns and were not converted, so those cells are n/r and the values appear above instead. power_w holds the chip (FPGA) power; wall power is listed above.

note:
Fraser et al. (2017) extend FINN to larger BNNs on an Alpha Data ADM-PCIE-8K5 board with a Kintex UltraScale KU115 FPGA running at 125 MHz. The main contribution is streaming padding with -1 values. This keeps the datapath binary: 0-padding would need ternary {-1,0,+1} values and a 2-bit datapath. In Table 1, -1-padding matches 0-padding (sigma=1: 88.3 vs 88.6; sigma=1/2: 85.2 vs 85.2). Both beat no-padding by about 4-5 points, but padding costs 2-3 times more operations per frame (Table 2).

Headline result: cnn(1), at 1.2 GOP/frame, runs at 12 kFPS with 671 µs latency, draws under 41 W of board power, and delivers 14.8 TOPS (Table 3: 14,814 GOps/s). The stated CIFAR-10 accuracy is 88.7.

Issues for critical reading:
(1) Accuracy doesn't match across the paper. The abstract gives 88.7, but Table 1 gives cnn(1) 88.3 with -1-padding and 88.6 with 0-padding.
(2) Power is only an upper bound for the whole board ("less than 41 W"). No power is reported per design. The resource counts include the PCIe infrastructure.
(3) The extracted Table 3 is garbled. LUT, BRAM and kFPS values are missing, and only GOps/s survives for the padded designs. All designs were built for the same target of about 12 kFPS.
(4) The GPU comparison (Titan X at 3.2 kFPS and 227 W on AlexNet) sets binary operations against 32-bit float and uses a different network and dataset. It is not a like-for-like comparison.
(5) The comparison with FINN mixes devices (Z7045 vs KU115). FINN's MLPs come closer to the theoretical peak. BRAM use is poor because weights are split across many PEs and SIMD lanes, which limits scaling to cnn(2).

Units: I copied values without conversion. In row 1, the fps value is in kFPS (12) and latency_ms holds 671 in µs (0.671 ms).

Survey paper (Schuman et al., 2017, arXiv 1705.06963). It reviews more than 3,000 neuromorphic papers published over 35 years, covering motivations, neuron/synapse/network models, and algorithms and learning. None of the supplied passages report a measured hardware result (no FPS, GOPS, latency, power, or resource figures for any system), so no benchmark rows were extracted. The only power figure is the ~20 W budget of the human brain (II. MOTIVATION), which is biological context, not a hardware measurement. Critical points: (1) This is a taxonomy and citation map, not a quantitative comparison, so it cannot be used as a source for benchmarks. Look up the cited primary works (e.g., SpiNNaker, the CNN implementations [1054]–[1075]) instead. (2) Table I (IV. ALGORITHMS AND LEARNING) compares back-propagation, evolutionary, Hebbian, and STDP learning with qualitative Yes/No/Maybe ratings, without a stated method or metrics. (3) The authors say low power is the main current motivation but do not measure energy efficiency. (4) They acknowledge that STDP has not shown broad applicability and that on-line learning algorithms are still an open problem. (5) Metadata was flagged for manual check (extraction ok=false), and the axes were inferred automatically.

note:
fpgaConvNet (NIPS 2017 MLPCD workshop; toolflow version, not the FCCM 2016 paper) maps Caffe ConvNets to streaming FPGA accelerators. It models each design as a Synchronous Dataflow graph, using a topology matrix and a workload matrix. Design space exploration is treated as an optimisation problem using four transformations: graph partitioning with full reconfiguration (for throughput, with batching to hide the reconfiguration cost), coarse-grained folding, fine-grained folding, and weights reloading (for latency, using one flexible architecture instead of reconfiguring). The paper also claims the first FPGA mapping of DenseNet-161.

Evaluation: Zynq 7045 (FXP16, 125 MHz) versus Tegra X1 (TensorRT, cuDNN v6, FP16) on AlexNet, VGG16, GoogLeNet and DenseNet-161. Power was measured with a power monitor, with idle power subtracted.

Results, with both platforms held to a 5 W budget (GPU clocked down to 76.8 MHz):
- Throughput-driven: up to 5.53x faster than the GPU, average 3.32x, geometric mean 3.07x.
- Latency-driven: up to 6.65x, average 3.95x, geometric mean 3.43x.
- Against the GPU at its full 998 MHz, GOp/s/W improves 1.17x for throughput-driven (geo. mean 1.12x) and 1.70x for latency-driven (geo. mean 1.36x).

Weaknesses:
- The text reports only speed-up ratios. Absolute throughput, latency and GOp/s for each network are only in Fig. 3, which was not supplied.
- The 270 GOp/s (FPGA) and 79 GFLOPS (GPU) figures are theoretical peaks, not measurements.
- No FPGA resource use (LUTs, DSPs, BRAM) and no accuracy impact of FXP16 are reported.
- The GPU is heavily throttled for the 5 W comparison, which favours the FPGA. Its memory bandwidth (12.8 GB/s) is also far higher than the FPGA's (4.2 GB/s).
- The latency-driven comparison is reported as 'throughput improvement', so the latency metric is unclear.
- The rows below are cross-benchmark aggregates. The 5 W value is the configured power budget, not a measured draw.

note:
NEURAghe (Meloni et al., arXiv 1712.00994) is a hardware/software design on a Xilinx Zynq Z-7045. A Convolution-Specific Processor on the FPGA fabric combines a SystemVerilog convolution engine with an OpenRISC microcontroller and runs at 140 MHz in its fast clock domain. The two ARM Cortex-A9 cores (800 MHz, with NEON) run fully-connected, marshaling and irregular layers. The NeuDNN software stack connects the two sides. All data is 16-bit fixed point (Q5.11) and no retraining is needed.

Measured results: VGG-16 uses an SVD-compressed FC6. Single-frame latency is 263.61 ms at 122.58 GOps/s. A 3-stage CPU/FPGA pipeline brings the per-frame time down to 181.2 ms, giving 169.74 GOps/s and 5.5 fps. Convolution layers peak at 225 GOps/s. The fully-connected layers are limited by memory bandwidth (about 70 ms at 1.02 GOps/s). ResNet-18 runs end to end in 150 ms (6.6 fps), averaging 58.4 GOps/s and peaking at 140 GOps/s across its convolution layers. The 7x7 convolution is split into 5x5 pieces and the 1x1 convolutions are mapped onto 3x3, and data marshaling takes about 42% of the time.

Resources: 864 of 900 DSPs (96.0%), BRAM 35.1%, logic LUTs 16.2%, shift-register LUTs 14.1%. Only percentages are given for BRAM and LUTs, so those fields are n/r. Table 5 gives LUT/FF counts, but the extracted text does not show which column they belong to.

Caveats:
- Power is only given as "~10W" in the comparison table, with no measurement method or scope. The abstract's 17 GOps/W is consistent with 169/10.
- No accuracy was measured on the accelerator. The 92.7 top-5 figure is from the original VGG paper, and the only accuracy statement for this work is that the SVD step loses less than 0.05.
- The fps and GOps/s figures come from pipelined throughput, not single-frame latency.
- The claim of 18-27% better VGG-16 performance than prior Z-7045 designs mixes designs with different quantization (Qiu et al. use 16/8/4-bit) and different end-to-end scope.
- The UltraScale (XCZU9EG) dual-CSP result is synthesis only.
- The metadata could not detect any sections, so every passage is under the heading "(préambule)".

note:
Penkovsky, Larger & Brunner (2018) build a single-node (time-delay) reservoir computer on an Artix-7 XC7A100T FPGA. The hardware was designed in Clash (Haskell), compiled to VHDL, then built in Vivado. The paper adds two ideas: (1) a PCA 'linear autoencoder' merged into the input mask (W_I2 = W_I·Wc^T·Wc), and (2) a genetic algorithm (GA) search over the reservoir dynamics parameters (τ, β, Φ0, ρ). The task is isolated-digit speech recognition on the clean Aurora-II subset (2412 samples, 64-dimensional Lyon cochleagrams).

**Reported results**
- Without PCA, the GA reaches a word error rate (WER) of 3.8. With PCA (7 components, 94.9 variance kept, about 9x input compression), it reaches 2.1. This is the '1.8-fold' improvement.
- These WER values come from offline simulation with two-fold cross-validation on 500+500 digits, not from the FPGA.
- The claim that the GA is 5,106 times faster than grid search is an extrapolated estimate for a four-dimensional grid, not a measurement.

**Limitations of the supplied passages**
- The only measured hardware figure is that the design takes 'about 23% of FPGA area' with N = 600 nodes. The passages give no LUT, DSP or BRAM counts, no clock rate, throughput, latency or power.
- The FPGA test-set WER (on a separate set of 1000 digits) is cut off in the passages, so no hardware accuracy can be recorded.
- Inputs are compressed on the PC and sent over serial UART. Readout weights are trained offline. Hardware quantization is only modelled as injected noise of about 2^-13 (the buses are 16+2 bits wide).

**Inconsistencies**
- The text limits Φ0 to [0, π], yet the reported optimal values are −1.33 and −3.3125.
- The PCA analysis finds the best result with 13 components, but later experiments use 7.
- The dataset is small, and the only baseline is the authors' own configuration without PCA.

note: Preußer et al. (Xilinx Research, arXiv 1806.08085, 2018) describe how they built Tincy YOLO, a real-time Pascal VOC object detector that runs end to end on an embedded Zynq UltraScale+ XCZU3EG. The work is mainly an integration effort. Darknet gets a generic offload layer that calls a FINN HLS QNN accelerator in the PL. That accelerator is a single reused conv+pool engine, because only one generalized layer fits on the XCZU3EG. It runs the hidden layers with binary weights and 3-bit activations (W1A3). The float or 8-bit input and output layers run on the Cortex-A53 cores with NEON. The authors also change the topology: ReLU instead of leaky ReLU, different channel counts, and the first maxpool is removed so the first conv uses stride 2. Finally, a 4-thread pipelined demo mode is added. Measured progression: 0.1 fps with generic Darknet (10,030 ms per frame, hidden layers 9,160 ms). With the PL offload the hidden layers take 30 ms (more than 300x) and the system runs at just above 1 fps. After the topology changes it runs at more than 5 fps, and with pipelining at 16 fps. The paper claims 160x overall. Workload is about 4.445 G ops per frame for Tincy YOLO, compared with about 6.97 G for Tiny YOLO. Critical points: (1) The text says retraining kept the accuracy loss within 3%. Table IV shows Tiny YOLO float at 57.1 mAP and Tincy YOLO W1A3 at 48.5 mAP, a drop of about 8.6 points. This is either a mismatch or a different meaning of "3%". (2) Tables I and III show that precision is mixed: 8-bit or float at the input and output layers. It is not clear whether Table IV's numbers include that exact configuration. (3) The paper reports no power, energy, LUT/DSP/BRAM use, clock frequency or GOPS, so efficiency cannot be compared. GOPS could be worked out (about 4.445 G ops x 16 fps), but the paper does not state it, so it is left as n/r. (4) Neither the Pascal VOC split (2007 or 2012) nor the mAP protocol is given. (5) End-to-end latency at 16 fps is not reported. A pipeline adds latency, so 1/fps is not the latency. (6) The extraction flagged the metadata as needing a manual check. Tables arrived partly garbled, and the NEON section is cut off, so NEON-only speedups are missing.

note: This is a survey of CMOS-memristive neuromorphic architectures for edge computing: synapse types (1M, 2M, 2M1R, 1T1M, 2T1M, 4M bridge), neuron circuits, and network types (ANN, DNN, CeNN, CNN, SNN, HTM). The paper reports no new experiments. Every number is taken from cited works. Many of those works are circuit simulations rather than fabricated or measured hardware, and the passages often don't say which. note:
FINN-L (FPL 2018) adds LSTM/BiLSTM layers to the FINN HLS library, with configurable precision and parallelism. It is tested on a single-layer BiLSTM for OCR, where accuracy is scored by Character Error Rate (CER). Training is quantization-aware in Torch7 and PyTorch, and the in-memory cell activations and output-layer weights are fixed at 8 bits.

Main claims:
- With 1-bit weights and multi-bit activations, the model can beat floating-point accuracy.
- Going above 3 bits adds hardware cost and power with almost no accuracy benefit.
- Quantizing output and recurrent activations separately (1/2/1/1) is 1.32 percentage points more accurate than 1/1/1, with no extra cost in the recurrent layer.
- On the ZCU104 (XCZU7EV) at 266 MHz, the 1/2/8 configuration reaches 3873 GOP/S for the whole network and 3435 GOP/S for the LSTM layer alone. The authors call this state of the art for dense LSTM models on FPGAs.

Critical caveats:
1. The ZCU104 throughput is described as "estimated" (Fig. 8). It comes from placing and routing multiple accelerator instances, not from a measurement on the board. Only the PYNQ-Z1 throughput (Fig. 7, 100 MHz) is described as measured, and the supplied text gives no numbers for it.
2. The number of instances was helped by weight sparsity: some arrays were optimized out, for example in 2/2/2. Results therefore depend on the specific weights and are not a worst-case figure.
3. GOP/S is counted analytically and ignores the rest of the network. Table II normalizes other designs' throughput to 142 MHz by assuming throughput scales linearly with frequency, which makes the comparison weaker.
4. Power figures come from vector-less Vivado Power Analysis (12.5% toggle rate), so they are not measured.
5. Accuracy, resource and power values appear only in figures (Fig. 4–6). The Table I hyperparameter values and the columns of Table II are garbled or missing in the extracted text: the "200/17894" throughput entry cannot be matched to a column reliably. For these reasons, accuracy, LUT, DSP and BRAM counts, and power are left as n/r.
6. The file's own metadata flags the extraction for manual checking.

- DSP usage is not reported.

Cerri et al. (JHEP 2019, arXiv:1811.10276) train a VAE on simulated Standard Model (SM) single-lepton LHC events and flag events whose reconstruction loss is above a threshold as anomalies. The VAE has 21 high-level input features, two dense layers of 50 nodes, a 4-dimensional Gaussian latent space with a learned prior, and 48 outputs that are parameters of per-feature probability distributions. β = 0.3. It was implemented in Keras/TensorFlow and trained on 3.45M events.

**No hardware result:** None of the supplied passages reports a hardware result. There is no FPGA or other device, latency, resource use, power or throughput. Deployment in the trigger (Section 6) is only proposed, with no implementation. The automatic 'autoencoder-fpga' axis looks wrong; this paper belongs under physics/algorithm background.

**Results:** The threshold is set so that about 5.4e-6 of SM events pass. Table 5 quotes 5.3e-6, and Table 3 gives about 1204 ± 167 SM events per month. Selection efficiencies on the benchmark new-physics (BSM) models are 2.8e-3, 6.7e-4, 3.6e-4 and 1.2e-3. The VAE's signal-to-background ratio is about 1.8e2 to 1.7e3 times that of a single-lepton trigger. Supervised boosted decision trees (BDTs) outperform the VAE on each model, which is expected; the VAE's advantage is that it does not depend on a specific model.

**Caveats:**
1. The PDF extraction lost the process labels in Tables 1, 2, 4 and 5 and the Table 2 AUC/TPR values. The mapping of efficiencies to specific BSM models (A→4ℓ, LQ→τb, h0→ττ, h±→τν) cannot be checked from these passages, so it was not recorded.
2. The conclusion says a sample about 30% pure, with about 43 events per day. This does not quite match S/B = 1/3, which is 25% purity, or about 1200 SM + 400 BSM events per month, which is about 53 per day.
3. All results come from DELPHES simulation.
4. Section headings were misdetected (an address line is used as the section title).

**Rows:** No benchmark rows are included because there is no measured hardware result, and physics-efficiency rows could not be tied to specific models reliably.

note:
This paper is a survey (Shawahna, Sait, El-Maleh, IEEE Access 2018, arXiv 1901.00121). It reviews CNN compression, ASIC accelerators (the DianNao family, ISAAC, PRIME) and FPGA accelerators, from CNP and MAPLE through DC-CNN, nn-X, Caffeine, fpgaConvNet, ALAMO, FP-DNN and FINN/BNN, up to loop-optimized VGG-16 on Arria 10. It offers no new design or measurement of its own. Every hardware number is taken from a cited work, so each row below is a secondary citation. Before any use, check the value against the original paper ([152] for Microsoft/Catapult; the VC707 HLS design is described next to the Roofline accelerator [55]).

Critical points:
(1) The survey mixes units and power definitions across the works it cites: GFLOPS vs GOPS, 'about 25 W' vs 'total power 18.6 W'. It also mixes baselines (CPU, GPU, or other FPGA designs), so the speedup factors cannot be compared with each other.
(2) The summary tables (Tables 2–5) came through extraction as captions only, so their contents cannot be used here.
(3) The section headings were split badly: almost every passage, including Sections II–III, is labelled 'I. INTRODUCTION I'. The metadata is also flagged for manual verification.
(4) For the VC707 design, the passage names neither the model nor the numeric precision. GFLOPS suggests floating point, but this is not stated, so both are recorded as n/r.

Other secondary results that could fill later rows:
- VC709 accelerators: 424.7, 445.6 and 473.4 GOPS for LeNet, AlexNet and VGG-S.
- Arria 10 GX 1150, VGG-16: 645.25 GOPS.
- DeepBurning on Zynq-7045: 1.13x slower but 1.45x more energy-efficient than [55].

Systimator (Ahmad et al., arXiv 1901.04986) is an analytical design space exploration method for systolic-array CNN accelerators on low-cost, memory-limited FPGAs. It models a generic architecture: an IFM buffer, a weight buffer, scratchpad rows, the systolic array, an accumulation block and a pooling/activation block. It supports two data traversal orders, feature-map reuse and filter reuse. Step 1 estimates on-chip memory layer by layer for I = P×Q×R design points and keeps only the points that fit N_DSP and M_BRAM. Step 2 ranks the remaining points by estimated total cycles T(i), using Eqs. 11–16 for DRAM load, scratchpad load, systolic array compute and write-back.

Case study: Tiny YOLO convolutional layers on an Artix-7 (86K slices, 220 DSPs, 4.9 Mb BRAM). The search covers 96 design points (F=4, P=6, Q=4, R=4; rt={104,52,26,13,7,4}; csa and chsa each {2,4,8,16}). The best estimates are 12.468 M cycles for feature-map reuse and 12.361 M cycles for filter reuse. The recommended configuration is a 16-column systolic array.

Critical points:
(1) Every result is an analytical estimate. The paper reports no synthesis, place-and-route or on-board measurement; the conclusion defers comparison with synthesized results to future work. There is also no clock frequency, so the cycle counts cannot be turned into latency or FPS. There are no accuracy, power, LUT, DSP-utilization or throughput figures. For these reasons no benchmark rows are extracted.
(2) The paper contradicts itself. Table I defines feature-map traversal as ρ=1, but Section III calls feature-map reuse ρ=0. The text also credits feature-map reuse with better performance because of lower communication overhead, yet the numbers it quotes favour filter reuse (12.361 < 12.468 M cycles).
(3) The figure references look wrong. Panels 'd and g' and 'c and g' are both cited, and the feasibility wording ('above the memory cut-off line') is unclear.
(4) The cycle model is simple. It adds the terms serially with no overlap of data transfer and compute, and it assumes a bus width W. Parallel IFM/weight transfer is listed as future work.
(5) Only the convolutional layers are evaluated. The dataset, quantization bit-width and detection accuracy are never stated.

Besta et al. (arXiv 1903.06697, 2019) is a survey and taxonomy of graph processing on FPGAs. It runs no experiments of its own. It sorts prior work by: generic framework vs. single-algorithm design; graph problem (BFS, SSSP, CC/WCC, PR, TC/GC, BC, MM, MST, SpMV); programming model (vertex-centric, edge-centric, GAS, BSP, MapReduce, substream-centric, graph virtualization, direct hardware mapping); language (HDL vs. HLS); multi-FPGA scaling; and where the input graph is stored (BRAM, DRAM, SRAM, HMC, or hardwired). It identifies two main bottlenecks: limited DRAM–FPGA bandwidth, which leaves graph workloads memory-bound with many random accesses, and limited on-chip BRAM. Techniques for these include HMC, update combining and edge sorting (FPGP/ForeGraph), graph compression (Lee et al. ExtraV, ratios 1.9–9.36), and partitioning into intervals and shards.

Critical remarks:
(1) All quantitative claims are taken from the cited papers. Examples: Umuroglu et al. use 82% of BRAM for the result vector and cannot go beyond about 2M vertices / 65M edges; GraVF's largest graph is 128k vertices / 512k edges on a Virtex 7; Zhang et al.'s HMC module holds 4GB; Convey HC-1 has 80 GB/s peak bandwidth. None of these are the authors' own measurements. The survey also does not compare throughput (e.g., MTEPS/GTEPS), power, or resource use across designs, so its tables cannot be used to rank performance.
(2) Table 3 compares works mainly by the largest graph each one handled (n, m). This measures scalability, not efficiency.
(3) Coverage ends in early 2019. HBM-based designs and later HLS frameworks are missing.
(4) Extraction problems: no section headings were detected (everything is under '(préambule)'); Table 3 check/cross symbols are garbled (\u0007); and the metadata header's running title ('Towards Understanding of Modern Graph Processing, Storage, and Analytics') differs from the paper title, so it should be checked by hand.

No benchmark rows were added. The passages report no hardware measurements by the survey's own authors. The cited figures from other works (Umuroglu, Zhang, GraVF, Lee) would be misattributed if entered under this paper_id; they should be taken from those original papers instead.

Critical reading note: Gallego et al., 'Event-Based Vision: A Survey' (TPAMI 2020, arXiv 1904.08405). This is a survey, not a hardware accelerator paper. It covers how event cameras work, the main sensor designs, event representations (event frames, time surfaces, voxel grids), SNN and bio-inspired processing, and applications such as feature tracking, optical flow, depth estimation, VO/VIO and image reconstruction. The only measured hardware result in the passages is the DVS128 pixel frequency response (Fig. 2). Pixel bandwidth is about 3 kHz under bright light, which the survey equates to an exposure time of about 300 µs. At 1000× lower intensity it falls to about 300 Hz, which is still ten times the 30 Hz Nyquist frequency of a 60 fps frame camera. Other numbers are approximate or taken from cited work, not measured by the authors: latency of about 10 µs on the lab bench, die power of about 10 mW, embedded system power of 100 mW or less, dynamic range above 120 dB (the abstract says 140 dB, the body says >120 dB, so the two are inconsistent), and readout rates from 2 MHz to 1200 MHz. The authors say the Table 1 numbers 'were not measured using a common testbed'. The survey stresses several times that there are no common benchmarks for optical flow or depth estimation, and that trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency and latency are not quantified. None of the passages report FPGA/LUT/DSP/BRAM, GOPS or FPS figures. I left latency (µs) and power (mW) values out of the rows because the columns use ms and W, and the task said not to convert units. Extraction caveats: PDF extraction flagged 'no sections detected', so almost every passage is labelled '(préambule)'. Metadata and axes still need to be checked by hand. The benchmark rows record pixel bandwidth in the accuracy fields as a proxy metric, so they are not comparable to accelerator benchmarks.

Blance, Spannowsky & Waite (2019, JHEP; arXiv 1905.10384) is a physics-only paper, not a hardware paper. It trains a dense autoencoder on background events only and uses it to spot unusual events in semileptonic ttbar final states from pp collisions at 14 TeV. The autoencoder has 21 inputs, hidden layers of 10, 3 and 10 nodes with sigmoid activations, and a linear output layer. The 21 inputs are the four-momenta of 2 b-jets, 2 light jets and 1 lepton, plus missing energy. An adversary network reads the autoencoder loss. It has two hidden layers of 20 ReLU nodes and a 3-class softmax output that predicts how the background was smeared: up, down or not at all. The combined loss is Ltot = Lauto - alpha*Ladv with alpha = 100. Training alternates between the two networks, with steps 3 and 4 repeated 1500 times, and uses Keras with a TensorFlow backend. The data are simulated with MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and Pythia 8.2. The benchmark signal is a Z' (mass 2 TeV, width 89.6 GeV). The detector smearing was deliberately inflated three times to be conservative. There are 100,000 events per sample, with 20% held out for testing. A supervised classifier (2x20 ReLU layers, sigmoid output) sets the upper benchmark. Main result: the adversarial training almost removes the effect of smearing direction on the loss distributions and ROC curves. Table 1 gives the overall AUC, the upper-minus-lower AUC gap and the cross-section limit (at 100 fb^-1, S/sqrt(B) > 2) for Z' widths of 10, 89.6 and 200 GeV, a scalar colour-octet and a colour-singlet. The authors say the limits are comparable to ATLAS results. Critical points: (1) The passages contain no numbers from Table 1 or the ROC figures, so no AUC or limit can be copied. (2) Everything is Monte Carlo pseudo-data. Applying the method to real data would need systematically smeared, labelled data, which the authors only propose. (3) The ATLAS comparison is loose: this paper uses a post-selection cross section at 14 TeV, while ATLAS uses an inclusive cross section at 13 TeV. (4) The overall performance of the autoencoder is much worse than the supervised classifier, and the passages do not quantify the gap. (5) The paper has no FPGA, hardware, latency, throughput, power or resource results, and no quantisation. Its 'autoencoder-fpga' tag appears to be auto-assigned and should be rechecked. No benchmark rows are given because none of the passages reports a measured hardware result or a copyable accuracy number. Extraction warnings: the metadata needs checking by hand, and no section headings were detected, so almost every passage is filed under '(préambule)'.

Critical reading note — Pomponi, Scardapane, Lomonaco, Uncini (arXiv 1909.03742, preprint submitted to Neurocomputing). This is a continual-learning (CL) algorithm paper, not a hardware paper. Contribution: Embedding Regularization (ER). It regularizes the second-to-last-layer embeddings of samples from past tasks, kept in a small external memory, using cosine dissimilarity. A dynamic distance-based sampling strategy fills that memory. ER is compared with GEM, online EWC, SI and an unregularized baseline. Both standard ANNs/CNNs and Kafnets (networks with trainable kernel activation functions) are tested.
Setup (section 4): Permuted MNIST with 4 tasks, using an MLP with 4 hidden layers of 400 ReLU units trained by SGD at lr 1e-3. CIFAR10 split into 5 tasks and CIFAR100 split into 10 tasks, using the CNN from [31] (kernels doubled for CIFAR100) trained by Adam at lr 1e-3. Kafnets have layers/kernels 30% smaller. Memory per task: 100 for ER versus 200 for GEM (500 for GEM on CIFAR100). λ = 1, or 5 on CIFAR100. Metrics are Accuracy, Remembering (1 − |min(0, BWT)|) and Positive BWT, all computed from the accuracy matrix R.
Claims (section 5): ER matches or beats GEM on accuracy and remembering, except on MNIST where GEM is better. Kafnets generally hurt CL. A Friedman test gives p = 0.01, and Nemenyi tests show ER differs significantly from the baseline, SI and EWC, but GEM is not in that list. On CIFAR10, ER takes about half of GEM's training time and scales better with the number of tasks because it avoids a per-step QP. Growing the memory raises training time from 10 to 20 seconds for both methods. ER peaks at about 100 samples per task, while GEM keeps improving with more memory. Distance-based sampling beats iid, usage-based and image-similarity sampling.
Caveats: The numbers in Table 1 are not in the supplied passages; only the caption and the text discussing it are. The fragment '2,266 / 4,456 / 2,040 / 1,050 / 1,500' next to the dataset names is unlabeled and cannot be attributed to a method or unit. Timing results come from figures, with no hardware platform, batch size or per-inference latency given. The accuracy formula shows a 2N(N+1) denominator that looks garbled by text extraction. The metadata is flagged for manual checking.
Rows: none. None of the supplied passages reports a measured hardware result (FPS, GOPS, latency, power, LUT/DSP/BRAM) on any platform. The only timing (10–20 s training time) is a software training-time observation on unspecified hardware. It does not fit the benchmark columns, and the per-method accuracy and remembering values are not available in the passages.

note:
REQ-YOLO (FPGA '19; arXiv 1909.13396) targets tiny YOLO (the YOLOv2-tiny variant with 9 CONV layers and 416x416 input). It combines three techniques: (1) block-circulant compression of CONV weights (model YOLO-3 uses block/FFT size 16); (2) ADMM-based quantization applied directly to the FFT-domain weights; (3) a per-layer heterogeneous scheme. In that scheme, DSP-based equal-distance quantization is used for accuracy-sensitive layers, and LUT shift-based mixed powers-of-two quantization for the rest. The platform is an Alpha Data ADM-PCIE-7V3 (Virtex-7 690t) at 200 MHz, built with Xilinx SDx 2017.4 HLS plus a template-based C/C++ code generator. All weights sit in on-chip BRAM, so off-chip DDR is never used for weights.

Measured result recovered: Table 1 gives total layer-wise latency for YOLO-3. Equal-distance is 4,801.0 µs with a 5.93 Mb model; heterogeneous is 3,183.6 µs with a 4.95 Mb model. The ratio is about 1.51x, which matches the claimed 1.5x speedup. These latencies are in µs. The schema column is in ms and unit conversion is not allowed, so latency_ms is n/r in the rows.

- Table 2's FPS, power and FPS/W values are missing from the supplied text. - The resource model contains an apparent typo: #CONVD appears in both DSP terms.
- The text says 'RNN designs' where it means YOLO.

The paper reports no experiments of its own and no FPGA work. Every number is a claim cited from another paper. Examples:
- DianNao: about 1000x speedup and more than 20x less energy than a 128-bit SIMD CPU.
- Deep compression: 2.9x throughput and 19x energy efficiency over DianNao. The survey credits this to Hinton et al. [70], which looks like a misattribution (it matches EIE by Han et al.).

Limitations: the cited figures do not share workloads, baselines or metrics, so they cannot be compared directly. Utilization and scaling efficiency are not accuracy or throughput. The PDF extraction found no section headings, so every passage sits under '(préambule)'. Metadata still needs checking by hand. The rows below are secondary figures cited by the survey. They are marked low confidence and should be checked against the original Horovod paper (Sergeev and Del Balso) and the Caffe2 paper (Goyal et al.) before any use.

Critical reading note (based only on the supplied passages).

Claim: The paper treats a synaptic weight w_ij as the probability of passing a spike along that synapse (p_ij = w_ij/w_max, applied weight w_max; inhibitory synapses use w_min). Over time, the expected input matches the deterministic one (Eq. 1). Each neuron's outgoing weights are sorted and one random value is drawn per spike, so propagation can stop at a termination point. This cuts the number of weight and index reads. It works on pre-trained, converted SNNs without retraining. Five termination methods are compared: deterministic (DET), binary search (BS), random index (RI), weight-transform function (TR) and 5-segment piecewise linear (PWL). The benchmarks are MNIST1 (fully connected 784-1200-1200-10), MNIST2 (conv) and CIFAR10 (conv). The work targets a co-processor on the ARM core of a Xilinx Zynq, keeping part of the weights and indices in on-chip BRAM.

Evidence: Table 3 gives average memory accesses per spike (MAPS), normalised to DET, for different fractions of weights stored on-chip. The text says that with about 40% of weights on-chip, off-chip accesses fall "to very low levels". Table 4 shows probabilistic accuracy converging to DET as simulation steps increase. The authors say total memory accesses stay below DET even with the extra steps. The table cells themselves are missing from the extraction, so no MAPS or accuracy values can be copied.

Limitations: (1) The passages give no measured FPGA results: no LUT/DSP/BRAM use, clock rate, latency, throughput or power. The Zynq architecture (Fig. 4) is only described, and all gains are memory-access counts from simulation or analysis. (2) The energy benefit is inferred from a cited off-chip vs on-chip energy ratio [8], not measured. (3) Probabilistic methods need more simulation steps, which raises latency. The net benefit rests on the authors' access-count argument, and the passages give no numbers to check it. (4) RI performs poorly when weights are not uniformly distributed. TR only holds if the sorted weight distribution roughly satisfies f(f(x)) = x. (5) Accuracy is compared only with the converted deterministic SNN, never with the source ANN. (6) Weights and indices must be stored in sorted order, which may not suit other architectures. (7) The extraction flags unverified metadata and no detected sections; every passage except the Abstract is labelled "(préambule)".

Rows: None added. No passage reports a measured hardware result, and the accuracy and MAPS table values are absent, so any row would contain only n/r placeholders.

note:
Wu et al. (UCLA, arXiv 2003.03852, 2020) propose an 8-bit low-precision floating-point (LPFP) quantization that needs no retraining. It uses an MaEb format with M4E3 on hardware (M5E2 was the most accurate in emulation) and a per-layer scaling factor chosen to minimise MSE. They also build a Kintex-7 KC705 processor that fits four 8-bit LPFP multiplications into one DSP: each multiplication is reduced to one 4-bit MAC plus one 3-bit adder. Products are M10E4 values converted losslessly to fixed point, so accumulation is done in fixed point.

Claims made in the supplied text:
- Average top-1 loss of 0.5 or less and top-5 loss of 0.3 or less against FP32 on ImageNet, across six CNNs (AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet50/101/152, DenseNet201). These figures come from software emulation in Darknet, not from runs on the FPGA.
- An average throughput of 1100.4 GOPS, or 1.43 GOPS/DSP.
- Speedups of 64.5× over an Intel i9 CPU and 1.5× over existing FPGA accelerators.
- For VGG16 and YOLO against six prior accelerators, average throughput gains of 3.5× and 27.5×, and per-DSP gains of 4.1× and 5×.

Limitations for critical reading:
1. The passages give Tables I and III–VII by caption only, so per-model FPS, latency, power, LUT/DSP/BRAM use (Table IV, XC7K325T) and the absolute YOLO numbers cannot be extracted.
2. The 1100.4 GOPS figure is an average across networks that have very different GOP counts. No per-model result is given.
3. The YOLO comparison gives only relative ratios. It is unclear which YOLO version, dataset or accuracy was used, and no detection accuracy is reported.
4. The accuracy figures come from emulated quantization run on the CPU and GPU, not from outputs measured on the FPGA.
5. Power and energy efficiency are not stated in the supplied text.
6. The accuracy loss is given as an upper bound ("within"), not as an exact average.

Metadata flags the extraction as incomplete: Section V was merged into the preceding section.

note:
Critical reading note: Ngadiuba et al. (2020) add binary and ternary dense layers to hls4ml, starting with tag v0.1.6. Two optimisations stand out. First, binary multiplications become XNOR operations. Second, batch normalisation (BN) followed by binary/ternary tanh is folded into thresholds that are computed at compile time, so no DSPs are needed. The paper tests six strategies (BNN, TNN, best BNN/TNN found by Bayesian optimisation, and hybrid ReLU/clipped-ReLU versions) on two small MLPs: MNIST (784x128x128x128x10) and LHC jet tagging (16x64x32x32x5).

Main claims:
- Straight binarisation or ternarisation works fairly well on MNIST but loses a lot of accuracy on jet tagging.
- Hybrid models recover about half of that loss, at a small DSP cost from explicit BN.
- The best TNN matches the best BNN's accuracy with the baseline's latency and far fewer DSPs, so ternary generally gives a better resource/accuracy trade-off.
- The baseline MNIST model's accuracy drop from 98 to 95 after <18,8> quantisation comes from the precision of the softmax lookup table (LUT). A <22,10> softmax LUT brings it back to 97.

Caveats:
- All hardware numbers are HLS estimates or post-logic-synthesis results. There is no on-board measurement, no power figure and no throughput in fps.
- The per-configuration resource and latency tables (Tables 4 and 6) are only captions in the supplied passages. The only hardware numbers given in the text are for the 3x256 MNIST BNN on a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ VU9P: initiation interval 28, maximum latency 0.31 µs, 0% DSPs, 7% FFs, 23% LUTs, 16% BRAM, reported as comparable to Ref. [18].
- In the row, latency_ms is n/r because the paper gives 0.31 µs and units must not be converted.
- LUTs, DSPs and BRAM are percentages of the device, not absolute counts.
- The clock frequency isn't given in these passages, so fps and GOPS can't be derived.
- The models were deliberately not architecture-optimised. The jet data set is simplified and leaves out the cost of computing the input features.
- Every passage has the section heading '(préambule)', because section extraction failed.

note: EBBINNOT (Mohan et al., arXiv 2006.00422) is a hybrid event-frame pipeline for traffic monitoring with a stationary DVS. It builds event-based binary images (EBBI) at 15 Hz (tF = 66 ms), denoises them with a 3×3 median filter, and proposes regions with CCL. A YOLO-inspired NNDC CNN then merges fragmented region proposals and classifies them into 5 classes (background, car/van, bus, bike, truck). A heuristic overlap tracker (OT) follows. Critical points: (1) No hardware implementation is measured in these passages. All pipelines ran in MATLAB, and the CNN was trained in Keras on an NVIDIA TITANX GPU. There are no FPS, latency, power, LUT, DSP or BRAM numbers. The 'hardware-efficient' claim rests on analytical operation and memory counts, not on silicon or FPGA results. The 'yolo-fpga' axis tag looks wrong; the only YOLO link is the detector design. (2) Computation comparisons are estimates. SiamMask is estimated at about 38000M ops/frame and about 157MB, about 12427× the compute and about 1450× the memory of EBBINNOT. EBMS needs 252 kops/frame, 12× lower than EBBINNOT, and 3.32KB. EvFT needs about 18 Mops/frame, about 5.89× EBBINN; this is the basis for the abstract's '≈6× less computes'. The KF tracker needs about 6.5× the ops of OT, but the NNDC dominates the pipeline cost. (3) Measured accuracy on the DAVIS240C test set (Table IV) is 85.07 per-sample and 95.39 per-track (unbalanced), and 77.70 / 92.70 (balanced). The per-class values in the passage are garbled and cannot be assigned to classes reliably. (4) F1 and EAO tracking results appear only in figures (8c, 10, 12b), so no numbers are available. The authors themselves say the claim of outperforming Siamese DNNs is only 'on-par' or 'marginally worse', which weakens the abstract's claim of 'outperforming state-of-the-art deep learning'. (5) Site 3 frames were rescaled to 120×90, and pedestrians were excluded. The rows below are software accuracy results, not hardware benchmarks.

note:
CoDeNet (FPGA '21; the metadata says arXiv preprint, but the passage says it appeared at FPGA '21) co-designs a hardware-friendly deformable convolution with the network. The changes are depthwise, bounded range, square-shaped sampling and offsets rounded to integers. The network is a ShuffleNetV2 + CenterNet anchor-free detector, quantized to 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations. It runs on an Ultra96 board (Zynq XCZU3EG) at 250 MHz, built with Vivado HLS as a dataflow design. The first layer and the split/shuffle/concat operations run on the ARM processor.

Hardware results:
- Kernel-level speedups are 1.36× for full deformable convolution and 9.76× for depthwise, measured on one synthetic layer (h=w=64, k=c=256). They are not end-to-end speedups.

- Config a (256×256) has 31 ms single-batch latency at 51.1 AP50.

- In the text, config a gets "53 AP50" (Table 3, likely FP32), but Table 5 gives 51.1 (w4a8).
- Config e has 72.4 AP50 in the text (FP32) but 69.7 in Table 5.
- The COCO sentence says CoDeNet2× gets "26.1 and 21.0 AP, with and without quantization respectively". This order looks reversed.
