note:
PP-YOLO (Baidu, 2020) takes YOLOv3, swaps the backbone for ResNet50-vd-dcn (deformable convolutions in the last stage only) and stacks existing tricks that barely change parameters or FLOPs. The tricks are larger batch size, EMA, DropBlock on the FPN, an IoU loss branch, IoU Aware, Grid Sensitive, Matrix NMS, CoordConv, SPP and a distilled ImageNet pretrain. The main claim is 45.2 mAP on COCO test-dev at 72.9 FPS on a V100, against YOLOv4's 43.5 mAP at 62 FPS.

Critical points:
(1) This is a GPU paper, not an FPGA one. The 'yolo-fpga' axis was auto-assigned and should be corrected. There are no LUT, DSP, BRAM or power figures.
(2) FPS and inference time exclude NMS (following YOLOv4) and use batch size 1. Results with TensorRT are only described qualitatively ('around 100%' relative speedup). Numeric values for the TensorRT case are in Table 2, which was not supplied.
(3) Numerical precision is never stated. The 72.9 FPS figure is presumably FP32 without TensorRT, but that is inferred.
(4) The ablation is incremental in the order the authors explored it, not a full factorial study. The authors admit that the tricks interact, so the contribution of each trick depends on the order.
(5) Some YOLOv4 and baseline numbers were re-measured in the authors' own environment ('+' and '*' marks), which can bias the comparison.
(6) The 72.9 FPS figure matches Table 1 row J (minival, 13.7 ms). The input size for the headline result is not stated in these passages, although sizes 320 to 608 are mentioned.
(7) Tables 1 and 2 report GFLOPs of model complexity, not throughput, so the gops column is n/r.

note: Critical reading: this is a CPU/GPU inference benchmark for soccer ball detection on a humanoid robot. It is not an FPGA paper, so the 'yolo-fpga' axis tag looks wrong and should be checked by hand. The paper compares SSD with MobileNetV2 (20 configurations, varying width multiplier α and input resolution) and SSD with MobileNetV3 (6 variants: large/small/min) using the TensorFlow Object Detection API. It also compares YOLOv3/v4 and TinyYOLOv3/v4 from the official darknet implementation. Training used a fish-eye, single-ball dataset of 4014 training and 250 test images at 1920×1080. Accuracy is test mAP taken at the end of training. Latency is the mean per-frame inference time on a 30 s robot video at 4 resolutions, measured on three machines: i5-4210U (constrained, CPU only, all cores), Xeon Gold 5118 (48 CPUs) and a Tesla V100. The per-model values in Tables 1–3 did not survive extraction; only table captions and row labels are present. The only measured numbers that survived are the aggregate MobileNet statistics over 104 values per hardware setting: i5 mean 68.292 ms (std 17.374), V100 mean 47.24 ms (std 8.756), Xeon mean 47.009 ms (std 8.981). A two-sample KS test gave p = 0.97371, meaning V100 and Xeon latencies are statistically similar. That in turn means the GPU gave no speedup for the TF-OD-API MobileNets, which may reflect pipeline or preprocessing overhead rather than compute. Qualitative claims: MobileNetV3 with α = 0.75 scores best on the i5 using a custom mAP/latency normalized score. MobileNetV2 with α ∈ {0.75, 1} is best on server hardware. Official YOLO/TinyYOLO are slowest on CPU but fastest on V100, with latency largely independent of input resolution. Limitations: the normalized score is ad hoc, as the authors admit. There are no power, energy, quantization or FLOP numbers. Results come from a single dataset and a single-object task. The two rows below are aggregate means across all MobileNet configurations, not per-model results; per-model mAP and latency must be taken from Table 1 of the PDF. Published version: J. Intell. Robot. Syst., doi 10.1007/s10846-021-01336-y.

note:
Critical reading note (only the supplied passages were used). The paper encodes soft X-ray (SXR) temperature profiles from the RFX-mod DSX3 camera, plus magnetic-state data, into latent codes. It uses variational autoencoders (VAEs) with NaN-Mask layers to handle missing data, and nests autoencoders to combine the two diagnostics. The full-precision VAE6 (4 ReLU layers of 300 nodes each, 6-D latent space) reports a validation mean squared error (MSE) of 0.6e-4 on normalized data (about 17 eV per point) over 6000 samples. Its missing-point recovery error has σ = 63 eV. These accuracy figures are for the float model; no accuracy is reported for the quantized FPGA encoder in the supplied passages (they point to Figure 9, which is not included).

The hardware result is a proof of concept. A quantized encoder, retrained with the Brevitas quantization-aware framework, ran on a Xilinx Zynq 7000 at 100 MHz with folding factor 8. It measured 125 µs average latency without pipelining and about 1.3×10^4 fps with a 64-frame FIFO pipeline. The latency_ms field is n/r because the source gives 125 µs and units were not to be converted.

Not reported: bit widths (only 'few bits' and 'binarized layers'), exact topology, LUT/DSP/BRAM usage, power, GOPS and a comparison baseline. The use of FINN is inferred from the acknowledgment and the folding terminology; the text does not state it. The control target is 'few µs', but the measured 125 µs does not meet it. The authors instead argue it is compatible with the roughly 1 ms plasma dynamics. The metadata author names look swapped between given and family fields (e.g. given='A. Rigoni', family='Garola'), and extraction ok=false, so check both by hand.

rows.accuracy_metric: average accuracy after task 10 (mean over 10 runs)

note:
Survey plus benchmark of class-incremental learning (class-IL) methods for image classification. The authors reimplemented about 14 methods in one framework: EWC, MAS, PathInt, RWalk, LwM, DMC, GD, GDumb, LwF, iCaRL, EEIL, BiC, LUCIR and IL2M. All methods share the same data splits and seeds. Hyperparameters are chosen with the Continual Hyperparameter Framework (De Lange et al.), which only uses data available at the current task. The main metric is average accuracy. CIFAR-100 results are means over 10 runs; domain-shift and architecture results are means over 5 runs. The backbones are ResNet-32 for CIFAR-100 and ResNet-18 for higher-resolution datasets, both trained from scratch.

Key findings:
(1) Finetuning with exemplars (FT-E) is a strong baseline. On CIFAR-100 (10/10) with a fixed 2,000-exemplar memory, FT-E reaches 37.9. Regularization methods extended with exemplars often do worse (EWC-E 28.1, LwF-E 30.8).
(2) Methods that correct task-recency bias do best in class-IL. BiC reaches 42.0 on CIFAR-100 (10/10) and 47.0 on (11/50-5), and the text says it is state of the art on ImageNet. IL2M is consistent across datasets.
(3) Herding and random exemplar sampling are nearly tied. The random-vs-herding differences are mostly not statistically significant under a Mann-Whitney U test (Table S6); p<0.05 only for LwF-E and EEIL after task 10.
(4) Returns shrink beyond about 20 exemplars per class. For BiC, going from 10 to 20 exemplars per class gains 6.2 points; going from 20 to 40 gains 4.8 points while doubling memory.
(5) Method rankings change with the network architecture.

Critical caveats:
- Standard deviations on CIFAR-100 are large (±2–8), and many ranking gaps fall within one standard deviation.
- The ResNet-18 RPS result (57.0) uses 89.56M parameters, versus 0.47M for the ResNet-32 baselines, so it is not a like-for-like comparison.
- The 5/20 bias-analysis numbers are given in the text without variance.

Hardware: none. This is not a hardware or accelerator paper. There is no FPGA/ASIC platform, no quantization, and no throughput or power data. The only runtime figure is training time per epoch in Table S3 (for example, FT-E 12.1 s), with an unspecified GPU. All hardware fields are therefore n/r. The rows below are accuracy benchmarks only.

Survey (Quraishi, Bank Tavakoli, Ren, arXiv 2011.09073, 2020) on FPGA virtualization for cloud and edge computing. It sorts prior work in two ways. First, by system-architecture stack: hardware (host interface on-chip/local/remote, shell, role with PRRs and DPR), software (OS, host application, and frameworks such as OpenStack), and overlay (intermediate fabrics and CGRA/NoC-based overlays). Second, by four objectives it proposes: abstraction, multi-tenancy, resource management, and isolation. It narrows the objective list from an earlier survey [13], arguing that scalability, performance, and resilience apply to cloud and edge computing in general rather than to FPGA virtualization specifically, and that flexibility and programmer's productivity belong to HLS. Tables 1–2 map each surveyed system (e.g., Catapult, Feniks, AmorphOS, VFR, RC3E, Ker-ONE, pvFPGA) to its host interface, shell, role, software stack, programming model, application, platform, and techniques. Stated future directions: vFPGAs that span more than one physical FPGA (most work limits a vFPGA to one PRR on one device), isolation (functional, performance, and fault), which is under-explored, and multi-tenant, scalable virtualization for DNN accelerators. Critical points: (1) The supplied passages contain no measured hardware results — no throughput, latency, power, resource-use, or overhead numbers — so no benchmark rows are given. The overheads of overlays and virtualization (lower performance, less efficient resource use, reconfiguration time) are described only qualitatively. (2) Claims such as 'an order of magnitude lower power' and 'up to two orders of magnitude more energy-efficient' than CPUs and GPUs are cited from other papers, not measured here. (3) The tables are summaries with many N/A and N/M entries, and the rows are truncated in the extraction. (4) Coverage stops in 2020. (5) The extraction reported that no sections were detected, so every passage except the Abstract is labelled '(préambule)'; metadata still needs checking by hand.

rows.accuracy_metric: ACC, FWT, +BWT, REM (from MRR and Hits@10); MS, SSS, LCA

note:
Critical reading note (supplied passages only). This paper is not about hardware. It adapts five continual-learning methods to knowledge graph embeddings (KGE): PNN, CWR, L2R, SI, and DGR with a VAE triple generator. Each is tested on TransE and Analogy embeddings. The task is triplet prediction on three 5-session datasets built by sampling: WN18RR-5-LS, FB15K237-5-LS, and AI2Thor. Batch serves as the upper bound and Finetune as the lower bound. The metrics are ACC, FWT, +BWT, and REM (computed from MRR and Hits@10 matrices), plus MS, SSS, and LCA. All are scaled to the range [0, 1]. Results are averaged over five runs and tested with repeated-measures ANOVA and Tukey's test (p < 0.05).

Qualitative findings: on the benchmarks, DGR has the best ACC and FWT, but its LCA is much lower because it retrains the generator every session. L2R has the smallest model-size growth (MS). PNN and CWR score below Finetune. On AI2Thor, the best choice depends on constraints: Batch when there are none, DGR when data is limited, and L2R or SI when both data and time are limited (capped at 100 epochs).

Caveats:
(1) The passages contain no numeric results. Every outcome appears only in Figures 2 to 4, so accuracy values are n/r.
(2) No hardware platform, latency, power, FPS, or resource figures are reported. Hardware constraints are only simulated, for example by the epoch cap. Every hardware field is therefore n/r.
(3) The AI2Thor statistics (#015) look corrupted by extraction. The training, validation, and test counts and coverage percentages match WN18RR-5-LS exactly, while |En| is only about 170. Check them against the PDF.
(4) The sampling strategy was designed by the authors, and they claim it is harder than entity sampling, but the passages show no comparison numbers.
(5) The metadata is flagged as unverified (extraction ok=false).

The one row below records the experimental setup only. It is not a measured result.

note:
Ducasse et al. (arXiv 2102.01341, SLOHA 2021) use Brevitas and FINN to benchmark a small 3-FC-layer MLP with HardTanh activations on Fashion-MNIST, with images resized to 32x32. They trained 49 weight/activation bit-width combinations from 2 to 8 bits. Only the equal-bit-width networks were deployed to a Pynq-Z1 (Zynq Z-7020), all with the same folding. A8W8 was not implemented, and A4W4 at PE/SIMD 16/16 did not fit on the board.

Main findings:
- Weight bit-width drives accuracy more than activation bit-width.
- Longer training closes the gap: 2-bit weights reach the error rate at 100 epochs that 8-bit weights reach at 40.
- BRAM use grows exponentially with activation bit-width because FINN uses threshold-based activations (2^k−1 thresholds).
- Throughput depends only on PE/SIMD, not on bit-width (A2W2, A3W3 and A4W4 are nearly identical).

Limitations and cautions:
- **Weak benchmark:** The model is a toy MLP with fixed, untuned folding. The paper reports no power, latency, clock or absolute LUT/DSP/BRAM figures in the text (resources are only in Figures 9 and 10, which were not supplied).
- **Accuracy not tied to a configuration:** "reaches 88%" is a general statement, not linked to any deployed configuration, so accuracy_value is n/r.
- **"62 times faster" claim:** This compares the PE/SIMD 16/16 and 2/2 settings (373,112/6,100 ≈ 61.2), so it measures parallelism, not quantization. The text says it comes from the compressed network being better parallelized.
- **Internal inconsistencies:**
  - The A2W2 8/8 throughput is printed as "96,5334" (likely 96,533).
  - The text says both "49" and "64" implementations.
  - The conclusion says MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, but the experiments describe only Fashion-MNIST.
- **Throughput measurement:** Throughput comes from FINN's remote test with a batch of 10,000. DRAM-in bandwidth was 382.06 Mb/s (A2W2) and 381.82 Mb/s (A3W3) at 16/16.
- **Metadata:** Extraction warnings say the metadata needs manual checking.

note: hls4ml (TinyML 2021) is mainly a workflow and tooling paper. It covers Python package internals, (Q)Keras/TF/PyTorch/ONNX converters, graph optimizers such as BN fusion, numerical profiling, QKeras QAT propagation, and the new quantization-aware pruning (QAP) method using Brevitas with lottery-ticket rewinding. It also covers reuse-factor parallelization, and Vitis Accel and Catapult ASIC backends. The supplied passages give few hard numbers. (1) For the jet tagging MLP (16-64-32-32-5), PTQ accuracy starts to drop below 14 bits, while QAT matches 32-bit float down to 6 bits. This comes from Fig. 4, borrowed from Ref. [11]. (2) After QAP, a 6-bit, 80%-pruned model uses 50 times fewer BOPs than the 32-bit unpruned model, with no loss in performance (Fig. 5). (3) The MNIST 784-16-10 MLP needs 12,704 multiplications and was swept over reuse factors from 14 to 12,544 (Fig. 6), but no resource figures appear in the text. (4) The FPGA results for 16-bit and 14-bit PTQ and 6-bit QAT are in Table 1, which is not included in the passages. The paper only says that DSP use is drastically reduced. note:
SCR (Mai et al., arXiv 2103.13885) swaps the Softmax classifier for a Nearest-Class-Mean (NCM) classifier in online class-incremental continual learning. It also trains the encoder with a supervised contrastive loss on the incoming batch combined with a replayed memory batch. Setup: reduced ResNet18, SGD with learning rate 0.1, stream batch 10, memory batch 100, temperature 0.1, reservoir update with random retrieval. Table 1 reports average end-of-training accuracy over 10 runs. SCR scores 35.4 on Mini-ImageNet (M=5k), 37.8 on CIFAR-100 (M=5k) and 65.7 on CIFAR-10 (M=1k). (1) This is not a hardware paper. There is no platform, latency, power or FPGA resource data. Run time appears only as a figure (Fig. 7) with no numbers, so every hardware field is n/r.

What the paper does: an unsupervised graph autoencoder built from EdgeConv layers, trained only on QCD jets. The training set is 200k simulated pp→jj events from MadGraph5. Each microjet (anti-kT, R=0.1) is a node with 5 features, and the graph is complete, with 3 features per edge (d_CA, log d_kt, log m_ij). An inner-product decoder rebuilds the edge features alongside the node features. The loss is a weighted RMSE (λ_node=0.3, λ_edge=1), and the latent dimension is fixed at 6 after scanning 2 to 12. The test set has 28k QCD jets and a similar number of signal jets.

Results: AUC is 0.74 for QCD vs W, 0.75 for QCD vs top and 0.81 for QCD vs φ (m_φ=700 GeV). The PGAE baseline (Appendix A, nodes only) scores 0.68, 0.57 and 0.78. The authors take this as evidence that reconstructing edges is what helps.

Caveats:
- All data is simulated, and the AUCs are modest.
- The loss is clearly correlated with jet mass (Appendix B), and the paper does not remove this correlation.
- The latent dimension was chosen by looking at signal AUCs, which leaks some signal information into an 'unsupervised' method.
- Section detection failed during extraction, so every passage is labelled '(préambule)'.

The rows below record accuracy only. They are the QCD-vs-top results for the proposed model and the PGAE baseline; the W and φ AUCs are listed above.

note:
What the paper does: few-shot, test-time domain adaptation for an autoencoder-based end-to-end communication system. The channel is modelled with a Gaussian mixture density network (MDN). When the channel changes, the MDN is adapted with one affine transformation per mixture component, trained with BFGS and a closed-form KL-divergence penalty that limits how far the adapted distribution can drift. The fitted transforms are then used to build a feature transformation at the decoder input, so the encoder and decoder networks are not retrained. It only needs a small labelled target set, and the labels come free because they are the transmitted messages.

Evidence: symbol error rate (SER) plotted against the number of target samples per class. Simulated shifts include AWGN, Ricean fading, uniform fading and random Gaussian mixtures with or without phase shifts. There is also a real over-the-air mmWave FPGA testbed (Lacruz et al. 2021: 2 GHz bandwidth per channel, 60 GHz SIVERS antennas) with 20%, 25% and 30% IQ imbalance. The only number stated in the text is a relative SER improvement of "around 69%" over the fine-tuning baselines at 30% IQ imbalance with 10 samples per class. All other results appear only in figures (Figs. 4–6), so no absolute SER values can be copied.

Critical points:
1. The FPGA is the testbed radio, not an accelerator. The passages give no throughput, latency, power or resource figures (LUT/DSP/BRAM), so those fields are n/r.
2. The method fails in the AWGN to Ricean fading case (Fig. 4c).
3. The fine-tuning baselines are weak: fixed epoch counts and no regularisation. The retrained oracle is shown only as a reference line.
4. The evaluation protocol, sample sizes and number of trials are in Appendix C.1, which was not supplied.
5. The claim of robustness when Assumptions A1/A2 are violated rests on appendix ablations that were not supplied.
6. Table 1 compares parameter counts only symbolically: k(d²+2d+2) for the proposed method against the full-MDN and last-layer counts. No numeric counts are given.
7. The extraction metadata says no sections were detected, so almost everything is labelled "(préambule)".

note:
Govorkova et al. (Nature MI 2022) put DNN and CNN autoencoders (AE) and variational autoencoders (VAE) on a Xilinx VU9P using QKeras and hls4ml, for unsupervised anomaly detection in the LHC Level-1 trigger. All models are 50% pruned. For the VAEs, the anomaly score is the KL divergence (D_KL) computed from the encoder's μ and σ. This drops the decoder, the Gaussian sampling and the input buffering, which roughly halves latency. Detection performance stays similar: AUC 84–95% across the four signals, and TPR at an FPR of 1e-5 is only about 0.05–6%. It is highest for A→4ℓ.

Latency and II are in ns: DNN VAE 80/5, DNN AE 130/5, CNN VAE 365/115, CNN AE 1480/895. The CNN AE fails the resource and II constraints. The only on-hardware check is the DNN VAE inside emp-fwk on a VCU118 at 240 MHz. There, the outputs matched the HLS C simulation, but no timing, resource or power values are given. A Virtex-7 690 estimate for the DNN VAE is also given: 205 ns latency, 9% LUT.

Limitations:
- No power, throughput or GOPS figures are reported.
- The floating-point Table I values are not in the supplied passages, so the compression cost cannot be quantified here.

- The abstract's 'less than 3% of logic' matches the DNN VAE's LUT estimate.

Critical reading note (Fraser et al., JHEP 2022, arXiv:2110.06948). This is a physics and ML methodology paper, not a hardware paper. None of the supplied passages mention an FPGA, a hardware platform, quantization, latency, throughput, power or resource usage. The 'autoencoder-fpga' axis was assigned automatically, so it is doubtful and should be checked manually.

What the paper does: it trains a convolutional VAE on QCD jet images only. The encoder has 1, 2 or 3 downsampling blocks, each with two 3x3 convolutional layers of 5 filters, ELU activations and 2x2 average pooling. These feed a 100-node dense layer and a 64-dimensional latent space; the decoder mirrors the encoder. The VAE is used to separate boosted top-jet and W-jet signals from background, scored by AUC.

Main findings:
1. Hyperparameters matter a lot. The best β values are 1e-7, 1e-7 and 1e-8 for MSE training with 1, 2 and 3 downsampling blocks, and 1e-5, 1e-8 and 1e-7 for Wass(1) training. The configuration with the lowest validation loss is not the best anomaly detector: the 1-block network has the lowest loss but is consistently the worst detector. The optimal settings also differ between the top and W signals.
2. Networks trained with MSE, using the full loss as the anomaly score, generally do best. Training with a Wasserstein loss does slightly worse, even though its latent space is more strongly correlated with Wasserstein distances.
3. Euclidean distances in the latent space correlate with 1-Wasserstein distances between images. Reported Pearson r values: about 0.77–0.78 in the latent space (Fig. 4); 0.75 after the first downsampling block and 0.87 after the second (Fig. 5); 0.44 between raw-image MSE and Wass(1) (Fig. 1).
4. A training-free alternative, the optimal-transport distance to QCD medoids, performs about as well as the VAE. 5–6 medoids work better than the 2–4 that the elbow method selects, and smaller p in the p-Wasserstein metric works better.

Limitations for the database:
- The AUC numbers in Tables 1 and 2 were lost in extraction; only headers and captions survive. No accuracy value can be copied.
- There are no hardware, FPS, GOPS, latency, power or resource figures.
- The dataset is described only as QCD background with top and W jet signals; the dataset section itself was not supplied.

Because no supplied passage reports a measured hardware result and no AUC value can be copied, no benchmark rows are included. If rows are wanted later, the numeric AUCs should be pulled from Table 1 (VAE) and Table 2 (medoid distances) in the original PDF.

note:
Critical reading note — Kwon et al., "Exploring System Performance of Continual Learning for Mobile and Embedded Sensing Applications" (SEC '21 / arXiv 2110.13290).

What the paper does: It is an empirical study, not a new method or accelerator. It tests six incremental-learning (IL) methods from three families on an LSTM base model: regularization (EWC, Online EWC, SI), replay (LwF) and replay with exemplars (iCaRL, GEM). No-IL ('None') and a jointly trained model ('Joint') serve as reference points. The data are six sensing datasets covering human activity recognition (HHAR, PAMAP2, Skoda), gesture recognition from sEMG (Ninapro per-subject and leave-one-user-out) and emotion recognition from speech (EmotionSense). There are three class-incremental scenarios: (1) N-1 classes then 1 class; (2) N/2 classes then N/2 classes; (3) N/2 classes, then one class per task, giving N/2+1 tasks. Metrics are average weighted F1 (A_k), forgetting (F_k), final-task F1 (a_k,k) and intransigence (I_k). All methods run on an Nvidia Jetson Nano GPU with PyTorch 1.1. Only iCaRL in Scenario 3 was also ported to a OnePlus 7 Pro CPU as an Android app using DeepLearning4j (app size 134 MB).

Main claims:
- iCaRL gives the best trade-off across all datasets and scenarios. In Scenario 2 it stays within 10% of the Joint model's F1, while other methods drop by up to 60%.
- SI and LwF lose roughly 40–50% of the F1 the Joint model reaches.
- EWC and Online EWC are a reasonable choice when storage is tight.
- Storage in Scenario 3 is small: at most about 17 MB for iCaRL/GEM on Skoda, under 2 MB (iCaRL) and under 3.4 MB (GEM) on EmotionSense, and under about 115 MB on the largest dataset (HHAR).
- Measured on-device times: IL time from a few seconds to 4 minutes, and training time from 1 to 75 minutes across datasets.

Caveats:
1. The supplied passages contain only the captions of Tables 2, 5 and 6, not their numbers. So per-dataset latencies and accuracies are missing here and are recorded as n/r.
2. The latency ranges in the abstract are pooled over both devices and all datasets, and are given in seconds and minutes. They were not converted to ms, so latency_ms is n/r.
3. Power and energy are not measured anywhere, which is a real gap for a 'system performance' claim about training on-device while charging.
4. Precision is never stated; FP32 is likely but unconfirmed.
5. Hyper-parameters, including the replay budget (1–20%, up to 40% for EmotionSense), are chosen using the test sets after the final task (Algorithm 1). This is optimistic model selection.
6. iCaRL classifies with a nearest-class-mean rule while the other methods use a softmax/cross-entropy classifier, so the comparison is not fully like-for-like.
7. The smartphone results cover iCaRL in Scenario 3 only, and training data were preloaded into memory, using memory-mapped files for Skoda. That may not reflect real streaming use.
8. The storage figures are an upper bound: the largest LSTM (2 layers, 64 hidden units) in Scenario 3.
9. There are no FPGA or accelerator resource metrics, so LUT, DSP, BRAM and GOPS are all n/r.
10. PDF extraction was flagged as unreliable, and Table 1 is partly garbled: dataset names and some counts are missing.

note:
MCUNetV2 (NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 2110.15352) finds that CNN peak memory is set by the first few high-resolution blocks. For example, the first 5 blocks of MobileNetV2 use about 8× more memory than the rest (1372kB vs 172kB, analytic profiling, int8). The paper runs those early blocks patch by patch. To reduce the repeated computation from overlapping patches, it moves part of the receptive field to later layers (MbV2-RD): overall overhead drops from 10% to 3% and ImageNet accuracy is unchanged (72.1 vs 72.2). Neural architecture search then jointly picks the architecture, per-block width w[], resolution r, and the patch settings p and n. Models are int8 and run on an extended TinyEngine on STM32F412, F746 and H743.

Main results:
- ImageNet top-1 of 71.8 on the H743 (465kB SRAM, 2032kB Flash) and 64.9 on the F412 (196kB SRAM).
- VOC mAP with YOLOv3 of 68.3 on the H743 and 64.6 on the F412.
- Visual Wake Words accuracy above 90 with 32kB SRAM.

Critical points:
(1) The detection gain is inconsistent: Section 4 says +16.7 mAP, while the Table 3 caption and the abstract say +16.9 (68.3−51.4=16.9).
(2) No numeric latency or FPS is given in the tables. Latency results appear only in figures (Figure 6, Figure 7), and the 4% latency overhead is stated only for MbV2-RD on the F746. Energy and power are never reported.
(3) Memory values mix analytic and on-device profiling. Table 2 SRAM/Flash values look like on-device figures but are not labelled. Table 3 peak SRAM is not stated as measured. The face-detection results (Tables 4 and 7) use analytic backbone memory (fp32 or int8), not deployment.
(4) The ImageNet comparisons are fair only among int8 models. The int4 and mixed-precision baselines are set aside as orthogonal work, although MCUNet int4 reaches 70.7.
(5) Section 4 wrongly cites RNNPool-Face-C as [30]; it should be [43].

rows.model: Double decorrelated autoencoder (DisCo-regularized, FC encoder 256-128-64-32-5, mirrored decoder) + ABCD background estimation

note: Critical reading note (based only on the supplied passages). This paper proposes a complete method for unsupervised anomaly detection when the signal does not form a resonance. It trains two autoencoders at the same time. A distance-correlation (DisCo) regularizer (Eq. 2) keeps them decorrelated, so their two reconstruction losses can be used for data-driven background estimation with the ABCD method (Eq. 3). Architecture: each autoencoder has five fully connected encoder layers (256, 128, 64, 32 and 5 nodes), and the decoder mirrors the encoder. Data: the ADC2021 dataset (simulated 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, Delphes Phase-II CMS card), with 2M training events and an independent 800k-event validation set of Standard Model events. There are four signal scenarios (LQ at 80 GeV, A→4l at 50 GeV, h0→ττ at 60 GeV, h±→τν at 60 GeV), each injected at 0.1% of the sample. Results: all signal scenarios reach a significance of about 1 to 4, while the Standard-Model-only sample deviates by less than 1. The standard deviation of the average significance across five random seeds is below 6%. The double autoencoder loses less than 30% of the significance of a single autoencoder, but only the double version supports background estimation. Without correcting for signal contamination, the ABCD significance is lower for Standard Model efficiencies above 1.5%. HARDWARE CAVEAT: the paper says the design is 'online-compatible' only because it uses fully connected layers. It cites earlier FPGA and hls4ml work [30, 96–101], but it reports no FPGA implementation and no measured latency, resources, throughput, power or quantization. The Section IV claim of a trigger-rate reduction of 'nearly two orders of magnitude' comes from the Standard Model efficiency in Fig. 3, not from hardware. The trigger-rate estimate (about 4ϵ with prescaled control regions) is only a proposal. Limitations: the dataset does not model differences between data and simulation, and the model is trained on pure background (tolerance to signal contamination was checked only for A→4l). Significance is given as ranges read from figures, not exact table values. The extraction metadata is flagged as needing manual checks, and the 'autoencoder-fpga' axis tag is overstated for this paper. The single benchmark row records the software/physics result only; all hardware fields are n/r.

rows.task: continual learning of referring expressions for colored tangrams (85 candidates)
rows.baseline: CLIP zero-shot 0.310; unseen color combinations CoLLIE 0.857 vs CLIP 0.317; synonyms CoLLIE 0.602 vs CLIP 0.290

note:
CoLLIE (Skantze & Willemsen) keeps CLIP frozen, with the ViT-B/32 backbone by default. It learns a transform of the text embedding, T(t) = t + A(t) × S(t). A(t) is an adjustment function that predicts a difference vector. S(t) is a scaling function (SVR, KNN, etc.) that decides how much of that adjustment to apply. The model keeps only the new examples' embeddings plus a fixed set of negative examples, and retrains the small transform after each round. The metric is MRR for ranking candidate images.

Experiment I (LAD, new pseudo-words for known objects, |Ctrain| = 50):
- CoLLIE reaches 0.618 MRR after 1 example and 0.750 after 5. CLIP's zero-shot MRR on the original words is 0.773.
- A logistic-regression few-shot classifier does slightly better on the new words (0.805 after 5 examples).
- Retention after the final round is 0.699 for Ctrain and 0.719 for Cother, against 0.760 and 0.769 for static CLIP.
- Without the scaling function, retention collapses to 0.260 and 0.242.

Experiment II (KTH Tangrams, 85 candidates):
- CLIP zero-shot MRR is 0.310. CoLLIE reaches 0.860 after 30 rounds, averaged over 3,000 iterations.
- Compositional test (train on 17 shapes in one color, test on other colors): 0.857 vs 0.317 for CLIP.
- Synonym test: 0.602 vs 0.290.

Critical points:
- (1) Evaluation is small-scale and synthetic: pseudo-words from the NOUN database, 85 tangram images, and a limited synonym test that the authors describe as limited.
- (2) Retention gets worse as N grows, especially with only 100 negative examples. The authors say scaling for large N is future work.
- (3) The few-shot baseline beats CoLLIE on pure label learning in Experiment I.
- (4) Performance is bounded by the frozen CLIP representation.
- (5) The retention figures are in the text, but the numeric contents of Tables 1–4 are missing from the supplied passages.
- (6) No hardware, latency, power or FPGA results are reported. All hardware columns are n/r. The schema field 'bram' is unrelated to co-author Bram Willemsen.

Metadata issues: the preamble shows the paper was published in JAIR 74 (2022), pages 1201–1223, not only as a 2021 arXiv preprint. Venue, year and type should be corrected. Extraction status is ok=false.

note:
Scope: the paper builds an RTL (SystemVerilog) version of FINN's Matrix-Vector Unit (MVU), the matrix-vector compute unit. It is a drop-in replacement for the HLS library. The authors compare it with the original Vivado HLS version by sweeping IFM/OFM channels, kernel size, IFM size, PE, SIMD and precision (1-bit XNOR, binary weights, or 4-bit weights and inputs). Target device: Xilinx Zynq-7000 XC7Z020-1CLG400C on a Pynq-Z1 board. Toolflow: FINN, with Vivado for RTL and Vivado HLS for HLS.

Claims (Abstract): For small designs, RTL gives much smaller circuits. For large designs, RTL uses up to about 15% more LUTs. HLS always uses more flip-flops (orders of magnitude more for small designs) and about 2× more BRAMs. RTL has a critical path up to about 80% shorter and synthesizes at least 10× faster. The results were checked on a 4-layer MLP for network intrusion detection (NID).

Caveats:
1. The reported numbers are out-of-context post-synthesis estimates, not post-place-and-route or on-board measurements. The paper says some designs were tested on the board, but it reports no board results.
2. The clock constraint was 5 ns, relaxed to 10 ns if either design failed timing. This means the Fmax comparison uses mixed targets.
3. The paper reports no power, throughput, FPS or model accuracy. The NID MLP accuracy and its absolute synthesis numbers (Tables 4, 5 and 7) are not in the supplied passages. Only the table captions are present.
4. The HLS designs keep an II=1 through heavy pipelining. That explains the extra FFs and is a design choice, not something inherent to HLS.
5. All comparisons are relative. The rows below therefore contain no absolute numbers (n/r).

Metadata extraction is flagged as unreliable, and no sections were detected. Every passage except the Abstract is labelled '(préambule)'.

Critical reading note (based only on the supplied passages): The paper adapts the method of Faucett et al. for mapping a network's decisions onto physical observables, applying it to convolutional-autoencoder anomaly detection in jet substructure. It proposes two surrogate strategies that use a small number of high-level observables. The first, a high-level neural network, regresses the autoencoder output directly. The second, a paired neural network, learns the difference between the autoencoder's outputs on a pair of events. The abstract claims that both strategies match the autoencoder's background decision ordering, that both independently select the same six high-level observables, and that both perform similarly to the autoencoder as anomaly detectors across several signals. This suggests that learning to order background events carries over to ordering signal events. Per the section list, there is also a comparison with Isolation Forests and an ablation using only prime EFPs. Limitations of this extraction: the supplied passages contain only the abstract, the table of contents, and author emails. They include no numerical results: no AUC or decision-ordering values, no names for the six observables, and no dataset or signal details. The paper reports no FPGA, hardware, latency, power, or resource measurements, so the 'autoencoder-fpga' axis tag looks wrong and should be removed or confirmed by hand. The extraction is also flagged ok=false, with a warning that section IV was merged into the previous section. Because no measured hardware or quantitative benchmark result was supplied, no benchmark rows are produced.

note:
Qin & Joty (2022, arXiv 2203.02135) define continual few-shot relation learning (CFRL) and propose ERDA. ERDA combines embedding-space regularization with self-supervised data augmentation. The regularization uses multi-margin, pairwise-margin and a hard-negative contrastive loss on memory data. The augmentation uses entity matching plus similarity search over unlabeled text. Memory holds only one sample per relation.

Benchmarks: FewRel is split into 8 tasks of 10 relations each. TACRED gives 8 tasks: 6 relations in the first, 5 in each of the rest. Task 1 has 100 samples per relation and the later tasks are 2-, 5- or 10-shot. Results average 6 runs with random seeds and task orders. With a Bi-LSTM + GloVe encoder, FewRel 10-way 5-shot final accuracy is 53.23 vs 40.56 for IDLVQ-C, a gain of 12.67 (p < 0.001). The reported gains in the 2- and 10-shot settings are 9.69 and 11.49.

Critical points:
1) This is an NLP / continual-learning paper. It reports no hardware results (no FPGA, throughput, latency, power or resource figures), so every hardware field is n/r.
2) The extraction put all experimental text under the heading '3.3.1 The Encoder Network'. Table rows in passage #011 have lost their method labels. The ERDA row (53.23) is confirmed by the ablation table, and IDLVQ-C (40.56) is labeled explicitly.
3) Joint training is not always an upper bound: ERDA beats it at 2 and 5 shots but falls short at 10 shots.
4) The data-augmentation module adds complexity, but ERDA without augmentation (51.51) still beats all baselines.
5) Variances are only in the appendix, which was not supplied. The λcon sweep changes results by about 1.2 points (51.95 to 53.38), which is comparable to some of the ablation deltas.
6) BERT results (Table 4, Figs. 6–7) are described only qualitatively in the supplied passages.
7) Metadata is flagged for manual verification.

note:
This is a survey/tutorial of GANs for NextG networks (spectrum sharing, anomaly detection, security). It includes one small case study of its own: f-AnoGAN (a WGAN-GP generator/discriminator plus an encoder, with the anomaly score = reconstruction MSE + κ·discriminator-feature MSE) for outlier detection on RFMLS 2016a (11 modulations, SNR -20 to 18 dB). It trains on one modulation and tests on all 11, with a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) as the baseline.

Findings:
- Detection performance depends strongly on which modulation is used for training.
- AUROC is above 0.90 when training on AM-DSB, CPFSK, GFSK or WBFM with the S-RP, H-RP or JSD measures, and f-AnoGAN beats the CAE there.

Tuned settings: 3 critic updates per generator update, λ=10, κ=1.

Hardware result: the only measurement is average end-to-end inference time on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU. This covers the encoder, generator and discriminator forward passes plus the score computation. It is 0.005784 s, or 172.9 samples/s, with no parallel processing (batch of one).
- The time is reported in seconds. Because the instructions say not to convert units, latency_ms is n/r and the value is kept here.
- 172.9 samples/s goes in the fps field.

note:
What the paper covers: exemplar-free, task-incremental continual learning on a lightweight ViT. The model has a convolutional stem, L=12 layers, K=12 heads and embedding size 192. The paper proposes Pooled Attention Distillation (PAD) on the attention maps taken before the softmax, and an asymmetric version that applies ReLU to the difference so that newly gained attention is not penalised. Both versions are applied to attention maps (ATT) and to contextualized embeddings (FUNC). They are compared with LwF, EWC and finetuning on CIFAR100/10 and ImageNet-32/6. The paper reports no hardware measurements: no platform, FPS, latency, power or FPGA resources. All hardware fields are therefore n/r, and the rows record accuracy only.

Main results. On CIFAR100/10, ATT(asym) reaches 57.3 last-task task-aware accuracy. In Table 1, FUNC(asym) Spatial reaches 57.26 last-task and 56.18 average incremental accuracy, against 55.93 and 54.81 for LwF. On ImageNet/6, FUNC(asym) reaches 27.55, which is 0.44 below its symmetric version.

Points to check critically:
(1) The best attention and functional results (57.3 and 57.26) are almost the same. Scores are averaged over 3 runs but no variance is given, so the claim in the abstract that functional distillation gives better overall accuracy is weakly supported.
(2) Units are inconsistent. Forgetting is "≈0.01%" and ImageNet stability is "≈0.23%", while CIFAR stability is "≈53%". These look like fractions mislabelled as percentages.
(3) The LwF last-task score of 47.74 in the plasticity discussion differs from the LwF last-task accuracy of 55.93 in Table 1. The first seems to be a plasticity (diagonal) value, but the text does not say so.
(4) Only task-aware scores are in the main text; task-agnostic results are in the appendix. Hyperparameters were searched only over [0.5, 1.0].
(5) Most results are shown only in figures (Figures 4 and 5), and many values are not stated in the text.

note:
Wasala & Kryjak (2022) implement a single-scale HOG+SVM pedestrian detector on an AMD Xilinx ZCU104 (Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC EV). It is written in SystemVerilog with Vivado 2020.2 and processes 3840x2160 video at 60 fps. The pipeline handles 4 pixels per clock, so the pixel clock needed for 4K at 60 fps drops from about 600 MHz to about 150 MHz (a frequency derived from the design, not a measured one). The design saves hardware in several ways. It approximates the gradient magnitude with max/min operations instead of a square root. It assigns orientation bins with a tangent look-up table instead of CORDIC. It builds histograms in registers with sum trees instead of BRAM. It normalises with a fast inverse square root (magic number 0x5F3759DF). It computes cell-based (rather than window-based) SVM partial sums and uses fixed-point arithmetic throughout. The ARM processor runs non-maximum suppression.

Critical points:
(1) The reported accuracy (98, versus 98.5 without the approximations) is the SVM's accuracy from the learning process on INRIA plus Oxford Town Centre (2600 positive and 24300 negative samples). It is not a hardware detection metric such as miss rate or AP, and no separate test split is described.
(2) Power of 9.579 W is an estimate, not a board measurement.
(3) The fixed-point bit widths in Table I and the resource counts in Table II are lost in the supplied text. The design is only described as using 'about half' of the ZCU104's resources. The Table II row for 'Ours' is garbled; its only number is 38.5, which cannot be mapped to a column, so LUTs, DSPs and BRAM are recorded as n/r.
(4) The detector works at a single scale only, so its 60 fps figure cannot be compared directly with multi-scale detectors. The paper gives no latency or GOPS figures.

note:
CVS (Continual-learner for Visual Search) targets continual learning for image retrieval. The main requirement is backward-consistent embeddings: gallery features extracted in earlier sessions are never re-extracted. Training combines three losses. Lc is an NSoftmax intra-session discrimination loss (T=0.05). Lm is a neighbor-session model-coherence loss, a 2-sample-3-embedding triplet distillation from the previous model (margin 0.1, α=10). Ld is an inter-session data-coherence loss that pulls current embeddings toward class means built from replayed old embeddings and data (β=1). The paper evaluates disjoint, blurry and a new general-incremental setup (new and old classes mixed per session). Datasets are CIFAR100 and Tiny ImageNet with ResNet-18, and Stanford Dog, iNat-M and Product-M with ResNet-50 and ImageNet pretraining. Embeddings are 128-d, the replay buffer is budget-limited (600 to 4,000 samples), and the metric is recall@K averaged over sessions (AR@K). On CIFAR100, CVS reaches AR@1 of 71.47 (disjoint), 47.47 (blurry) and 73.95 (general). These beat all compared continual-learning methods (Rainbow, RWalk, EWC, LWF, MMD, BCT) but stay well below the Joint Train upper bound (83.39, 55.10, 81.97).

Critical points:
(1) There are no hardware, latency, throughput or power measurements. The efficiency claim (avoiding gallery re-extraction) is argued, not measured, so every hardware field is n/r.
(2) Most baselines are classification continual-learning methods adapted with NSoftmax. BCT was given the authors' own exemplar mining. The comparison fairness depends on these re-implementations.
(3) The gap to the upper bound widens as sessions grow, especially in the blurry setup, as the authors admit. At AR@4 the margins shrink or tie (Tiny ImageNet general, Stanford Dog).
(4) Model selection uses best validation recall@1 from a split sampled out of the training data. Hyperparameters are in the supplement, which was not supplied.
(5) The Tiny ImageNet figure legend (e.g., CVS 38.78 general) is not labeled with its dataset in the passage, so it was left out of the rows.

The two rows below are accuracy-only results for CIFAR100. Both values are confirmed as AR@1 by the embedding-distillation comparison text.

note:
QONNX (Pappalardo et al., arXiv 2206.07527, 2022) is a format and tooling paper, not a hardware benchmark paper. Its contributions:
(1) Two backward-compatible ONNX variants for sub-8-bit quantization. Both insert integer Clip nodes: the quantized-operator format with clipping, and QCDQ (quantize-clip-dequantize).
(2) A higher-level dialect with three operators: Quant, BipolarQuant and Trunc. Each one quantizes and then dequantizes (float32 in and out). Scale, zero_point and bit_width are tensors, so broadcasting covers both per-tensor and per-channel quantization.
(3) Python utilities for execution, shape inference, constant folding and conversion from channels-first to channels-last layout.
(4) Import paths from QKeras (via tf2onnx) and Brevitas, and ingestion into hls4ml and FINN. FINN converts Quant nodes into its own MultiThreshold nodes and only supports ReLU, hardtanh and identity activations.
(5) A model zoo.

Critical points:
- None of the supplied passages reports a measured FPGA result. There is no throughput, latency, power or resource figure (LUTs, DSPs, BRAM) for any hls4ml or FINN build. The value to hardware work is shown only in qualitative terms.
- Table I compares formats with self-assessed checkmarks, not experiments.
- The QCDQ and clipping variants only work at or below 8 bits, and they cannot express a separate bit width per channel.
- The QONNX execution engine is meant for checking correctness, not for speed.

Table III (model zoo) has only accuracy and complexity figures (MACs, bit operations (BOPs), weights). In the text extraction its columns are run together: the input, weight and activation bit-width cells are missing and the numbers are merged. Accuracies were not checked against the original PDF.

rows.source_section: II. Approaches of implementation of YOLO and CNN
II. Approaches of implementation of YOLO and CNN

note:
This is a narrative review, not a primary study. It contains no hardware experiments of its own. Every number in it is quoted from cited work without platform, dataset or setup details, so all rows are secondary and low confidence.

Critical points:
1. The English is badly garbled, apparently from automated paraphrasing ("frames consistent with 2d", "curling gold detection", "sluggish Vicinity"). This makes technical claims hard to verify.
2. Section II has an internal contradiction for the YOLOv2 curling system [18]: it gives 13 fps once and 30 fps once, both with 94.3% precision. The row below uses 13 fps, the explicitly measured test figure. The 30 fps value is unreliable.
3. The FPGA-relevant citation [5] (improved YOLO on Xilinx ZYNQ with 16-bit fixed-point weights) gives no numbers for throughput, resources, power or accuracy. It only says cost was "significantly reduced while maintaining accuracy," so it cannot fill a row.
4. The improved YOLOv3 road-detection claim [6] (+3.17% accuracy, -5.62% miss rate, extra 104x104 detection layer) has no hardware platform.
5. It repeats the original YOLO figures of 45 fps and 125 fps for Fast YOLO from [2] without naming the GPU.
6. The conclusion calls YOLOv4 the "second major version," which is factually wrong.
7. It miscategorizes CNN/RNN as "classification-based" versus YOLO as "regression-based."

Use this only as a pointer to primary sources ([5], [18], [2]), not as a source of benchmarks.

YOLOv6 (arXiv 2209.02976) is a GPU paper, not an FPGA one. Every speed result in these passages was measured with FP16 and TensorRT on an NVIDIA Tesla T4. TensorRT 7.2 is the default unless the paper says otherwise, and the input size is 640×640 on COCO 2017 val. There are no FPGA resource or power figures, so the 'yolo-fpga' axis tag should be checked by hand. The claims focus on deployment: throughput at batch size 1 or 32, and GPU latency rather than FLOPs. Main measured claim: YOLOv6-L-ReLU reaches 51.7 AP at 8.8 ms latency and beats YOLOX-L, PPYOLOE-L and YOLOv7 on both accuracy and speed. Relative gains are given for the other variants: N is +7.9 and +2.6 AP over YOLOv5-N and YOLOv7-Tiny at 416; S is +3.0 and +0.4 AP over YOLOX-S and PPYOLOE-S. Some models use self-distillation (‡), which makes some comparisons uneven. Several baselines were re-evaluated (∗). note: EfficientAD (Batzner, Heckler, König; MVTec Software, arXiv 2303.14535) is a GPU anomaly-detection method, not an FPGA one. The automatic 'autoencoder-fpga' axis should be checked: the only link is that an autoencoder handles logical anomalies. The method uses a 4-layer patch description network (PDN) as both teacher and student. The PDN is distilled from WideResNet-101 features on ImageNet, has a 33×33 receptive field, and uses strided average pooling to downsample early. A hard-feature loss and a pretraining-image penalty create loss-induced asymmetry between student and teacher. An autoencoder catches logical anomalies, and quantile-based map normalization combines the maps. Evaluation covers 32 scenarios from MVTec AD, VisA and MVTec LOCO. Measured results in the supplied passages: (1) the abstract gives about 2 ms latency and about 600 images/s, measured on a 'modern GPU'; Section 4 says Table 1 timings use an NVIDIA RTX A6000, latency at batch size 1 and throughput at batch size 16. (2) PDN feature extraction takes under 800 µs for a 256×256 image on an RTX A6000 (Section 3). This is not a row because the value is in µs, the rule forbids unit conversion, and it is an upper bound for the feature extractor only. Table 1–5 numbers were not extracted (only captions and fragments are available), so no AU-ROC or AU-PRO values can be filled in for the default model. Ablation deltas (Table 4, average AU-ROC): map normalization +0.8, hard feature loss +1.0, pretraining penalty +0.4. Isolated removals (Table 5) cost -0.7, -0.7 and -0.4. With early stopping (tuning on test images, which is disabled by default), the paper reports 99.8 image-level AU-ROC on MVTec AD. Strengths: fair-comparison fixes (SimpleNet test-set tuning disabled, PatchCore center crop disabled, FastFlow early stopping disabled) and timing on several GPUs (A6000, A5000, V100, 3080, 2080 Ti). Caveats: the abstract does not say which variant (S or M) gives 2 ms / 600 fps; no power, FPGA resources or quantization are reported; the GCAD comparison uses only one ensemble member. Metadata extraction was marked ok=false, so title, authors and venue need a manual check.

note:
What the paper does: it trains a 16-QAM mapper and demapper ANN end-to-end over an AWGN channel in PyTorch. The demapper is 2 inputs, 3 fully connected layers of 16 neurons, ReLU and sigmoid. The demapper ANN can then be retrained on an Avnet Ultra96-V2 board (ZU3EG) using Vivado HLS 2019.2 and layers from the FINN library. After retraining, the paper samples the decision regions, computes one Voronoi centroid per region, and passes the centroids to a suboptimal max-log soft demapper for inference.

Communication results (Table 1, on-board retraining after a pi/4 phase offset):
- At 8 dB SNR, the baseline BER is 0.0103. Before retraining, BER is 0.316 for AE inference and 0.323 with centroids. After retraining, it is 0.0127 for AE inference and 0.0143 with centroids.
- At -2 dB SNR, the baseline BER is 0.19. Before retraining it is 0.318 and 0.319. After retraining it is 0.199 and 0.2005.
- The authors say BER matches a conventional demapper up to 10 dB and drops slightly at 12 dB.

Hardware results (Table 2):
- Soft demapper: latency 5.33e-8 s, throughput 7.50e7 symbols/s, power 5.5e-2 W, energy 7.33e-10 J/symbol.
- AE inference: latency 8.10e-8 s, throughput 1.23e7 symbols/s, power 4.53e-1 W, energy 3.67e-8 J/symbol.
- AE training: latency 2.67e-7 s, throughput 3.75e6 symbols/s, power 5.47e-1 W.

Caveats:
1. The Table 2 extraction is garbled. The soft demapper's BRAM, DSP, FF and LUT cells are missing. The AE inference row has only three resource numbers (18.5, 10895, 11343) for four columns. I read them as BRAM, FF and LUT with the DSP cell lost, because a ZU3EG has only 360 DSPs. That mapping is uncertain.
2. Latency is reported in seconds, so latency_ms is left n/r to avoid a unit conversion. Throughput is in symbols/s, not frames/s, so fps is n/r. Power scope is not stated.

note:
ULEEN proposes a weightless neural network (WNN) built from Bloom-filter lookup tables instead of arithmetic. It adds ensembles, 30% pruning, thermometer encoding and a multi-shot training method inspired by BNNs. The paper compares an FPGA version against FINN BNNs on a Zynq Z7045 at a 200 MHz target, and a 45nm ASIC version against Bit Fusion running ternary LeNet-5 (FreePDK45 library, 500 MHz), all on MNIST.

Main FPGA result (ULN-S vs FINN SFC): 0.21 vs 0.31 µs latency, 14,286 vs 12,361 kIPS, 1.1 vs 7.3 W, 17,319 vs 91,131 LUTs, and 96.20 vs 95.83 accuracy. The authors report 1.4-2.6x lower latency, 1.2-2.6x higher throughput and 6.8-9.6x lower energy at batch 1.

- **Power is not measured.** FPGA power comes from Vivado reports and ASIC area and power from Cadence RTL Compiler, so power_scope is set to estimated. Key observations:

note:
YOLOBench (Deeplite, arXiv 2307.13901) benchmarks 550+ YOLO-based detectors. The models combine YOLOv3–v8 backbones and necks with depth factors {0.33, 0.67, 1.0}, width factors {0.25–1.0} and input resolutions from 160 to 480 in steps of 32. They are tested on 4 datasets (VOC, SKU-110k, WIDERFACE, COCO) and 4 embedded devices: Jetson Nano GPU (ONNX Runtime FP32), Khadas VIM3 NPU (INT16), Raspberry Pi 4 CPU (TFLite/XNNPACK) and an Intel CPU. All models share a fixed YOLOv8 anchor-free head, the same losses and the same Ultralytics training pipeline, so differences come only from the backbone and neck.

Main findings:
- Which models are Pareto-optimal depends on the device. VIM3 favours YOLOv6. The CPUs mix YOLOv5 and YOLOv7. The Jetson Nano is the most heterogeneous.
- With modern heads and training, older YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 backbones can still reach competitive trade-offs.
- In optimal models, depth and width are reduced before input resolution.
- Most zero-cost NAS proxies do worse than MAC count, but pre-activation NWOT helps predict Pareto-optimal models. Using it, the authors found YOLO-FBNetV3-D-PAN-C3, which they report is faster and more accurate than YOLOv8s and YOLOv8s-HSwish on Raspberry Pi 4 (TFLite FP32, 640x640, COCO).

Caveats:
- This is not an FPGA paper. There are no LUT, DSP or BRAM figures, no power measurements and no GOPS.
- The Table 4 text was garbled during extraction. Only the standard deviations survived (latency ±1.49, ±7.34, ±9.93 ms; mAP ±0.00–0.23%), so the mean latency and mAP values are recorded as n/r.
- Table 1 latencies (0.1, 0.05 and 0.5 s) are selection thresholds, not measurements.
- The authors say their YOLOv8s baseline scores slightly below Ultralytics' published numbers.
- The Intel CPU runtime is cut off in the supplied text.
- The metadata is flagged for manual verification.

note:
SATAY (Imperial College London, arXiv 2309.01587, 2023) is a toolflow that turns YOLO ONNX models into streaming FPGA accelerators. It uses SAMO as its base and Vivado 2020.1 for synthesis. The design is a deeply pipelined dataflow architecture: every layer gets its own hardware block, and all weights stay on-chip in URAM/BRAM. New blocks handle YOLO-specific operations (Resize, HardSwish, Leaky ReLU, Split/Concat/Add). Long skip connections are buffered in off-chip memory through a software FIFO, and fine-grained quantization (W8A16 in Table III) reduces on-chip memory use. The paper evaluates YOLOv3, YOLOv5 and YOLOv8 on U250, ZCU104, VCU110 and VCU118, and says this is the first FPGA implementation of YOLOv8.

Claims in the text:
- The YOLOv8s VCU110 design has 8% higher GOP/s/DSP than the next-best fixed-point accelerator.
- GOP/s/DSP is 1.1–3.4× higher on YOLOv3-tiny than [10], [34], [35], and 7.3× higher on YOLOv5s than [26].
- Speed-up averages 79× over an ARM Cortex-A72 and 3.6× over a Jetson TX2, using FPGA designs picked for similar energy.
- ZCU104 performs much better than the Jetson TX2 at similar power (Table IV).

Critical points:
1. The extracted Tables III and IV are garbled. Their numbers (LUT, DSP, BRAM, latency, power, GOP/s, mAP) cannot be matched reliably to model/device columns, so every absolute metric below is n/r.
2. The 1.1–3.4× and 3.6× figures are ranges or averages over hand-picked comparison points. Choosing FPGA designs by matching energy is a comparison method the authors picked themselves.
3. GOP/s/DSP rewards designs that use LUT-based arithmetic, and the binarized design [8] still has higher efficiency.
4. Accuracy is reported as mAP50 on COCO 2017 val in Table III but mAP50-95 in Fig. 10, and prior works use different datasets (for example, PASCAL VOC for [8]). This limits how comparable the numbers are.
5. It is unclear whether the power numbers are board-level or chip-level.
6. The metadata extraction is flagged for manual checking.
7. Recover the Table III/IV values from the original PDF before filling in any absolute numbers.

(2) Rows below are limited to the recoverable FPGA mAP for YOLO v2 on VOC with INT8 (Table IX/X baseline row). The values are Ultra96 63.78 and ZCU102 64.56. The paper does not explain this beyond "low-level optimizations", which suggests the models or preprocessing differ rather than it being a pure effect of quantization.
(3) Pruned variants on the same pair of boards (Ultra96 first, then ZCU102): 22g 62.94/63.10, 24g 61.41/61.96, 26g 61.59/61.25. The claim that pruning gives efficiency "for free" can't be checked without the missing power and throughput numbers.
(4) Tiny YOLO v3 on the FPGAs reaches only 4.6 mAP (COCO), which makes it close to useless in practice. YOLO v3 on Berkeley has two FPGA variants, (A) 19.44 and (B) 55.20, and the text does not define them clearly.
(5) Batching tests used YOLO v3 on COCO. The ZCU102 scales up to 4–8 threads, while the Ultra96 is already saturated. The 500 and 2500 FPS at 13 and 25 W figures are for AlexNet classification on TX2 and Xavier, not the FPGAs.
(6) The metadata is flagged as unverified, table references are garbled ("Table VI-A" and similar), and there is no DOI or venue. Treat all extracted values as medium confidence and check them against the PDF.

note:
LifeLearner (SenSys'23) proposes rehearsal-based meta continual learning. It combines three parts: (1) inner-loop and outer-loop updates at deployment time; (2) latent replay from the frozen feature extractor's last layer, compressed with a sparse bitmap and product quantization (PQ); (3) an INT8 feature extractor (QNNPACK on Jetson Nano and Pi 3B+, TFLM on STM32H747), with a custom Eigen-based backprop engine for the classifier on the MCU. There is no FPGA or accelerator design, so the LUT, DSP and BRAM columns do not apply.

Critical points:
- The headline gains (178.7x memory, 80.8-94.2% latency and 80.9-94.2% energy reduction) are measured against ANML+AIM. That baseline is very heavy and often runs out of memory on Jetson Nano. Against Oracle, compression is only 2.5-3.5x.
- LifeLearner is slower than plain ANML on the same architecture: 415 s vs 343 s end-to-end on CIFAR-100 on Nano. On the MCU, Tiny LifeLearner takes 832 ms vs 579 ms for Tiny ANML (CIFAR-100). The cost of compression is only partly offset by INT8.
- Power is never reported directly. Energy is Tegrastats power multiplied by elapsed time (Nano CIFAR-100: 1.9 kJ vs 32.7 kJ for ANML+AIM). So power_w is n/r.
- The Nano end-to-end latency is given in seconds (415 s). Converting it would be needed to fill latency_ms, so that field is left n/r.
- In the supplied text, Table 3 has no dataset labels. The first block is read as CIFAR-100 because the prose cites 579 ms vs 561 ms for CIFAR-100.
- The prose gives a Tiny LifeLearner SRAM range of 181-281 kB. The 181 kB figure is Tiny ANML's GSCv2 value; Tiny LifeLearner's table minimum is 212 kB. This is an internal inconsistency.
- The passages do not give accuracy values for Table 3 or Figure 5, so accuracy is n/r. Only relative claims are made: within 2.8% of Oracle, and 4.1-16.1% better than other meta continual learning methods.
- MCU memory is SRAM 236 kB and Flash 825 kB. These are not FPGA BRAM, so the bram field is n/r.

note:
What the paper does: it proposes two particle-based VAE anomaly detectors for jets. Set-VAE uses a conditional VAE with Chamfer loss. CLIP-VAE stops the KL-divergence term from back-propagating for the samples with the highest reconstruction loss, so KL divergence alone can serve as the anomaly score. Models are trained only on QCD (q/g) jets from JetClass. The paper reports signal efficiency at a background rejection of 100 for 9 signal classes, averaged over 5 runs. It compares DeepSet and Transformer backbones, each with and without particle-type (PID) information. The baseline is an n-subjettiness logistic regression.

Main findings: in the Set-VAE setting, DeepSet with PID beats Transformer with PID while using about 13x fewer FLOPs (13.8M vs 171M; 205K vs 1.81M parameters). CLIP-VAE roughly halves the compute (DeepSet 6.95M FLOPs / 103K parameters) with similar efficiencies overall. Some classes drop, though: H->qql falls from 57 to 35 and t->bl from 77 to 53. The authors say this similarity supports calling the performance 'similar'.

Critical caveats:
(1) No FPGA or other hardware was implemented or measured. The abstract's '2x acceleration in latency' is inferred from FLOP counts, not measured. The claim that avoiding input caching is cheap on FPGAs is not quantified.
(2) The 2x signal-efficiency gain over n-subjettiness can't be checked, because the baseline numbers are 'N/A' in the supplied tables.
(3) The comparison is not controlled: Table 2 models have about half the parameters of Table 1 models, so the savings come partly from model size and partly from the paradigm.
(4) Efficiencies are very uneven across classes (H->gg is 0.2 to 0.6), and variance is high for some entries.
(5) This is a short NeurIPS workshop paper. Architecture and training details are deferred to GitHub, and there is no quantization or resource analysis.

About the rows: they are algorithm-only results. All hardware fields are n/r. For consistency, accuracy_value is the t->bqq signal efficiency.

rows.task: unsupervised zero-day intrusion detection (CAN bus anomaly detection)
rows.accuracy_metric: average accuracy across unseen DoS, Fuzzing, RPM and Gear spoofing attacks
rows.dataset: Car Hacking dataset (attack-free for training; DoS, Fuzzing, Spoofing RPM/Gear for test)
rows.baseline: state-of-the-art GPU- and CPU-based supervised/unsupervised IDSs (e.g., GIDS, MTH-IDS, NovelADS, iForest)

note:
Khandelwal & Shreejith (arXiv 2401.10724, 2024) propose an unsupervised convolutional autoencoder IDS for automotive CAN. It is trained only on benign traffic and takes a window of 100 CAN IDs in binary as input. Its layers are 2 Conv2D (128, 64 filters) + 2 Conv2DTranspose (64, 128) + a sigmoid Conv2D output. Attacks are flagged when the reconstruction Hamming distance exceeds a threshold of 10, which was chosen on benign data. The model is quantised to 8 bits with Vitis-AI (QCAE) and runs on a Zynq UltraScale+ XCZU7EV DPU. The B4096 configuration was picked over B512 and B1152. Ping-pong buffers overlap inference with collecting the next window.

Reported results: an average accuracy of 99.61 on unseen DoS, fuzzing and RPM/Gear spoofing attacks from the Car Hacking dataset, and 0.43 ms per 100-message window. That is under the 1 ms it takes to fill a window at 100% high-speed CAN load. The paper also claims about 2x lower power than state-of-the-art IDSs.

Critical points:
1. The supplied passages give only table captions for Tables II–VII, so the per-attack accuracy, precision/recall/F1, DPU resource use and absolute power (W) are not available. LUT, DSP, BRAM and power fields are therefore n/r.
2. The 2x power claim cannot be checked without the numbers in Table VII.
3. The detection threshold was set on the benign test split, and each attack set is cut down to 200k messages. How the benign data was split and how this affects generalisation is unclear.
4. Detection happens per window, not per message. Worst-case detection latency therefore includes filling the window (up to about 1 ms), not just the 0.43 ms inference.
5. The only input feature is the CAN ID. Payload-only attacks that do not change the ID sequence may not be detected.
6. Comparisons with the literature mix platforms (GPU, CPU, FPGA) and metrics.

The extraction warnings (metadata and section detection) also apply.

rows.baseline: MTH-IDS on Raspberry Pi 3, 0.574 ms per CAN frame
MTH-IDS on Raspberry Pi 3, 0.574 ms per CAN frame

note:
Khandelwal, Walsh & Shreejith (arXiv 2401.12240) build 4-bit quantised MLP intrusion detectors for automotive CAN networks. They trained the models with Brevitas/FINN and run them as custom IP in the programmable logic of a ZCU104 (XCZU7EV) board, which acts as the ECU. There are two separate models, one for DoS attacks and one for Fuzzy attacks, both trained and tested on the Car Hacking dataset.

**Headline results**
- Latency: 0.12 ms per CAN frame, which the paper calls a 4.8x improvement over MTH-IDS on a Raspberry Pi 3 (0.574 ms).
- Throughput: "over 8300" messages per second at maximum payload. This fits 1/0.12 ms ≈ 8333.
- Power: 2.09 W, read from the device power rails with PYNQ-PMBus.
- Energy: 0.25 mJ per inference. This matches 2.09 W × 0.12 ms.
- Accuracy (Table I, as parsed): F1 99.99 and FNR 0.01 for DoS; precision 99.68, recall 99.93, F1 99.80 and FNR 0.07 for Fuzzy.

**Caveats**
1. **Latency comparison.** Table II mixes block-based detectors (29 to 5000 frames per decision, on GPU or Jetson) with per-frame ones. The authors themselves note that the block latencies leave out the time needed to collect the frames. So only the MTH-IDS comparison is like-for-like, and it runs on a different kind of platform.
2. **Power scope.** The 2.09 W was measured while the ECU was also running Linux and other tasks. It is not isolated accelerator power. It is also not stated whether it was measured for one model or for both. I recorded it as chip-level (device rails), but that is my reading.
3. **GPU energy figure.** The GPU reference of 9.12 J per inference is for a different 8-bit model on an A6000. It looks implausibly high and has no stated method, so the energy claim is not fully like-for-like.
4. **Accuracy table extraction.** Table I did not extract cleanly. Some baseline rows have missing or shifted cells: DCNN on DoS shows only 3 values, and TCAN-IDS on Fuzzy shows F1 99.22. Treat baseline numbers as unreliable.
5. **Missing details.** No LUT, DSP or BRAM counts are given, only "less than 4% of resources". Neither the MLP topology nor the clock frequency appears in these passages. The latency and throughput are reported once for "4-bit-QMLP", so assigning them to the Fuzzy model is an inference on my part.
6. **Metadata.** The metadata extraction was flagged ok:false and needs checking by hand.

PDGNNs-TEM (MLP f_out, 2-layer, 256 hidden, L=2, f_topo S1)

note:
Critical reading: PDGNNs-TEM decouples the trainable parameters from the ego-subnetwork topology. It stores fixed-size Topology-aware Embeddings (TEs), which cuts replay-buffer space from O(ndL) to O(n). It also adds coverage-maximization sampling, motivated by a proven "pseudo-training" effect on neighbouring nodes.

Strengths: large class-IL gains. Average accuracy (AA) on OGB-Arxiv is 53.2 versus 49.9 for SEM-curvature. On OGB-Products it is 73.9 versus 65.1. Buffer memory is the smallest reported: for example, 9M float32 values on Reddit, against 193M for SSM/SEM.

Caveats:
(1) Baseline results are copied from the original works [95, 96, 98] rather than re-run, so the setups may not match exactly.
(2) PDGNNs beats joint training, the supposed upper bound (53.2 vs 46.4 on Arxiv; 73.9 vs 71.5 on Products). The authors explain this by differences in optimization and noise, but give no controlled evidence.
(3) Average forgetting (AF) on OGB-Arxiv is worse than SSM/SEM (-14.7 vs -10.7/-8.4). On Reddit, AA is below SEM (94.7 vs 96.3).
(4) Under task-IL, PDGNNs does not clearly beat SSM or SEM.
(5) Coverage-maximization sampling helps mainly when the buffer is tight. The gain disappears at larger ratios (53.4 vs 53.3).
(6) Memory is counted in float32 values, not measured in bytes or runtime. There is no hardware, latency or power evaluation, so all hardware fields are n/r.
(7) Metadata issue: the passages say KDD '24 with DOI 10.1145/3637528.3671732, but the metadata lists "arXiv preprint" with no DOI. This should be checked by hand.

All passages sit under "(préambule)" because section detection failed during extraction.

note:
Critical reading (from the supplied passages only): The authors train a Bayesian binary ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with BayesBiNN, which gives Bernoulli weights in {-1,+1}. They convert it to an 8-bit SNN through a quantized ReLU with L=8, then map it to a Zynq-7000 (PYNQ) PS–PL accelerator. The accelerator has 64 multiplier-less mux-based PEs and a 16-LFSR PRNG bank that takes 4 random numbers from each 32-bit LFSR.

The Bayesian SNN has lower ECE than the STE frequentist baseline, even when its accuracy is lower.

Measured hardware results:
- Table I gives 1.06e-5 ms to generate 64 random numbers with the LFSR at 94 MHz, for both the no-reuse and max-reuse versions.

- The extracted text of Table III has no numbers for power, GOPS, frequency or GOPS/DSP. The abstract's '6.5x GOPS/DSP' and 'up to 30x less power' are relative claims that cannot be checked here, so power and GOPS are n/r.

- There is no end-to-end inference latency or FPS figure. The 1.06e-5 ms is PRNG time only, so row 1 leaves latency as n/r.

- The toolflow (e.g. Vivado/HLS) and the exact Zynq part are not stated.

note:
Sharma, Haq & Darak (2024) build channel estimation (CE) for pilot-based OFDM on a Xilinx ZC706 Zynq SoC, with a dual-core ARM A9 and a 7-series FPGA. They compare four estimators: LS (least squares), LMMSE (linear minimum mean square error), iResNet (the prior state-of-the-art deep-learning CE, put on hardware here for the first time) and their proposed LSiDNN, an LS-augmented interpolated two-layer DNN. They use hardware-software co-design (splitting work between the ARM processor and the FPGA fabric) and choose fixed-point word lengths by comparing MSE against single-precision float. The chosen formats are (12,4) for LS, (16,4) for iResNet and (26,8) for LSiDNN.

Table X gives two LSiDNN variants. The low-latency one (LSiDNN LL) runs in 0.08632 on the FPGA, which the text calls 86% faster than on the ARM, and is close to LS at 0.070558. The low-complexity one (LSiDNN CE) runs in 0.714885. The paper says LSiDNN CE uses 97%, 85%, 80% and 67% fewer BRAM, DSP, LUT and FF resources than LSiDNN LL.

Critical points:
1. **Time units are unclear.** Table X's header says execution time is in seconds, but the text says the ARM-only iResNet takes 40 µs, which matches the table's 40.25315. The values are probably microseconds, so I left latency_ms as n/r rather than guess.
2. **Resource counts are missing.** The absolute BRAM, DSP and LUT numbers were lost in text extraction; only relative percentages survive. Those columns are n/r.
3. **Power source is not stated.** The table gives "Total" and "Dynamic" power, but the passages don't say whether these are Vivado estimates or board measurements, so power_scope is unspecified.
4. **No accuracy numbers in the hardware table.** The paper claims fixed-point versions match float MSE/BER, but only shows this in figures; no number is given in the text.
5. **Generalization is weak.** The authors admit DL-based CE degrades badly when test channel conditions differ from training.
