rows.task: continual knowledge graph embedding / link prediction
continual knowledge graph embedding / link prediction

note:
IncDE (Liu et al., arXiv 2405.04453) is a continual knowledge-graph-embedding method built on TransE. It has three parts: (1) hierarchical ordering, which groups new triples into layers using BFS from the old graph (inter-layer order) and then splits each layer into chunks of at most M triples (intra-layer order); (2) incremental distillation, which distills each entity from its representation in the nearest previous layer, weighted by structural importance; and (3) two-stage training, which first freezes old embeddings and then trains all of them.

The authors test on 7 datasets: ENTITY, RELATION, FACT and HYBRID from Cui et al. 2023, plus three new ones (GraphEqual, GraphHigher, GraphLower). Each has 5 time steps with a 3:1:1 train/valid/test split per step. They report IncDE beating all CKGE baselines on MRR, Hits@1 and Hits@10. Incremental distillation is credited with 0.2–6.5% of the MRR gain. M=1024 is the best layer size in most datasets.

Critical points:
- This is a pure ML/algorithm paper. The supplied passages contain no hardware measurements at all: no platform, FPS, latency, power or FPGA resources. Every hardware field is therefore n/r, and the rows record accuracy only.
- The Table 3 fragment is missing its column headers and the IncDE row label. I assigned column 1 to GraphHigher and column 2 to GraphLower because (a) the caption lists them in that order, and (b) the text's gains of +2.0% on GraphHigher and 1.8% on GraphLower match 0.227−0.207 and 0.228−0.210 against LKGE. The unlabeled last row repeats as the full model in the ablation Table 5, which supports reading it as IncDE.
- Gains on RELATION and FACT are small (0.6–0.7% MRR). There are no variance or significance tests, and the case study rests on a single query.
- Three of the seven datasets were built by the authors themselves.
- The efficiency claims (lower training cost than full retraining) are not backed by any runtime numbers in these passages.

rows.toolflow: custom SystemVerilog RTL (PL) + PS classifier head

note: EFGCN (Jeziorek et al., arXiv 2406.07318) is a hand-written SystemVerilog pipeline for graph convolutional networks on event-camera data. It runs on the ZCU104 board (XCZU7EV-2FFVC1156) at 200 MHz. Feature extraction runs in the programmable logic (PL). The linear classifier head runs on the ARM processor (PS). All weights and feature maps stay in on-chip memory (BRAM, URAM and distributed RAM), so no off-chip DRAM is used. Main design choices: directed graph generation using a neighbourhood matrix of β×β entries with radius R=3, a first convolution that processes each event as it arrives, a 4×4×4 3D MaxPool that turns later layers into synchronous processing of 'temporal channels', and memory buffers shared between layers. Graph generation needs 15 clock cycles per event, and this is the bottleneck. The resulting throughput is 13.3 million events per second (MEPS). This figure was first estimated analytically and then confirmed in simulation. It was not reported as measured on the board. A new prediction is produced every TIME_WINDOW/4, covering the most recent TIME_WINDOW of events. Two configurations are supported: β=128 with a 100 ms window and β=256 with a 50 ms window. Software ablations on N-Cars with the Base model: 3D MaxPool adds about 0.3–0.4% accuracy over 2D pooling, and 'divide position' costs about 0.1–0.2%. Removing pooling multiplies the operations in later convolutions by about 50. Swapping in their modules shrinks AEGNN from 30.4k to 5.0k parameters and EvGNN from 4.8k to 4.2k, with slightly better accuracy in both cases. With quantisation-aware training (QAT), 6-bit quantisation cuts model size by about 23% with little accuracy loss. 4-bit quantisation loses considerable accuracy. The hardware targets 8-bit. Going from 8 to 6 bits reduces memory and LUT/FF usage, but DSP usage stays the same because DSPs only do the 32-bit requantisation. Limitations: the supplied passages contain only the captions of Tables 7 and 8. The actual LUT/DSP/BRAM counts, latency, power and accuracy numbers are missing, so the row below holds mostly n/r. Throughput is given in events per second, not FPS or GOPS. The authors also admit that FLOPs per event does not fully capture FPGA implementation cost. For testing, events were replayed from an SD card, with a DVS camera connected to the PL also demonstrated. Values to check against the full paper: Table 7 (resource use, accuracy and latency compared with state-of-the-art FPGA work) and Table 8 (scalability as the number of multipliers m changes, at 8 and 6 bits).

rows.baseline: YOLOv10 Nano, YOLOv8 Nano, YOLOv9 Tiny
YOLOv8, YOLOv9; classic inverted bottleneck (pw), expansion x3

note:
LeYOLO (arXiv 2406.14239) proposes LeNeck, a detection neck that works with any lightweight classifier, and LeYOLO (Nano to Large), a YOLO-style detector built for parameter and FLOP efficiency. Both are trained and evaluated on MSCOCO (mAP) with 4×P100 GPUs.

Critical points:
1. There is no FPGA work in these passages. The 'yolo-fpga' axis was assigned automatically and looks wrong: hardware results are on STM32 MPUs/MCUs (STM32MP257FAI3, STM32N6570-DK, STM32H7/F7/F4 DISCO boards).
2. PDF extraction failed for the tables. Tables IV–XI show only captions and headers, so no latency, mAP, FLOP or parameter values can be copied. Every numeric field is therefore n/r.
3. The text gives only qualitative or relative claims:
   - Real-time at 320×320.
   - Under 1 s per inference at 640×640 on STM32. This is an upper bound, not a measured value.
   - The optional-pointwise inverted bottleneck saves 8.5% inference time versus the classic inverted bottleneck.
   - An expansion ratio of 2 instead of 3 gives 17% faster inference (Table IX).
   - LeNeck is 'nearly as fast' as SSDLite with better mAP.
   - LeYOLO-Small 'matches' YOLOv8–v10 accuracy.
4. No power, energy or memory-footprint measurements are reported, even though the paper is framed around low power.
5. Quantization and deployment toolchain are not stated beyond 'ONNX' in the Table IV–VI captions. It is unclear whether the MCU runs used int8 (e.g., via STM32Cube.AI).
6. The title-page author list omits Gaveau, while the metadata includes them. This should be checked by hand.

Before these rows are used, the table values must be pulled from the original PDF.

rows.baseline: LKGE MRR 0.144 (T 1,073 s); EWC MRR 0.136 (T 1,013 s)

note:
FastKGE (IJCAI-style arXiv 2407.05705) is a continual knowledge-graph-embedding method, not a hardware-accelerator paper. It uses TransE as the base model, with incremental LoRA adapters and adaptive rank allocation. New entities are split into layers using BFS distance from the old graph plus degree centrality. The only hardware context is training on one NVIDIA RTX 3090Ti with PyTorch. The paper reports no FPGA, power, throughput or resource figures, so those fields are n/r.

**Claims.** Compared with the fastest baseline, training time drops by 34-49% on ENTITY, RELATION, FACT and HYBRID, and by 51-68% on the two new datasets, FB-CKGE and WN-CKGE. On the four public datasets, average MRR is 21.0 vs 21.1 for the best baseline: competitive, not better.

**Caveats:**
1. FastKGE's own T(s) values are missing from the extracted Table 3 and Table 4 text, probably because they were bold or underlined. The time savings therefore cannot be checked against the passages, and no time value is recorded in the rows.
2. The Table 3 header was truncated to "WN-CKGE". Mapping the three column blocks to HYBRID, FB-CKGE and WN-CKGE relies on the caption order, so the rows are set to medium confidence.
3. The abstract says link prediction improves by 1.5 on the new datasets. The table gives 0.223 vs 0.218 (EWC) on FB-CKGE and 0.159 vs 0.144 (LKGE) on WN-CKGE, so the 1.5 matches only WN-CKGE.
4. Results are said to be the mean of 5 runs, but no variance is reported.
5. Early-stopping patience of 3 directly affects the time comparisons.
6. The batch-size grid lists 258, which is probably a typo for 256.
7. The "no extra inference cost" claim is asserted, not measured.
8. Numeric precision is not stated. Extraction warnings: the metadata needs checking by hand and no sections were detected.

rows.baseline: Google Edge TPU [13]: 2.2 W, 7.66 FPS, 3.48 FPS/W; paper claims 7.7x faster, 19.5x more energy efficient

note:
Posso, Bois and Savaria (arXiv 2407.06170, 2024) run a mixed-precision Mobile-URSONet (MobileNetV2 backbone, 240x240 input) for spacecraft pose estimation on the SPEED dataset. They build it with FINN/Brevitas as a dataflow accelerator with one unit per layer and on-chip weights, clocked at 187.5 MHz on a ZCU104 (Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC).

Measured on the board: 58.7 FPS at 0.865 W, or 67.9 FPS/W. The Vivado post-implementation estimate was 250 FPS at 3.83 W (65.3 FPS/W). The passages do not say how the board power was measured (rail, board or dynamic), so power_scope is marked unspecified.

Critical points:
1. The real board is more than 4x slower than the estimate. The authors blame too few BRAMs, which made the FIFOs too small. FPS per watt stays about the same only because power drops by 4.4x as well.
2. Only the backbone runs on the FPGA. The network head runs on the CPU. The passages don't say whether the reported FPS covers the whole pipeline or just the backbone.
3. Accuracy drops a lot. The ESA score (lower is better) goes from 0.296 in Float32 to 0.307 in Int8, then to 0.411 in mixed precision. Orientation error rises from 13.0 to 18.7 degrees and position error from 0.71 to 0.91 m. The paper calls this "manageable", but the claims of 7.7x speed and 19.5x efficiency are made without matching accuracy against the baselines.
4. The comparisons are across platforms and against other papers' numbers: Edge TPU [13] at 7.66 FPS and 2.2 W, and Intel Atom [6] at 6.58 FPS and 3.7 W. The ratios check out: 58.7/7.66 ≈ 7.7 and 67.9/3.48 ≈ 19.5. However, the power measurement methods are probably not the same across these works. The Ultra96 works [11] and [12] cannot be compared because they report no throughput.
5. Resources are given only as percentages: LUT 91, BRAM 90, DSP 32, FF 26. The table records these bare percentages, not absolute counts. The exact per-layer bit-widths are not in the passages. Activations below 4 bits caused errors.
6. Latency and GOPS are not reported.

The FPGA outputs match Brevitas bit for bit, so the pose metrics on the board and on the computer are identical.

rows.toolflow: Ultralytics YOLOv8 code with custom PoT QAT; OpenVINO INT8 quantization

note:
PowerYOLO (Przewlocka-Rus, Kryjak, Gorgon, arXiv 2407.08272) quantizes YOLOv8s for detecting cars and pedestrians in GEN1 event-camera data (10 ms event frames, 2 classes). The convolution weights use 4-bit power-of-two (logarithmic) values trained with quantization-aware training. Activations are 8-bit linear, calibrated with OpenVINO. Bias is 32-bit. The paper also proposes a way to fuse convolution and batch-normalization layers that keeps the weights as powers of two.

Main claim: mAP 0.301 on GEN1, with almost 8x less memory than the float model (7.2M parameters). The passages do not say whether 0.301 is mAP50 or mAP50-95. The numbers in Table II are missing from the extracted text.

Accuracy drops versus the full-precision baseline, as stated in the text:
- INT8: about 1 (mAP50) and 3 (mAP50-95).
- LOG4: 3.5 and 8.3.
- Mixed precision: 5.5 and 11.5.
- 4-bit uniform quantization: the gap is about twice that of LOG4.

Critical points:
1. **No hardware measurements.** The paper reports no FPS, latency, power or FPGA resource use. The 1.4x power-efficiency figure is from earlier work [19], a single convolution-layer accelerator on a ZCU104, not from PowerYOLO. Energy savings from bit-shifts are argued, not measured. The Results section says it will "show the applicability" to a hardware accelerator, but the supplied passages contain no such numbers.
2. **The state-of-the-art claim is narrow.** It only holds among compressed models. Full-precision methods reach 0.406–0.484 (GET), and the gap to YOLOv5l [30] with augmentation is more than 20.
3. **The low-bit comparisons are not like-for-like.** The comparison with [22] (post-training quantization) and [34] (which also quantizes activations) mixes different setups, and the authors admit they cannot say which model is better.
4. **The fusion method's cost is unclear.** It may add computation at inference time.
5. **Metadata and axes are auto-flagged for manual checking.** The yolo-fpga axis looks weak because there is no FPGA implementation.

I made one row, for accuracy only.

rows.baseline: Comparison baseline for ZCU104 DPU (ZCU104 reported 2.6x faster, 3.6x more energy efficient)

note:
Castelino et al. (arXiv 2407.17647, 2024) present an unsupervised 6-layer 2D convolutional autoencoder (CAE) that flags artefacts in hyperspectral images (HSI) on board a satellite. An image is flagged when its reconstruction error is above a threshold of about 70000. The model is trained on Indian Pines, Salinas Valley, Pavia University and Kennedy Space Center, using 144x144 patches. It is quantised to uniform INT8 with Vitis-AI post-training quantisation plus 50 epochs of fine-tuning, and runs on a DPU B4096 on a ZCU104 (XCZU7EV) at 300/600 MHz.

Measured results:
- **Accuracy:** F1 is 92.77 after quantisation, against 94.05 for FP32.
- **Speed:** 4.0 ms per inference, averaged over 1000 runs, which gives 250 FPS.
- **Power and energy:** 5.38 W of active power, read from the PYNQ-PMBus rails, and 21.52 mJ per inference.
- **Resources:** only the BRAM/URAM entry survived extraction, as 35.42 / 47.92 %. The LUT, FF and DSP values are missing.

Against other devices, the authors report being 2.6× faster than INT8 and 4.7× faster than FP16 on a Jetson Xavier NX. They also report 1.27× lower latency and 7.5× lower energy than CloudSatNet.

Critical points:
1. **FPR = 0 is a design choice, not a result.** The threshold was chosen to give 0% FPR, at the cost of a 13.48% FNR. The FPR is therefore tuned on the same data and says nothing about how well the model generalises.
2. **The accuracy comparisons are not like-for-like.** The CloudScout and CloudSatNet baselines are supervised RGB cloud classifiers on different datasets. The claimed accuracy gains of +6.4, +6.7 and +3.8 compare different tasks and data.
3. **Inconsistent quantisation claims.** The text describes CloudScout Extended as INT4/FINN in one place and INT8 on the ZCU106 in another.
4. **Power scope is unclear.** It is not stated whether "active power" is total or idle-subtracted. The Pidle and Ptot values in Table VI were lost in extraction.
5. **The Jetson baseline is not like-for-like either.** It used a different training and quantisation flow and got a higher F1 of 95.29. Its absolute latency and power are not given in the text, only as ratios, so the Jetson row has many n/r fields.
6. **Units are ambiguous.** The abstract says "each spectral band" while the body says "per HSI image", so it is unclear what one inference covers.
7. **Tables were garbled in extraction.** Tables III to VI came out mostly without their values, so resource numbers are only partly verifiable.

rows.toolflow: cgra4ml (qkeras -> SystemVerilog CGRA RTL + C firmware, Vivado TCL flow)

note:
cgra4ml (Abarajithan et al., ACM TRETS 2026 / arXiv 2408.15561) is an open-source framework built around the idea that it is meant for deployment rather than for exploring architectures. It generates vendor-agnostic SystemVerilog for a parameterised R×C CGRA of simple MAC PEs. It uses a single dataflow for conv and dense layers: columns regroup at runtime by KW, weights are held in ping-pong caches, and a pixel shifter reuses data vertically. The IP is wrapped with AXI and open-source DMAs. The framework also generates C firmware (bare-metal, PetaLinux or PYNQ-style ctypes) and TCL flows for Vivado, Genus/Innovus and DC/ICC2. Its main claimed difference from hls4ml, FINN, VTA and Vitis AI is verification: the production C runtime is linked into the SystemVerilog testbenches via DPI-C, with randomised AXI valid/ready backpressure, aiming for bit-exact agreement with a golden model. It is meant to fix hls4ml's scaling limit, since reusing layers lets it run larger models such as ResNet-50 and PointNet.

Critical points:
(1) The supplied passages contain no measured numbers. Only the captions of the result tables survive: Table 3 (ResNet-50, PointNet and Autoencoder on ZCU104), Table 5 (Jet-tagger, cgra4ml vs hls4ml across reuse factors) and Table 6 (8×24 PPA at 28/65/7 nm). The claim of 'competitive performance-per-watt' therefore can't be checked from this text.
(2) Pooling, normalisation, residual adds and writeback all run on the host CPU. The end-to-end latency on small trigger-style models may be dominated by this CPU work (the authors admit this and point to Table 4 and Sec. 6.2), so the CGRA's peak throughput overstates what a user would actually see.
(3) The idle-PE figures (1, 5 and 8% for KW=5, 7 and 11 at C=96) come from analysis, not measurement.
(4) The ASIC results are first-order PPA estimates from synthesis and place-and-route. The ARM NanoSoC tape-out is only mentioned as a partnership, not reported as silicon results.
(5) Table 6 uses different tool flows for different nodes (Cadence at 28/65 nm, Synopsys at 7 nm), so comparing across nodes is confounded.
(6) Comparing a layer-reuse CGRA with fully pipelined hls4ml on the tiny Jet-tagger mixes throughput and latency regimes. Check which metric Table 5 fixes.

Extraction status: I made one placeholder row, with low confidence, to record the ZCU104 ResNet-50 experiment named in the Table 3 caption. All of its metrics are n/r because the table body is not in the passages. Pull the values from the full PDF before using this row.

note: Critical reading: The paper proposes TinyML continual/incremental learning that stores a distilled replay set (distribution matching with DSA, distilled on ConvNetD4) and grows the model when validation accuracy falls below a threshold (ConvNetD2→D3→D4). None of the supplied passages reports a measured hardware result: there is no MCU deployment, latency, power or memory measurement. Cost is reported only as training FLOPs relative to a fixed ConvNetD4 (43% CIFAR10*, 49% CORe50, 36% Speech Commands/HAR/MNIST), so claims about energy and time savings are inferred, not measured. Issues: (1) *The results text cites 'Table 1' without naming its dataset. CIFAR10 is inferred only because the discussion matches CIFAR10 to 43% FLOPs, and the supplied captions label Table II as CORe50 and Table IV as MNIST. (2) The accuracy-loss claims disagree: the abstract says ~1%, the conclusion says 0.4% on average, and the discussion gives +0.3% for CIFAR10 and −2.8% for CORe50. (3) The optimizer is contradictory (SGD with momentum 0.9 vs Adam at lr 0.01). (4) 'Baseline' in Results means cumulative full-data training, but in Related Work 'baseline' (19.39) refers to the naive approach. The comparison with CWR, LwF and EWC from [5] uses a different model and a different resolution (128 vs 64). (5) Several adaptive-model accuracies are only approximate ('~70', '92% range', 'mid-60%'), so no rows were made for them. (6) The kernel description '8, 64, 128 kernels' per depth is ambiguous. The rows below are algorithm-level results from simulation, not hardware benchmarks.

note:
Empirical benchmark of 8 detectors (YOLOv8 n/s/m, EfficientDet Lite0-2, SSD MobileNet V1, SSDLite MobileDet) on 9 edge platforms (Pi 3/4/5 CPU-only, each Pi with Coral Edge TPU, Pi 5 with AI HAT+ (Hailo-8), Jetson Nano, Jetson Orin Nano). Accuracy is COCO val mAP (5,000 images, scored with FiftyOne). Latency is server-side service time in ms and excludes network delay. Energy is reported only as mWh per request above idle, from a UM25C USB meter, so there are no watt figures and power_w is n/r.

Points to check before reusing these numbers:
(1) The platforms don't use the same inputs. YOLOv8 runs at 320x320 on the TPU but 640x640 on CPU, Hailo and TensorRT, so TPU speedups mix hardware gains with the smaller input. The authors say this themselves, and TPU YOLOv8 mAP drops to 16/25/32.

(3) Jetson Nano and Orin Nano report identical mAP, and the Jetson latency passage is cut off, so no Jetson latency figures are available here.

(5) No FPS, GOPS or FPGA resource figures are reported (this is not an FPGA paper). Batch and concurrency settings from Locust are not given.

Row 1, Pi 5 + AI HAT+ running YOLOv8n: energy per request above idle is 0.2 mWh (Fig. 2(h)).
Row 2, Pi 4 + TPU running SSD v1: energy is 0.10 mWh per request, and the same model takes 209 ms on the CPU-only Pi 4.

rows.source_section: 2. MANUAL NETWORK DESIGN FOR EMBEDDED COMPUTING SYSTEMS

note:
Critical reading: this is a broad survey (manual/automated network design, compression, on-device learning, LLMs, software/hardware, applications) with no original experiments. Every quantitative figure in the passages comes from cited work or vendor spec sheets.

(1) The only measured on-device results are second-hand: DeiT and PiT latency on iPhone 12 (10.99 ms vs 10.56 ms, citing [124]), and a transformer translating a 30-word sentence in 20 seconds on a Raspberry Pi (citing [95]). The survey uses the iPhone result to argue that 3× fewer FLOPs need not mean lower latency. It does not give quantization, framework or batch settings, so these numbers can't be reproduced from the survey. EdgeViT is compared with MobileNetV2 on Samsung Galaxy S21 "under comparable latency constraints", but no latency value is given.

(2) Table 4 is a list of vendor specs, not benchmarks: launch prices, power ranges, and peak TFLOPS/TOPS at mixed precisions. These are not comparable across devices. The table caption also mislabels it as "software frameworks".

(3) Extraction and consistency problems:
- The Table 3 fragment mixes in a bar chart comparing ResNet-50 and MbV2-1.4 memory (Param 102 / 24 MB; Activation 1414.4 / 1252.8 MB) with no context.
- Reference numbers in the Fig. 4 timeline don't match the text: Transformer [90] vs [92], GPT-3 [48] vs [50], ViT [107] vs [109].
- The text says ViT was proposed in June 2020, while Fig. 4 dates it 2020.10.
- The text gives over 87 MB of storage for ResNet50, while the figure gives 102 MB of parameters.
- INT8 is glossed as "8-bit weights" only.
- There is a typo, "Facebool".

(4) Accuracy figures for efficient CNNs and ViTs (e.g., EfficientViT 78.6 at 406 M FLOPs, EdgeNeXt 75.0) are ImageNet top-1 taken from the original papers under different training recipes, as the survey itself notes. They carry no hardware measurements.

Rows below record only the cited iPhone 12 latency pair, with low confidence because the result is secondary. Use the original sources for the database.

rows.model: Continual LLaVA (frozen LVLM + dual increment embeddings, 0.75M tunable params)
Continual LLaVA (frozen LVLM + dual increment embeddings, 0.75M tunable params)

note:
Continual LLaVA is a rehearsal-free method for continual instruction tuning of large vision-language models (LVLMs). The LVLM stays frozen. The method trains a low-rank pool of proxy-increment pairs (0.75M tunable parameters), selects the top-M pairs by cosine similarity with a Sentence-BERT embedding of the instruction ("intrinsic increments"), and combines a learnable weighted sum of increments chosen in earlier tasks ("contextual increments"). The dual increment embeddings are re-parameterized into the output linear layer. The paper also introduces the COAST benchmark with three settings: domain, capability and dataset. The supplied passages contain no hardware measurements (no FPS, latency, power or FPGA resources), so the rows record accuracy and forgetting results only.

Headline results on COAST-domain: average accuracy 37.08, which is 13.06 above sequential training. Average forgetting is 2.58, compared with 15.83 for sequential training and 15.61 for rehearsal. These numbers average three task orders.

Caveats:
- Accuracy is graded by GPT-4o rather than exact match, so it depends on the grader and is hard to reproduce.
- The parameter counts don't match. The tables list 6.76B parameters for full tuning, but the text says 7.67B.
- The comparison mixes different parameter budgets: the prompt-based baselines use 0.75M parameters, while full fine-tuning uses 6.76B.
- Task order matters on COAST-capability: the dcrf order gives 51.47 accuracy and 8.96 forgetting.
- Ablations: removing the alignment loss costs 6.80 accuracy, and removing the intrinsic increment ∆θ costs 3.71. Choosing output-layer adaptation over all-layer adaptation rests on a 0.09 gap.
- The supplied text does not state the LVLM backbone or its size.

note: ICHEP 2024 proceedings (CMS collaboration): two L1 anomaly-detection triggers. AXOL1TL is a VAE on L1 objects (10 jets, 4 e/γ, 4 μ, MET; pT/η/φ as raw integers; latent size 8). Only the encoder runs online, and the anomaly score is Σμ². CICADA is a convolutional AE on an 18x14 calorimeter image, compressed by knowledge distillation. Both use QKeras QAT, go through hls4ml to HLS, and run on Xilinx Virtex-7 in the CMS Global Trigger test crate. The text says the FPGA outputs are bit-exact (Fig. 2). Critical reading: (1) The text reports no measured hardware numbers: no LUT/DSP/BRAM counts, no measured latency, no power, no bit widths. (2) The 46% efficiency gain over the rest of the L1 menu at 1 kHz for H→4b is described as estimated, not measured on hardware, and the text does not say how the comparison was matched. Survey (no original experiments) of end-to-end autoencoder (AE) transceivers for wireless, optical-fiber, optical-wireless, semantic and quantum communication. It covers AE variants, loss functions, GCS vs PCS, and a FLOPs-based complexity analysis. The supplied passages contain no measured hardware result: no FPGA or ASIC implementation, and no throughput, latency, power or resource figures. So no benchmark row is extracted. The comparison tables (II–XII) only survived extraction as captions, so their content, including any hardware numbers they may cite from other work, can't be checked from these passages.

Critical points:
(1) The complexity metric is inconsistent. The abstract says "floating-point operations per second (FLOPS)", while the acronym table defines FLOPS as "Floating-Point Operations". Treat Table IV and the complexity section as operation counts, not throughput.
(2) The claim that the bottleneck is "typically composed of one or more un-trainable layers" is questionable. Section IV also calls the AE unsupervised, but communication AEs are usually trained on known transmitted messages and a CE/BCE reconstruction target.
(3) Claims that AEs beat traditional systems and get closer to the Shannon limit rest on cited work, with no quantitative evidence in these passages.
(4) Metadata needs checking. The year says 2026 but the arXiv ID is 2412 (Dec 2024). The DOI points to IEEE OJCOMS 2026. The byline in the preamble lists 6 authors, while the metadata lists 8 (Atalla and Mansoor are missing from the preamble). The 'autoencoder-fpga' axis is not supported: FPGA appears only in the acronym list. Extraction was flagged not-ok, and sections VII/VIII were merged into earlier sections.

note:
TreeLUT (Khataei & Bazargan, FPGA '25; the metadata says arXiv preprint, but the passages cite the FPGA '25 proceedings) is an open-source Python tool. It trains XGBoost gradient-boosted decision trees on inputs quantized before training (min-max normalization to w_feature bits), quantizes the leaves to w_tree bits using per-tree min shifts and a global scale, and writes Verilog directly without HLS. The design is a fully unrolled 3-layer architecture (key-generator comparators, then MUX-based trees, then adder trees). Pipelining is controlled by [p0,p1,p2] to reach II=1. It is evaluated on MNIST, JSC and NID using post-place&route Vivado results, with accuracy from post-implementation functional simulation. Claimed results: on MNIST, about 97% accuracy with 4.2x to 101x lower area-delay product than LUT-based neural networks (18.4x vs PolyLUT-Add for TreeLUT (II); 881.5x vs POLYBiNN (I)); on JSC, 471.9x lower area-delay product than hls4ml (Fahim et al.), which uses 38 DSPs; on NID, 2.7x vs Alsharari et al. (II).

Caveats:
(1) The baseline numbers are quoted from the original papers, not re-run. They mix post-synthesis and post-place&route results and probably different FPGA parts. The baseline for each dataset was chosen as the one closest in accuracy, which is a selection that favors TreeLUT.
(2) The target FPGA device is not named in the supplied passages.
(3) Table 5 rounds accuracies to whole percentages. Precise values come from Tables 2 and 3.
(4) There is an inconsistency: the DWN comparison (Table 6) gives TreeLUT MNIST at 96.6% with 2,278 LUTs, while Table 5 gives TreeLUT (I) at about 97% with 4,478 LUTs. This suggests a different device or setup that the passages do not explain.
(5) The table extraction is garbled. Fmax, latency, FF and some LUT values are missing, and area x delay (LUT x ns) is reported instead of latency. Latency was not derived.
(6) Only area-delay product is compared. There is no power or energy data.
(7) The DSP and BRAM values of 0 come from the abstract's statement that the design uses no BRAMs or DSPs. The table cells for those columns were not recovered.
(8) On NID, accuracy after quantization (92.7) is higher than before (92.0), which may be test-set noise.

note:
Kwok, Yip & Chng (arXiv 2501.07875) is a continual-learning ASR paper, not a hardware paper. None of the supplied passages reports a measured hardware result such as throughput, latency, power or FPGA resources. The only hardware detail is that training takes up to six days on one NVIDIA A40 GPU. The rows below are accuracy (WER) results only, and every hardware field is n/r.

**Method.** The authors add two things to Experience Replay (ER) with Whisper:
1. **Embedding Layer Surgery (ER-E):** each new language gets its own copy of the vocabulary token-embedding table. Special and language-ID tokens stay shared, so the model can still identify the language itself before switching to the right table.
2. **Task-wise beam search (ER-E-B):** the decoder keeps the top N=2 language-ID hypotheses, transcribes each one, and picks the one with the higher ASR log-probability. It is switched off for an utterance when a hypothesis is shorter than Mlen=5 words or overlaps other paths by more than Moverlap=3 words.

**Setup.** CL-MASR subsets of Common Voice: 10 h train, 1 h validation and 1 h test per language. Only the decoder is fine-tuned, for 2 epochs. The replay buffer holds 1 h per language.

**Main result (Table 2, Whisper-small, new languages eo/ia, forgetting measured on en/de).** In the language-agnostic setting, ER-E-B reaches an average WER of 15.9, against 17.3 for ER and A-GEM (tied as the best baselines) and 52.3 for full fine-tuning (FT). English WER goes from 18.26 with ER to 14.83, close to the unadapted 14.57. In the language-aware setting, ER-E and ER-E-B give identical numbers (15.7). This fits the claim that the beam search only helps when the model has to identify the language itself.

**Whisper-large-v2, 10 languages in sequence.** Average WER on the pretrained languages falls from 14.2 to 11.9 compared with ER. This number is given only in the Abstract and prose (the plot is Figure 4, which isn't in the passages), so it isn't entered as a row.

**Ablations.**
- Table 3 (en/eo, language-agnostic): the beam search lowers average WER from 19.4 to 18.3 for ER and from 19.2 to 17.6 for ER-E.
- Table 4: separate embeddings lower average WER from 16.4 to 15.7. A variant that only updates the tokens seen in the new language (ER-E-part) gets 15.9.

**Caveats.**
- Only two new/old language pairs are reported in the tables.
- Gains are relative percentages against FT. The margins over the best baseline are small (about 1–1.4 WER), and no variance or significance tests are given.
- Hyperparameters were swept for all methods, but the tuning budget isn't specified.
- Dynamic-architecture baselines are excluded because they aren't language-agnostic.
- The index terms list "speech emotion recognition" and "instruction-tuning", which looks like a template error.
- Metadata extraction was flagged ok=false, so the bibliographic data should be checked by hand.

note:

Because the task is this easy, the mAP50-95 values (about 0.72–0.86) do not transfer to real UAV scenes. INT8 costs a lot of accuracy: YOLOv8n mAP50-95 drops from 0.8422 to 0.7190 on the Orin Nano. In return, the Orin NX reaches 65.83 FPS and 0.179 J/inference.

Problems found:
(1) The power column in Table 4 is labelled 'Energy Consumption (W•s)' but the text treats it as mean power in W. The measurement scope (board vs. module, and which sensor) is not described.
(2) The text says the Orin Nano's power rises from 7.4 W (FP32) to 8.7 W (INT8). Table 4 shows the opposite direction: 8.790 for YOLOv8s FP32 and 7.483 for YOLOv8n INT8.
(3) Inferences per minute do not match FPS. For example, 3443 inferences/min is about 57.4/s, while the reported speed is 65.83 FPS. So the energy-per-inference figure (EPI = power×60/IPM) and FPS come from different measurements.
(4) The 35.09 ms edge round-trip time in Table 6 is attributed to the Orin Nano with YOLOv8s FP16. In Table 5, however, 35.09 ms is the Orin NX value; the Orin Nano with YOLOv8s FP16 is 49.44 ms.
(5) Table 7 gives mAP50 as 0.7190 for NX YOLOv8n INT8. In Table 4, 0.7190 is the mAP50-95 value; mAP50 is 0.8276.
(6) The '52 FPS' in the abstract is the FP32 result on the Orin NX (52.19).
(7) Mean iteration times in the text are 15.16 ms (NX) and 23.16 ms (Nano) for YOLOv8n INT8. They are not directly comparable to Table 4 FPS or the testbed processing times (14.29 ms and 20.54 ms).
(8) The Raspberry Pi 5 could not complete the realistic testbed runs.

The rows below take the clean, unmerged Table 4 lines. Confidence is medium because the extracted table is partly garbled and the power units are unclear.

The workflows are TensorFlow-GPU and cuDNN on Jetson AGX Xavier, TVM on the CPUs of Ultra96/ZCU104, FINN on ZCU104, and Vitis-AI on ZCU102. The authors say the U-Net has 16x fewer parameters and MACs than the original while keeping accuracy, and that it beats the Inria FCN+MLP baseline on building IoU and pixel accuracy. note:
Replay4NCL (DAC 2025; arXiv 2503.17061) builds on SpikingLR [25], a latent-replay neuromorphic continual learning (NCL) method. It runs a 4-layer recurrent SNN (700 inputs → 200 → 100 → 50 → 20 classes) on the SHD dataset with fewer timesteps (100 → 20 in the case study). To make up for having fewer spikes, it adjusts the threshold potential Vthr (spike-timing-based or sigmoid schedule) and uses a learning rate for the CL phase of η_cl = η_pre/100. It compresses the latent replay (LR) data and inserts it at a chosen layer. The authors claim, against SpikingLR: old-task Top-1 accuracy of 90.43 vs 86.22, 4.88x latency speed-up, 20% latent-memory saving and 36.43% energy saving.

Critical points:
(1) The only hardware is a GPU running a Python implementation (the paper says 'Nvidia RTX 4090 Ti', which is not a standard product name). It has no neuromorphic or FPGA deployment and no power measurement. The paper does not explain how energy was obtained, and latency and energy appear only as values normalized to SOTA, with no absolute ms or J.
(2) The headline numbers don't match the figure results. The body reports up to 2.34x speedup across LR insertion layers but the abstract says 4.88x, and energy saving is up to 56.7% across layers but 36.4% at layer 3. At LR insertion layer 3 (50 epochs), Replay4NCL is actually lower than SpikingLR on old tasks (88.24 vs 90.19) and new tasks (67.19 vs 71.88). The 90.43 vs 86.22 headline appears to come from a different setting that isn't stated, possibly the 150-epoch run in Fig. 13.
(3) Memory saving is 20–21.88%, which is modest given the 5x timestep reduction.
(4) Only one dataset and one small network are evaluated, with no variance reported.

Row 1 holds the abstract's headline claim. Row 2 holds the per-configuration result at LR layer 3. Neither passage reports FPGA resources, GOPS, FPS or absolute power.

rows.source_section: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS A. Pareto Optimal Model Search

note:
N-TORC is a two-phase flow for building models that must meet a hard latency limit. First, Optuna/BoTorch searches network settings, trading accuracy (RMSE) against workload (number of multiplies). Second, a Mixed Integer Program (MIP) solver sets the HLS4ML reuse factor for each layer so the whole network fits a 200 µs latency budget with minimal LUT, DSP, register and BRAM cost. The solver relies on data-driven latency and resource models trained on synthetic layers. The case study is DROPBEAR: predicting roller position from vibration data sampled at 5 kHz, using networks built from Conv1D, LSTM and Dense layers.

Main claims:
- The resource and latency models are more accurate than those of Wu et al. (Tables I and II; the numbers in those tables are not in the supplied passages).
- The MIP solver matches the quality of stochastic search or simulated annealing run for 1M trials, in 1000X less search time.

Hardware evidence:
- The results appear to be HLS synthesis/report estimates, not measurements on a board. The passages say "high-level synthesis results" and "estimated resource cost, estimated latency."
- On the XCZU7EV, the deployed networks run in "slightly less than" 200 µs. Effective throughput is 11–39 Mops/s. They use 3.7–18.8% of the available LUTs and 0.58–4.5% of the DSPs.
- These are ranges or percentages, and throughput is given in Mops/s, not GOPS. So the numeric columns are left as n/r rather than converting units or filling them with ranges.
- Power, quantization/precision, fps and exact per-model RMSE are not reported in the passages.

Caveats:
- The authors admit their resource model has "imperfections": the rows 8 and 9 models use more LUTs than the rows 10 and 11 models, even though the latter need more multiplies.
- The extracted text of Tables III and IV is garbled, so per-model values could not be reliably extracted.
- There is a possible mix-up in the passages: row 4 is called model 1 but plotted as "model 2", and vice versa.
- The 1000X speed-up is compared only against naive search baselines. There is no comparison against another deployment optimizer.
- The paper is a preprint and its metadata is flagged for manual checking.

note:
RAMAN is a sparse tinyML accelerator (12 PEs × 4 MACs, 8-bit weights and activations, 24-bit partial sums). It runs the encoder of a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) that compresses 96-channel × 100-sample LFP windows from two macaques (K and L, from dataset [53]). The compression ratio is 150 for DS-CAE1 and 37.5 for MobileNetV1-CAE(0.25x). On the Efinix Ti60 FPGA, Table I lists one set of resources for both models: 37.3k LUTs, 8.6k FFs, 52.3k XLR cells (86%) and 61 DSPs. Memory blocks, clock, latency and power differ by model. The balanced stochastic pruning uses an LFSR (32 LUTs + 20 FFs), and the passages give its parameter-memory saving as 15.7–32.4% versus magnitude pruning, with nearly the same SNDR and R2.

Caveats:
(1) Power is estimated, not measured. The FPGA figures (47.91 mW at 2 MHz, 53.97 mW at 7 MHz) are about 94% static. The 65-nm ASIC figure (1.45 mW, 15.1 µW per channel) comes only from post-layout simulation, not silicon. That makes the per-channel comparison against fabricated chips in Table V uneven.
(2) Latency is about 45–48 ms per 50 ms window at 2–7 MHz. Throughput is only just real-time, and the paper reports no FPS or GOPS.
(3) The passages don't say whether the SNDR and R2 values in Table V come from RAMAN's on-FPGA output or from the QAT model in PyTorch. I assume the 8-bit, 75%-pruned configuration shown in Fig. 9.
(4) The per-cell values in Table III and Table IV were lost in extraction, so the stochastic-vs-magnitude pruning numbers can't be checked.
(5) The prior works in Table V use different signal types (EEG, spike, ECoG, LFP) and bit precisions, and lossless and lossy methods sit side by side. Only Valencia et al. [54] uses the same dataset, so it is the only like-for-like baseline.

Row choices: the LUT count is copied exactly as '37.3k'. BRAM is the count of 10 kB memory blocks. Accuracy is the Monkey K SNDR; Monkey L is 27.43 dB for DS-CAE1 and 28.49 dB for MobileNetV1-CAE(0.25x).

Scope: this is a software benchmark of the smallest YOLO variants (v5n6u, v8n, v9t, v10n, v11n). They are compared on CPUs (Intel i7-13700, AMD Ryzen 7 5800X) and a GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3070), using ONNX, PyTorch, IPEX, OpenVINO and TensorRT through Ultralytics 8.3.39. There is no FPGA work at all, so the auto-assigned 'yolo-fpga' axis is wrong and should be removed. None of the supplied passages give numeric speed, latency or power results. Speed findings appear only in figures (Fig. 2–4) and in qualitative statements: OpenVINO is best on CPU, the AMD system beats the Intel one, and TensorRT is by far the fastest on GPU. The only numbers are accuracy values from Tables I and II, and those are platform-independent. Critical issues: (1) Eq. 4 is labelled 'Throughput' but actually computes mean per-image time (pre-processing + inference + post-processing), which is latency. (2) The captions and the text disagree. The Table I caption refers to objects at 1%/2.5%/5% of the image, but the columns say Small/Medium/Large. The text cites Table II for the 5% COCO result, although that result appears to be in Table I. One column is labelled 'mAP@0.95 (Small)', which is probably a typo. (3) Some claims in the text don't match the tables. For medium objects on DOTA, the text says v9 leads v8 by 9 points, but the table shows 11.43 at mAP@0.5 (74.01 vs 62.58) and 6.94 at mAP@0.5:0.95. The claimed 'nearly 4 points' lead of v8 over v11 on small DOTA objects is 3.55. (4) The authors deliberately left out mask annotations, so their mAP values are not comparable with the numbers Ultralytics publishes. (5) Each run was repeated five times, but no variance is reported. (6) Explanations based on architecture (C2f, PGI, attention being overwhelmed) are speculation with no ablations behind them. (7) The 1024x1024 DOTAv1.5 results come from models trained for 100 epochs with AdamW, but the training details for each dataset are not clear. Both rows below are accuracy-only; the hardware platform is n/r because the tables do not link accuracy to a specific device.

(3) The FINN-R throughput "50 TOPS (1 bit)" was lost as a section heading during extraction. The FINN-R row (VU9P, ~900k LUT, >100 GOPS/W) is incomplete, so no row was made for it.
(4) Several values are given in units the schema doesn't have and were not converted: FINN ~5 TOPS, FlightLLM ~55 tokens/s, and efficiency in GOPS/W (FlightLLM 300–400, SSR 246–453). SSR reports "up to 26.7 TOPS int8" on VCK190 with 394/400 AIEs, but it has no LUT/DSP figures, so it has no row.
(5) The MAESTRO/Timeloop 3×3 conv case study (ResNet-50, 256 PEs, about 5e5 vs 4.5e5 cycles, off-chip traffic 0.87 MB vs 440 MB) models a hypothetical accelerator. It is not a hardware measurement, so no row was made.
(6) The paper contradicts itself on Eyeriss: it calls it "OS-like", but also names it as the origin of Row-Stationary.
(7) The HLS/DSL/RTL overhead figures (+10–30% and +20–40% LUT/DSP; about 5× shorter design time) have no sources.
(8) Approximate values were written as bare numbers: "~50k LUT" became 50000 and "574k LUT" became 574000.

Critical reading note — Query Drift Compensation (QDC), Goswami et al., arXiv 2506.00037 (2025).

Problem: When a dense retrieval embedding model is trained on new datasets over time (Continual Document Retrieval, CDR), queries encoded by the updated model no longer match corpus embeddings that were indexed with the old model. Re-indexing (back-filling) fixes this but costs a lot of compute.

Method: The setting is task-incremental and exemplar-free. The base model is the pre-trained nomic embedding model (137M parameters, 768-dim, modified BERT-base). It is fine-tuned on 5 BEIR tasks in this order: MS MARCO → NQ → HotpotQA → FEVER → FiQA-2018. Training uses a contrastive loss with in-batch negatives plus H=7 hard negatives mined with gte-base, 1 epoch per task, batch size 128, learning rate 2e-5 and weight decay 0.01, on 4 NVIDIA L40S GPUs. Two additions:
(1) Embedding distillation (KD): minimises the cosine distance between old-model and new-model embeddings of both queries and documents.
(2) QDC: estimates one drift vector per task transition and subtracts it from new-model query embeddings at retrieval time. This maps queries back into the old space so they match the old index, without re-indexing.

Claimed results (the passages give only relative numbers; Tables 3 and 4 contain no absolute values here):
- KD improves over plain fine-tuning (FT) by 1.4 on average but hurts plasticity (FEVER drops by 4.5).
- QDC improves over FT by 4.1 on average.
- QDC on top of FT+KD adds 3.3 on average and is claimed best overall, performing similarly to joint training.
- QDC also beats FT with re-indexing.
- Using 20 drift vectors instead of one gains only 0.3–0.7 on some tasks.
- Analysis: corpus embeddings drift more than query embeddings, and longer texts drift more (Table 5). The authors link this to an information imbalance between short queries and long documents.

Critical points:
- The comparison with joint training uses per-dataset hard negatives rather than jointly mined ones, which may understate the joint-training upper bound.
- The claim that QDC beats re-indexing depends on the unequal-drift explanation, which is correlational (Table 5).
- Retrieval uses task-ids, which makes the setting easier than class- or domain-incremental retrieval.
- There is one task order and one backbone, and the passages report no variance.
- Drift vectors are estimated from new-task data only, because old queries are not accessible. It is unclear how well this holds when domains shift a lot, for example the finance domain of FiQA.
- Costs are never quantified. The paper argues that re-indexing is expensive but gives no measured indexing time or retrieval latency.

Benchmark rows: none extracted. The passages contain no measured hardware result (no throughput, latency, power or resource figures; the GPUs are mentioned only as training infrastructure). The absolute nDCG@10 values in Tables 3 and 4 are also missing from the passages, so no row could be filled without inventing values.

note:
ETT-CKGE (arXiv 2506.08158, 2025) is a regularization-based continual knowledge graph embedding method. It learns a small set of task-driven tokens Z (T ≤ 10, D = 200). These give importance masks σ(ZE) that are multiplied together into an aligned mask, which weights an L2 distillation loss between old and new snapshot embeddings. This replaces the traversal-based or heuristic importance scores used by LKGE, FMR, IncDE and FastKGE. The task is link prediction on six benchmark datasets. All experiments ran in PyTorch on one NVIDIA A6000 GPU. This is a GPU software paper, not an FPGA paper: the 'versal' tag and the 'platforms' axis look wrong and should be fixed in the fiche. There is no FPGA, power, LUT, DSP or BRAM data.

Measured results:
- Accuracy (Table 3): ETT-CKGE has the best or tied-best MRR on 5 of 6 datasets, but the margins over IncDE are small (about 0.001–0.007 MRR). On WN-CKGE, FastKGE is better (0.160 vs 0.153).
- Speed and memory: training time is reportedly 50–96% lower than the second-best model and 1.6–2.3x faster than FastKGE. Peak memory is 150MB–2GB lower, and about 2,000 parameters are updated per snapshot. Most of these efficiency figures come from figures that were not supplied, so they could not be checked.

Caveats:
- The PDF extraction is garbled. The Table 3 training-time columns are missing. Table 4 has fewer T(s) values than its headers imply, and the headers show only 5 dataset names for 6 MRR/T pairs.
- Table 4 gives the full model 0.222 MRR on what appears to be HYBRID, while Table 3 reports 0.224, which may be an inconsistency in the paper.
- The abstract claims 'superior' performance, but the results text says 'competitive... without overclaiming superiority'.
- Baselines were rerun 5 times and tuned. No variance is reported.

Training time in seconds (for example 784 s total on ENTITY in Table 4) is not a per-inference latency, so latency_ms is left as n/r.

note:
Critical reading (from supplied passages only). This paper is a side-channel reverse-engineering attack on FINN dataflow accelerators, not an accelerator design. Victim: a 5-layer CNN for MNIST built with FINN 0.9 on a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq Z7020). The design uses no DSPs, stores all parameters on-chip, and runs at 100 MHz. There are 8 victim variants: folding 1x/2x/4x/8x × 4-bit/6-bit quantization. A 128-latch TDC sensor from SCABox runs on the same fabric at the same clock. The dataset has 6400 traces (800 per configuration), split 5120 train / 1280 test. Traces are trimmed to a window of about 129k samples, with the first 258k samples of dataflow loading discarded. Method: PCA (scikit-learn) followed by one lightweight classifier per parameter (k-NN or RF). The baseline is tsfresh feature extraction as in [17].

Measured results:
- Preparation time on the database is 15.7 s for k-NN and 17.7 s for RF with PCA, versus about 4.62 h with tsfresh (>940×).
- Attacking one trace takes 337 ms (k-NN, PCA) and 421 ms (RF, PCA), versus >110 s with tsfresh.
- k-NN (ncomp=12, k=13) reaches 91.84 folding accuracy without averaging and 96.78 with averaging over 4 traces.
- RF (PCA) reaches over 93.7 for quantization without averaging and 99.96 for both parameters with averaging over 4 traces (PCA-A4).

Caveats:
1. The abstract attributes 337 ms to RF and 421 ms to RF with 4-trace averaging. The body text and Table II instead give 0.337 s for k-NN (PCA), 0.421 s for RF (PCA) and 0.79 s for RF (PCA-A4). Rows follow the body text.
2. The Table III text extraction is garbled. Per-configuration cells cannot be reliably mapped, and the 91.84/96.78/96.70 'Avg' values are only partly tied to specific metrics in the prose.
3. The timings are for attack computation on a dual AMD EPYC 7443 server, excluding trace acquisition. They are not accelerator inference latency.
4. The paper reports no victim accelerator throughput, GOPS, power or resource utilisation. 'No DSP' is a design choice, not a reported utilisation figure.
5. There is only one victim model and one board, and the attacker is assumed to know all candidate configurations. Generality to other models or devices is not shown.
6. The note that separation is weaker at low folding comes from Fig. 4, which is not reproduced here.

rows.dataset: SATLIB uniform Random-3SAT, size 250 (first satisfiable instance)
rows.baseline: CPU implementation mimicking 16-bit noise; median TTS99 on FPGA = 0.89 us (fastest schedule); claimed 2500-3000x FPGA speedup (sentence truncated)

note:
Critical reading note (from the supplied passages only).

What the paper is: a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine. It uses an 'autoencoder' structure in which clause outputs Tk are projected onto latent spin neurons (encoder, weights diag(J)H^T) and then reconstructed back into clauses (decoder). Latent thresholds are annealed with an emulated Fowler-Nordheim (FN) schedule tau(t)=tau0/log(1+t/C). Graph colouring (DSATUR or greedy) allows parallel updates. The main claim is that resource complexity does not depend on interaction order (O(n^2) dense; n*q + m*p sparse). Quadratized second-order solvers need auxiliary spins and couplings with more precision and range.

Axis caveat: the 'autoencoder' is a fixed, problem-derived mapping (H, J), not a trained neural network. It has no learned weights and no reconstruction-loss training. Tagging this paper under autoencoder-fpga is questionable and should be checked by hand in /paper-fiche.

Hardware evidence:
- The graph-coloured variant runs on an FPGA with a PS/PL split driven through PYNQ, an AXI DMA IP, 16-bit noise samples streamed from the PS (one sample per clock) and a 100 MHz clock.
- The FPGA part, LUT/DSP/BRAM usage and power are not given in these passages (they are deferred to SI S8).
- The only concrete measured numbers are for MAX-3SAT size 250 at the fastest schedule: median TTS97 = 0.34 us and median TTS99 = 0.89 us. The passage also claims a 2500-3000x speed-up over a CPU emulating 16-bit noise, but the sentence is cut off.

Concerns:
1. Units: at 100 MHz, 0.34 us is only about 34 clock cycles for a 250-variable instance (about 1065 clauses). That is implausibly short and may be a unit typo or a count that excludes some cycles. Check it against Fig. 4.b/c and SI S9.
2. The latency_ms field is left as n/r because the source value is in us and unit conversion is not allowed. The raw us values are in the baseline field.
3. TTS is a median with failures assigned a large value. The error bars run from the 6th to the 94th percentile. Results come from a single instance per size (the first satisfiable SATLIB instance) with 100 trials each.
4. The MAX-CUT FPGA comparison (G4/G11/G15 against dSBM, Fig. 2.c) is cut off in these passages, so no numbers were extracted.
5. The higher-order vs second-order comparisons (Fig. 3; 250-variable instances fully satisfied) and the MAX-5SAT/7SAT results (>99% of clauses satisfied after 10^8 iterations) come from CPU simulations, not hardware.
6. Energy-to-solution is not reported. The FN annealer is emulated digitally, and its noise is generated on the PS rather than on the chip.

rows.model: Q-ConvLSTM (DeepLOB-style ConvLSTM without inception blocks, LSTM 64 hidden units, seq len 25, ~141K params)
rows.task: Stock mid-price trend classification (limit order book, 3 classes)
rows.quantization: Mixed-precision quantised (Brevitas QuantLSTM/QCDQ); INT8 input features
rows.toolflow: FINN with FINN-GL LSTM extensions (ONNX Scan, Vitis HLS, Vivado IPI, PYNQ)
rows.baseline: DeepLOB (F1 76.59) and float ConvLSTM (F1 76.22) for Downward-0 class

note:
FINN-GL extends the FINN compiler so it can handle LSTMs. It models the LSTM recurrence with the ONNX Scan operator, which gives a QCDQ graph where each of the 11 internal QuantLSTM quantisers can have its own bit-width. It adds new or modified streamlining transformations (Table I) and an HLS backend that implements the recurrence as a loop bounded by sequence length. As a case study, the authors built a DeepLOB-style ConvLSTM without inception blocks: 2 conv blocks, an LSTM with 64 hidden units, input size 40 and sequence length 25, then FC 256 and FC 3, about 141K parameters. They trained it on FI-2010 (z-score version) with INT8 input features and deployed it on a ZCU104 (XCZU7EV) at 150 MHz. The compiler settings were mvau width = 36 and target fps = 1000. That fps figure is a compiler target, not a measurement.

Measured result: batch-1 latency of 4.3 ms. This matches the Vitis HLS cosimulation but excludes data movement. Resource use is reported only as percentages: about 49% of LUTs, 13% of flip-flops and 15% of DSPs. The supplied text does not give absolute LUT, DSP or BRAM counts, so those fields are n/r.

Accuracy (Table III): Q-ConvLSTM F1-scores are 77.54 (downward), 78.07 (stationary) and 76.60 (upward). The float ConvLSTM scores 76.22, 76.09 and 75.56, and DeepLOB scores 76.59, 80.36 and 76.68. So quantisation does not hurt accuracy, but on the stationary class the model trails DeepLOB.

Critical points:
1. The prediction horizon (k) behind Table III is not stated.
2. The paper names macro F1 as its main metric but does not report it in the supplied text. The per-class values are not averaged here.
3. There are no power or energy measurements.
4. There is no hardware comparison with FINN-L, hls4ml-LSTM or other FPGA LSTM accelerators. Only accuracy is compared (Table IV, whose contents were not supplied, and the claims of beating SVM by 42% and MLP by 29%).
5. The bit-widths of the mixed-precision weights and activations are not given in these passages.
6. The paper frames the work around HFT, where events can be nanoseconds to microseconds apart, yet the design reaches 4.3 ms. That is justified only against FI-2010's roughly 192 ms event interval.
7. The extraction flags say the metadata needs manual checking. The case-study text (Section IV) is filed under "III. DEVELOPMENT STAGES", so that heading is used as source_section.

note:
MoCa (Chen et al., arXiv 2506.23115) turns causal VLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL 3B/7B) into bidirectional multimodal embedding models in two stages. Stage 1 is modality-aware continual pre-training: joint MLM on text plus MAE on image patches, about 30B tokens, 32 H100 GPUs, lr 2e-6, MAE loss weight 0.5. Stage 2 is heterogeneous contrastive fine-tuning: about 2M pairs, batch 2048, task-aware batching, tau 0.03, 2 hard negatives. Embeddings are mean-pooled. Evaluation uses MMEB (36 tasks, Precision@1) and ViDoRe-v2 (7 tasks, NDCG@5).

Critical points:
(1) This is not a hardware or accelerator paper. The H100s are only for training, and no throughput, latency, power or FPGA resource figures are given, so every hardware field is n/r.
(2) The extraction is poor (extraction.ok=false). Tables 1 and 3 have no numbers in the passages. Table 2 keeps only 2 numbers per row out of 8 columns, so which column each number belongs to is uncertain. I guessed they are the first two (ESG_Human, Eco_Mul) and marked both rows low confidence. Check them against the PDF.
(3) Claims to check: the 'new SOTA on ViDoRe-v2' claim is not visible in the numbers we have. GME-7B gets 62.9 against MoCa-3B's 62.8 in the first extracted column. The abstract's SOTA claim is explicitly about MMEB, but the text says 'outperforms all strong baselines on both benchmarks'. The claim that 3B beats 7B on ViDoRe-v2 is explained by overfitting, which is not tested.
(4) The ablation (Table 3) and the scaling claims (about 2,200 CPT steps ≈ 20B tokens; Figure 3) can't be checked here. The hyperparameter study reports MMEB test scores after choosing settings on validation sets built from the training data.
(5) The 'micro-batch size of 12,800' is unclear (it is probably tokens, not samples).
(6) The metadata axis 'continual-learning' is probably a misclassification. The method is continual pre-training for representation learning, not continual learning in the catastrophic-forgetting sense. Also, every passage is labelled '3.1.1 Modality-aware Continual Pre-training Stage' even when it covers results or ablations, which looks like a sectioning error.

note:
Quantised SuperPoint for visual odometry on Zynq UltraScale+. The authors deploy it in two ways. The first uses Vitis AI with the INT8 DPU (DPUCZDX8G B4096) on the Kria KV260. The second uses Brevitas and FINN at low bit-widths (8, 4 and 3 bits, plus a mixed 4-2-4 variant) on the KV260 and the ZCU102. Unlike earlier FPGA SuperPoint work (FCCM'20, TCASI'22, APCCAS'24), they keep the original network architecture unchanged. The two FINN builds reach 27 FPS on the KV260 and 54 FPS on the ZCU102 at 640×480. The rows below cover only these two measured FINN builds.

Critical points:
1) Power figures are estimates from the Vivado Power Analysis tool, not board measurements. Total power is 3.307 W and 4.607 W, and the PS accounts for most of it. The DPU power (2–4 W) and the DPU's LUT/DSP/BRAM figures come from documentation, not from a post-implementation report.
2) The text of Table IV is garbled in the extraction. Matching 3.307 W to the KV260 build and 4.607 W to the ZCU102 build is inferred from column order. Frequency, latency and DSP/BRAM values for the FINN builds cannot be recovered.
3) The passages never state which bit-width the deployed FINN builds used. The mixed INT 4-2-4 variant is only implied by Table I. Accuracy numbers from Tables I and V are also not recoverable, except the APE figures quoted in the text. Those are for TUM: FP32 is 7.61°/0.31 m, INT8 is 9.39°/0.38 m, INT4 is 10.41°/0.36 m, and INT3 has a rotation error of 12.24°. The mixed 4-2-4 variant has the largest trajectory error.
4) The comparison with prior work mixes different frameworks, boards and resource-accounting methods, so the 'outperforming state of the art' claim deserves caution.
5) The DPU at INT8 reaches 58.6 FPS. The truncated passage suggests this is on the KV260, but the configuration and resolution are unclear, so no row was created for it. The quantised network also detects 10–15% fewer feature points than the full-precision version.

rows.task: object detection and classification (general objects + traffic signs)
rows.baseline: Table I: Valadanzoj et al. YOLOv4-Tiny ZC706 (79%, 55 FPS, 13.6 W); Nguyen et al. YOLOv4-Tiny ZCU104 (78%, 125 FPS, 26.4 W); Heller et al. YOLOv4-Tiny KV260 (75%, 15 FPS, 8 W); Amin et al. YOLOv3-Tiny KV260 (99%, 15 FPS, 3.5 W); Ngo et al. YOLOv3-Tiny KV260 (91.87%, 25 FPS, 7.9 W)

note:
YOLOv5 was trained in PyTorch with SGD (lr 0.01, batch 32, 100 epochs) on COCO and GTSRB. It was quantized from FP32 to INT8 after training and compiled with Vitis AI for the DPU on a Xilinx Kria KV260. The only hardware result reported is 98.6 'classification accuracy', 9 FPS, 3.5 W and 2.6 FPS/W. This comes from 72 curated test images drawn from both datasets.

Points to read critically:
(1) Accuracy is not stated consistently. The abstract says 99 while the results section and Table I say 98.6. The metric is not defined either: it is not mAP, and COCO and GTSRB are not reported separately.
(2) 72 images is too small a test set to support comparisons with other work. Most rows in Table I report mAP on different datasets, so the accuracy comparison is not like-for-like.
(3) The paper does not say how the 3.5 W was measured (board or chip, idle or under load). Latency is claimed to be 'real-time' and 'low', but no latency number is given. 9 FPS is weak for real-time ADAS use.
(4) The paper claims to be 'resource-efficient' but reports no LUT, DSP or BRAM use and no DPU configuration. No input resolution, YOLOv5 variant (n/s/m) or FP32-vs-INT8 accuracy comparison is given.
(5) The method is contradictory: it is described as post-training quantization but also credits 'quantization-aware techniques'. The abstract says 'GTSRD' instead of GTSRB. Future work promises 'multiclass detection', yet the system already uses 80-class COCO.
(6) Some Table I baseline figures don't match elsewhere. The Ngo et al. entry lists 25 FPS, but the related-work text says up to 29 FPS. Amin et al.'s 15 FPS / 3.5 W works out to 4.29 FPS/W, but the table lists 4.2. The paper's own efficiency checks out: 9 / 3.5 = 2.57, rounded to 2.6.
The claim that it 'improves energy efficiency' over prior work is not supported by its own table: 2.6 FPS/W is lower than 4, 4.7, 4.2 and 3.1.

Critical reading: This paper is a software-only feasibility study. It trains a small spiking-neural-network autoencoder (SNN-AE) for trigger-level anomaly detection on the CMS ADC2021 dataset. The network has an encoder of (19, 24, 12) neurons, a latent space of 4, and a decoder of (12, 24, 19). It uses leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with T in [5, 10] steps, a firing threshold (u_thresh) of 1.2 and a decay factor (β) of 0.9. It is built in PyTorch/snntorch, trained on 100k background events, and uses only the 19 transverse-momentum (pT) and missing-energy (MET) inputs. The comparison baseline is a DNN autoencoder with the same shape and ReLU activations.

No FPGA or neuromorphic deployment is reported. The claims about latency, efficiency and FPGA suitability are argued qualitatively (Sec. 2), and deploying to hardware (FPGA, Loihi) is left as future work in Sec. 5. For that reason, all hardware fields in the rows are n/r.

Table 1 (mean ± std over 5 runs) shows the SNN-AE slightly behind the DNN-AE on every signal:
- AUC: h0 0.719 vs 0.737; h+ 0.899 vs 0.903; A4l 0.880 vs 0.890; phi 0.802 vs 0.852.
- Inverse background efficiency at 30% signal efficiency (ε_b⁻¹ at ε_s = 0.3): h+ 71.3 vs 101.8; A4l 217.3 vs 360.3.
- Reconstruction loss is about 4× higher for the SNN-AE: 20.24e-5 vs 5.19e-5.

So "competitive" is a generous reading. The claims of better robustness (lower variance across latent size and training-set size) rest on figures that are not included in these passages.

The rows report the h+ AUC as the representative accuracy value. Confidence is medium because the table text was extracted by PDF parsing and the value comes from a single signal. The extraction metadata also flags the paper metadata as needing manual checking.

rows.model: LeNet-5*, MobileNetV1, ResNet50, VGG16, MobileNetV2, DenseNet121 (aggregate)
rows.platform: AMD Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 (custom ISA-extended trv32p3 RISC-V soft core)
rows.dataset: StanfordCars + COCO (64x64x3); handwritten digits 28x28 for LeNet-5*
rows.toolflow: MARVEL (Apache TVM + Synopsys ASIP Designer/Chess + Xilinx Vivado)
rows.baseline: Synopsys trv32p3 RISC-V (v0): 2x inference speedup, up to 2x energy-per-inference reduction, 28.23 area overhead

note:
MARVEL is an automated flow that profiles TVM-generated bare-metal C for CNNs and turns the patterns it finds into custom RISC-V ISA extensions. It takes Python/Keras models, uses Apache TVM to emit generic C, then Synopsys ASIP Designer (nML/PDG plus Chess compiler rewrite rules) to extend the trv32p3 core, and Vivado to target a ZCU104 FPGA. The processor versions build on each other: v1 adds mac (fixed registers x20–x22), v2 adds add2i (5-bit and 10-bit unsigned immediates), v3 adds fusedmac and v4 adds zero-overhead hardware loops (zol).

Strengths: the extensions come from instruction-level profiling rather than assumed hotspots. The add2i immediate coverage is reported per model (100 for LeNet-5*, 86.03 for MobileNetV1, 75.19 for ResNet50, 66.89 for VGG16, 71.39 for MobileNetV2, 95.13 for DenseNet121). The paper also counts blt executions to justify the hardware-loop extension. Unlike AI-RISC, it needs no changes to TVM.

Weaknesses and caveats:
- The only measured hardware figures in these passages are aggregates in the Abstract: 2x inference speedup, up to 2x less energy per inference, and 28.23 area overhead versus the trv32p3 baseline on ZCU104. Per-model latency, energy, power and LUT/DSP/BRAM numbers were not supplied; Tables 8 and 10 appear only as captions.
- The models are simplified. Inputs are 64x64x3 and the task is binary Car/Not-Car, fine-tuned on StanfordCars and COCO. No accuracy figures are given.
- Profiling was done on MobileNetV1 only; the claim that the patterns hold across the model class rests on pattern counts.
- Fixing the mac registers reduces register-allocation flexibility.
- The LLVM front-end cannot infer custom instructions, so the choice of front-end matters.
- Metadata tag 'finn' is misleading: FINN is mentioned only as a contrasting tool and is not used. The 'mobilenet' and 'zcu104' tags are correct.

BAKE (Li et al., arXiv 2508.02426; the passages give the venue as WWW '26) treats continual knowledge-graph embedding (CKGE) as sequential Bayesian inference. It uses a mean-field Gaussian posterior with precision-weighted updates, where the old posterior becomes the new prior. On top of TransE and the usual KGE loss it adds a KL-style regulariser (L_Bayes, with weight beta) and a continual clustering loss. The clusters have a fixed size K and are built from entities sorted by importance, rather than by re-running k-means for each snapshot. The paper evaluates on 8 benchmarks (ENTITY, RELATION, HYBRID, GraphLower/Equal/Higher, FB-CKGE, WN-CKGE), each with 5 snapshots. Metrics are MRR and Hits@1/3/10, averaged over the current and all earlier test sets and over 5 runs. Training ran on 8 V100 GPUs.

Critical points:
(1) This is not a hardware or FPGA paper. There are no measured throughput, latency, power or resource numbers, and the GPUs are only the training setup. So no hardware row is required.
(2) The PDF extraction dropped every absolute value from Tables 1–3. Only the 'Improve' percentages survived, and they cannot be matched reliably to dataset and metric columns because some cells are '-'. So I did not create any accuracy rows.
(3) The paper overstates its claims. The results text says it is state of the art on 'all benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics', but the abstract says 'the vast majority of cases', and the Improve row has missing entries.
(4) The paper claims 'theoretical guarantees' and insensitivity to data order. In practice the method is a precision-weighted L2 penalty (operationally close to EWC-style regularisation), and the passages show no proof. The precision update is also additive, so it may make parameters too rigid over many snapshots. The authors do not discuss this.
(5) The paper motivates CKGE by efficiency (retraining YAGO from scratch is too costly), but reports no training-time or cost comparison.
(6) The case-study prose does not match Table 4. The prose says competitors placed the true answers 'beyond the top 100', but the table shows ranks of 26 and 3 for Blade Runner and 25 and 69 for Netherlands.
(7) The ablation results are given only as relative drops, e.g. an average H@1 drop of about 11.16% without clustering and an H@10 drop of 5.37% on ENTITY without the Bayesian module.
(8) Metadata to fix: the author appears as 'Tashi Nyima' in the paper, and the venue should be WWW '26 rather than a preprint. No section headings were detected, so almost everything is filed under '(préambule)'.

rows.task: continual knowledge graph embedding / link prediction
rows.accuracy_metric: MRR improvement over SOTA CKGE baselines (avg over 7 datasets, %)
rows.dataset: ENTITY, RELATION, FACT, HYBRID, GraphEqual, GraphHigher, GraphLower
rows.source_section: 1. Extract and mark features of historical graphs

note:
SAGE (Li et al., KDD '25; arXiv 2508.11347) is about continual knowledge graph embedding (CKGE). It is not a hardware or FPGA paper. None of the supplied passages report a hardware measurement: there is no platform, throughput, latency, power or resource usage. All hardware fields are therefore n/r. Table 5 gives only an estimated training cost in FLOPs, and its values are not in the passages.

What the method does: (1) it estimates how much the graph grew and sets the embedding dimension from a fitted logarithmic curve P = a·log_b(N), with P = d·(|E|+|R|); (2) it replays hard past examples and expands the embeddings using a learned mapping; (3) it updates old embeddings with a distillation loss weighted by how new and how reliable each entity or relation is (L = L_itg + α·L_dwt).

Evaluation: link prediction (MRR, H@1, H@10) on seven benchmarks, each with 5 snapshots: ENTITY, RELATION, FACT, HYBRID, GraphEqual, GraphHigher and GraphLower. Baselines are Fine-tune, PNN, CWR, GEM, EMR, DiCGRL, SI, EWC, LKGE, IncDE and FastKGE. The paper also proposes a new forgetting metric, RtF.

Reported gains: averaged over the seven datasets, +1.38% MRR, +1.25% H@1 and +1.6% H@10 over the strongest recent CKGE methods. Against conventional methods the gains are 4.2–20.5% MRR. On ENTITY and RELATION the MRR gains are 2.7% and 1.8%. In the ablation on GraphLower, removing LE lowers MRR by 0.038, removing DI by 0.032, and removing SE by 0.019.

Weaknesses:
- The absolute SAGE scores were lost when the PDF was extracted; the table fragments only show some baseline values, such as IncDE 0.239/0.143/0.426. The row below therefore records a relative gain, not an absolute score.
- The passages do not say whether "1.38%" means percentage points or relative improvement.
- The FACT and HYBRID margins are small, and the passages report no variance or significance tests.
- The log-scaling law is fitted on only four datasets, and the constants a and b are not given.
- RtF is a metric the authors defined themselves, which makes comparison with earlier papers harder.
- The metadata needs fixing: this is KDD '25, DOI 10.1145/3711896.3737115, and the section headings were mis-segmented during extraction.

rows.model: QONNX model zoo QNN workloads (average across workloads)
rows.baseline: FINN without SIRA optimizations; average reductions with SIRA: LUT 17, DSP 66, accumulator bitwidth 22 (percent, out-of-context synthesis)

note:
SIRA (Umuroglu et al., arXiv 2508.21493, preprint) is a static analysis pass. It uses interval arithmetic to find the range, scale and bias of every tensor in a QONNX graph. It works one node at a time, with separate propagation rules for Quant, Add, Mul and MatMul/Conv. Scales and biases only pass through affine regions. MatMul needs weight/activation scaling that is at most per-channel, and the weights must have zero bias. The authors use this information in FINN in three ways: (i) collapsing scales and biases into one aggregated Mul/Add, so MatMul runs on pure integers; (ii) shrinking accumulators without losing accuracy; and (iii) a generic version of streamlining that turns layer tails into multi-thresholding. It fixes four stated gaps in the original streamlining work by Umuroglu & Jahre: no concrete algorithm, only one conversion example, a dependence on a later thresholding step, and no analysis of trade-offs.

Motivation (Table 1): a 3-bit ResNet-8 on CIFAR-100 loses more than 2 percentage points with the least expressive scale factors compared with the most expressive. The float32 reference is 70.52.

Headline result (abstract): on average across the QONNX model-zoo workloads, SIRA cuts LUTs by 17%, DSPs by 66% and accumulator bitwidth by 22%.

Critical points:
- The supplied passages give only the captions of Tables 5–8, not their values. So there are no per-model LUT/DSP/BRAM/FPS figures, no FPGA part, and no power figure here.
- The results come from out-of-context synthesis, not board measurements.
- Interval bounds can be loose because of the dependency problem.
- Thresholding cost grows exponentially with activation bitwidth. Table 7 shows cases where thresholds use more LUTs than float operations. So SIRA does not always help.
- Whether fixed-point aggregated scales cost any accuracy is not quantified in these passages.

Before trusting this row, check it against Table 6.

Critical reading note — Kurpukdee & Bors (arXiv 2508.21773, 2025), "Unsupervised Video Continual Learning via Non-Parametric Deep Embedded Clustering".

What it does: The paper sets up unsupervised video continual learning (uVCL), where the model gets no labels and no task boundaries. A frozen VideoMAE V2 encoder, pre-trained without labels on Kinetics-700, extracts a 1024-dim feature per video (16 frames of 224×224×3). Mean-shift then clusters these features using a Gaussian KDE. A novelty detector adds new clusters when a sample is far from existing ones. There are two variants:
- uVCL-KDE uses a distance threshold Θ1, set from the maximum distance between cluster centres in the first task (16.53 / 16.92 / 15.98).
- uVCL-KDE-RBF adds an RBF-style linear layer trained with focal loss (γ=2) and uses a probability threshold Θ2 (best value 0.3).
A replay buffer stores features for N=20 videos per cluster.

Setup: PyTorch, Adam with lr 0.001, up to 50 epochs, batch size 8, on one GTX 1080 Ti 11GB. Datasets are UCF101, HMDB51 and SSv2 with labels removed, split into 13 / 37 / 659 tasks of 256 videos each.

Reported results: uVCL-KDE-RBF is reported as best on all three datasets, ending with 100 / 42 / 133 clusters (bandwidth h=17 for UCF101 and SSv2, h=19 for HMDB51). Ablations:
- A 30-sample buffer works better on UCF101; a 10-sample buffer works better on HMDB51.
- Θ2=0.3 beats 0.7 and 1.0.

Limitations of the evidence:
1. The extracted Table 1–3 text is garbled. Only scattered forgetting values survive (for example -0.11, -0.15, -0.001), and none of the CAcc/ACAcc accuracy numbers can be recovered or matched to a method or dataset.
2. Baselines on SSv2 were run only for the first 30 tasks because of cost, so the SSv2 comparison is incomplete.
3. Bandwidth h and the thresholds were tuned on the evaluation results, and no separate validation protocol is described.
4. Using cluster count as a proxy for the number of classes assumes the classes match the clusters.
5. The conclusion says the method reduces computation and training time, but the evidence is only in Appendix F, which was not supplied.
6. Baseline descriptions (Appendix C) and metric definitions (Appendix D) were also not supplied. In the Table 2 header the arrows on BWF/FWF are the opposite of Tables 1 and 3, which is an inconsistency.

Why there are no benchmark rows: None of the supplied passages reports a measured hardware result (no FPS, latency, power, GOPS or FPGA resources). The GTX 1080 Ti is only the training setup. The accuracy values that could be read cannot be reliably tied to a model or dataset, so no rows were produced.

rows.model: ResNet with HAPM pruning + Dynamic Sparsity Bypass (Peccia et al. [76])

note:
Survey (Sali, Meribout, Majeed, arXiv 2509.04153, 2025) of FPGA CNN deployment for detection, classification and tracking. It covers LUT-DSP, SoC and ACAP (Versal) platforms, parallelism and pipelining, quantization, DSP packing, pruning and toolflows (Vitis AI, FINN, Intel FPGA AI Suite). The paper runs no experiments of its own. Every hardware number here comes from a cited work. That includes Tables VII–IX, H2PIPE [73] (>1000 FPS ResNet-50 on Stratix 10 NX), Peccia et al. [74] (two INT8 MACs per DSP48E2, 60% mean speed-up over Gemmini) and HAPM [76]. The rows below are secondary data and should be checked against the primary papers.

Problems with the source:
- The comparison tables leave out quantization, dataset and power measurement scope. Power values mix boards and conditions, e.g. 1.11 W versus 77 W.
- Table VIII puts U-Net (segmentation) and RBPnet4's F1 score under a "Top 1" accuracy column.
- The GROBID extraction garbles some columns. One example is Table VII [100], where LUTs and DSPs are merged ("484209 1153").
- Some entries look suspect: 19 BRAM for LCAM-YOLOX, and 1609 FPS at 77 W for the custom SSD.
- The GOPS/W comparison in Section II (Zynq 7z100 at 16.7 versus RTX 3090 at 6.32 [132]) is taken from one cited source and does not compare like with like.
- The peak-TOPS figures in Table IV are vendor ranges, not measurements.

The survey does raise useful open problems: RTOS-level management of PS-PL interaction, the cost of balancing a pipeline, and the fact that sparsity alone does not guarantee a speed-up (YOLOv7 pruning [77]).
