note: Critical reading: This paper benchmarks 12 YOLO variants (v8, v9, v10 and v11 in n/t, s and m sizes) for single-class deer detection. It introduces a curated Cameratraps dataset of 3,095 images from Idaho camera-trap footage, split 2,578 train / 517 val. Inference runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 (CPU only, Cortex-A76, 16 GB) and an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier. The paper has no FPGA implementation, so the automatically assigned 'yolo-fpga' axis looks wrong and should be checked by hand. Strengths: the cross-dataset test shows a clear domain gap. YOLOv11n scores AP@0.5 0.9920 on Roboflow but only 0.7395 on Cameratraps, with AP@50_95 dropping from 0.8475 to 0.5341. The dataset is public. Weaknesses: (1) The Table 5 values did not survive extraction; only headers remain. The passages give only bounds for edge results: YOLOv9t on Pi 5 takes >250 ms (<4 FPS), YOLOv8m on Pi 5 takes >1.5 s per frame, YOLOv11n and YOLOv10n on Jetson reach >40 FPS, s-models on Jetson reach >20 FPS, Jetson inference stays <70 ms, and Jetson AP@0.5 stays >0.85. (2) The 'total' and 'inference' timings are defined inconsistently: FPS comes from total time, including pre- and post-processing, and the authors blame the gap on software inefficiency. (3) The passages mention no precision, TensorRT, INT8 or hardware-specific optimization, and the conclusion defers that work, so the edge results are probably unoptimized framework inference. (4) No power measurements are given, even though the discussion argues that energy efficiency is a key point. (5) The high-end GPU used as the reference is not specified in these passages. (6) The summaries do not fully agree: the abstract says >30 FPS on Jetson and the conclusion says >25 FPS. Because only bounds are available, the numeric fields in the Jetson row are n/r. rows.task: object detection (metal sheet defect detection: surface scratches, irregular holes)
rows.platform: PC: Intel i7-13700K CPU + NVIDIA RTX4080 16 GB GPU
rows.dataset: Custom metal sheet defect dataset (no ConSinGAN augmentation)

note:
Critical reading: The paper compares YOLOv3, v4, v7 and v9 for detecting metal-sheet defects (surface scratches and irregular holes), with and without ConSinGAN single-image augmentation. It reports that YOLOv9 with ConSinGAN is best: mAP0.5 91.3, PRE 98.8, REC 85.7, F1 91.0, detection time 146 ms.

Hardware and tagging: All timings come from a PC with an Intel i7-13700K and an NVIDIA RTX4080 (16 GB), Windows 10, Anaconda. There is no FPGA, quantization, power or resource data, so the auto-assigned 'yolo-fpga' axis looks wrong and should be checked.

Issues found in the passages:
(1) The test set is not independent. Only 10 original sheet images were used. From these, 35 defect crops of 512x512 were cut and augmented to 735 images, then split at random 80/10/10. Near-duplicate synthetic images from the same source crops very likely appear in both train and test, which would inflate the metrics.
(2) The abstract and contributions call the 91.3 value 'accuracy', but it is mAP0.5.
(3) Some F1 values do not match their PRE and REC. For YOLOv4 with ConSinGAN, F1 is 76.2 while PRE is 73.1 and REC is 73.9; F1 cannot be higher than both. For YOLOv3, PRE 70.1 and REC 78.5 imply F1 of about 74.1, but 65.4 is reported.
(4) The text says average detection time is about 210 ms. The mean of the 8 values in Table II is about 191 ms.
(5) Augmentation only changes training data, yet it changes detection time (for example YOLOv9 goes from 161 to 146 ms). The timing protocol is not described: batch size, whether pre/post-processing is included, and whether the time is per image.
(6) There are no model sizes, no inference resolution beyond the 416x416 training size, no variance or repeated runs, and no external baseline.
(7) Some descriptions are wrong: PGI is called 'personal growth initiative' (it is Programmable Gradient Information), and YOLOv4's SAM is called 'segment anything model' (it is a spatial attention module).

Rows: Values are copied from Table II. That table was extracted under the 'V. CONCLUSION' heading, so that heading is used as source_section. Detection time is entered as latency_ms, with medium confidence because the timing scope is unclear. The dataset is described in 'IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS'.

Survey/review (Sapkota & Karkee) of Ultralytics YOLOv5 → YOLOv8 → YOLO11 → YOLO26 → YOLO27, plus some non-Ultralytics detectors. It contains no FPGA work, and none of the results come from the authors' own measurements. All numbers are copied from vendor or original-paper reports.

Key claims:
- YOLO27 splits the family into two designs by model size. n/s use dual-scale CNNs with an optional NMS-free mode. m/l use query-based transformer decoding, and YOLO27l adds an UltraViT backbone.
- Preliminary COCO mAP50:95 at 640 px ranges from 42.3 (n) to 60.4 (l), with 0.62–2.32 ms latency using TensorRT 11 FP16 on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000. YOLO27l reaches 61.2 at 800 px.
- YOLO26 removes DFL and NMS, and adds ProgLoss, STAL and MuSGD.

Critical points:
1. Latencies come from different hardware and runtimes: CPU ONNX for Table 3, T4 TensorRT for Table 4, and RTX PRO 6000 TensorRT 11 for YOLO27. They cannot be compared across tables.
2. The YOLO27 figures are called "preliminary", with no independent check and no batch size, preprocessing or NMS-timing details.
3. Claims about YOLO26 quantization ("INT8 retains nearly the same mAP") and the ~43% CPU speedup ("early previews") have no numbers or source.
4. Table 4 gives YOLOv13 latencies of ~41–67 ms on a T4, versus 1.64–6.14 ms for YOLO12. This is probably a units or source error and needs checking.
5. The dates are inconsistent: YOLO26 is dated 2025 in the text but 2026 in Table 1, the metadata says 2025, and the preprint is dated 2026-09-17.
6. No power, energy or FPGA resource figures are reported, so the automatically assigned 'yolo-fpga' axis looks wrong.

The PDF extraction found no section headings, so every passage except the Abstract is labelled "(préambule)". The two rows below are secondary-source GPU results, not FPGA results.

Critical reading note (based only on the supplied passages). CICADA is a CMS Level-1 Trigger anomaly detector. A convolutional autoencoder teacher (~300k parameters) is trained on 2017 Zero Bias CMS Open Data. Its behavior is transferred by knowledge distillation (MAE loss on the target Qlog = quantize(log(32·loss)), plus outlier exposure using ttbar→2l2ν) to a ~10k-parameter CNN student. The paper compares three ways of making the student cheap enough for hardware: QKeras quantization-aware training (the baseline), HGQ (bitwidths learned per weight, with an EBOPs term weighted by β and an L1 term with γ=1e-8, and β scanned), and a logic gate network (LGN, with architectures and input bit representations scanned). Physics performance is measured with EMD between teacher and student scores and with ROC AUC on the ttbar signals. Hardware cost comes from Vitis HLS synthesis on an AMD Virtex-7 XC7VX690T, reporting latency in clock cycles (1 cycle = 6.25 ns), DSPs, FFs and LUTs.

Caveats: (1) The hardware numbers are pre-place-and-route HLS estimates, not measurements on a board. The authors say place-and-route is still needed to get the real cost. (2) The Table 1 passage lists only row labels (QKeras, HGQ-1E-5, HGQ-1E-4, HGQ-mixed, LGN-LT2) and column names. No numeric values were extracted, so none of the claimed resource savings can be checked here. (3) No ROC AUC or EMD values appear in the passages. The claim of "comparable performance with significantly reduced resources" therefore cannot be quantified. (4) "Sub-200 ns" is a design target or bound for the deployed model, not a per-model measured value. (5) The signal samples are limited to ttbar channels, which are the only ones available in Open Data. This limits how well the results generalize to realistic new-physics signals. (6) Convolutional LGNs have not been synthesized yet. (7) The metadata warnings (extraction ok=false, axes inferred automatically) mean the metadata should be checked by hand.

Rows: none. The instructions require a row only for a measured hardware result, and there is none. The only hardware figures are HLS estimates, and their numbers are missing from the extracted table. Re-extract Table 1 from the PDF to fill in the rows.

note:
Critical reading note (arXiv 2511.06955, Parameshwara & Mokashi, 2025). Claim: custom "RISC-V ISA extensions" (FPGA.VCONV, FPGA.GEMM, FPGA.RELU, FPGA.CUSTOM) backed by FPGA accelerators on a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) give an average 2.14× speedup and a 49.1% energy reduction over an ARM Cortex-A9 baseline on MobileNet V2, ResNet-18, EfficientNet Lite and YOLO Tiny. The baseline is GCC 11.2 -O3 with NEON and ARM Compute Library v23.02 at a fixed 666 MHz. The accelerators use INT16 fixed point (Q8.8 activations, Q12.4 weights) with per-tensor calibration on 1,000 ImageNet/COCO samples. Per-extension speedups: VCONV 7.2×, GEMM 4.2×, RELU 3.0×. VCONV accounts for 60–75% of saved time.

Problems to check before using any numbers:
(1) Architecture is unclear. The title says RISC-V, but the system diagram shows an ARM Cortex-A9 @ 650 MHz driving FPGA accelerators, and VCONV is said to replace about 800 ARM instructions. It is not clear what actually runs the custom instructions.
(2) Resource figures don't agree. The base core is listed as 229 LUTs (0.43%), 0 DSPs and 16×36 Kb BRAM. That BRAM is reported as "256 KB, 5.2%", but 16×36 Kb is about 72 KB, and 16 of 140 blocks is about 11%. The text also mentions a separate 64 KB BRAM. "4.9 MB total" should be 4.9 Mb. The integrated bitstream uses 9.6% LUTs, 8.2% FFs, 40.7% BRAM and 43.6% DSPs (96 of 220, which is consistent). This makes the "0.43% LUTs, minimal resources" claim misleading.
(3) The core and accelerator both run at only 50 MHz, while the CPU runs at 666 MHz.
(4) The accuracy loss is exactly −0.1% for every model, including YOLO Tiny mAP. The FP32 and INT16 absolute values were not in the supplied text.
(5) The statistics don't add up. "15 runs × 2 configurations = 60 inferences" doesn't match 4 models, which would be 120. A single t(14) is reported for all models combined.
(6) Tables III–XI were not in the supplied passages (captions only). So there are no per-model latency, energy, FPS or GOPS values; the table cells are n/r.

Power: 1.85–2.14 W measured with onboard sensors (INA226, 1 kHz). The 1.85 W idle power is subtracted when computing energy.

Toolflow: not stated.

note:
Critical reading: The paper compresses YOLOv8n with iterative L2-norm structured pruning (70% ratio, k=6 steps, 30 fine-tuning epochs per step) and integer quantization, and uses 224x224 inputs. It deploys the result with STM32Cube.AI on an STM32U575ZI (Cortex-M33, 160 MHz) to detect weeds in CropAndWeed (74 species). Caveats:
(1) This is a microcontroller deployment, not an FPGA one. The 'yolo-fpga' axis tag is wrong, so LUT/DSP/BRAM do not apply.
(2) The paper claims 'real-time' detection, but inference takes about 1.5 s per frame and wakes every 30 s. That is duty-cycled monitoring, not real-time.
(3) The passages never state the quantization bit width. They discuss 8-bit only in general terms. Granularity and the PTQ vs QAT choice are also not given.
(4) Accuracy is reported on the 80/20 validation split with no held-out test set. The passages give no accuracy for the uncompressed baseline, so the drop caused by compression cannot be quantified. The pruning figures give only the mAP loss (0.15 at 70%).
(5) Table III compares against GPU/Jetson models at 640x640, which is not like-for-like. Those models' mAP50 above 93% is not comparable to this work's 0.517.
(6) There are internal inconsistencies. Table II lists 3200M parameters for the baseline, but the text says 3.2x10^6. The RAM constraint is given as 768 KB while the SRAM spec is given as 786 KB. The 1.1 mA measured in Stop2 is far above the 8.95 uA datasheet figure, which suggests board-level overhead.
(7) The paper reports energy per inference, not average power. The extracted Table IV text does not give an FPS value, so power_w and fps are left as n/r and no values were derived.

rows.accuracy_metric: Ωbase (Hits@3-based retention) improvement vs Random init (%)
Ωnew (Hits@3-based acquisition) improvement vs Random init (%)

note:
Critical reading note — Pons, Bilalli & Queralt (2025), arXiv 2511.11118. Machine learning / continual learning paper; no hardware.

What the paper proposes: a "Schema" initialization for new entities in continual knowledge graph embedding (KGE) learning. Each new entity starts at the mean of its class centroids, taken from previously learned embeddings. A small random offset is added, scaled by γ times the per-class standard deviation. The method works with any KGE model and any continual learning method.

How it was evaluated:
- Datasets: three datasets derived from FB15K-237 (FBinc-S, FBinc-M and FBinc-L). Each has a base snapshot plus 4 snapshots, growing the triple count by 2%, 12% and 25%. Entity classes come from mapping entities to DBpedia.
- Continual learning methods: fine-tuning, EWC, EMR, LKGE and incDE.
- Baselines: random (Xavier) initialization and model-based initialization (the expected position under TransE).
- Metrics: link prediction MRR and Hits@3, plus Ωbase (knowledge retention) and Ωnew (knowledge acquisition), both computed from Hits@3.
- Protocol: results are averaged over 5 seeds, with Wilcoxon significance tests (appendix).

Claims backed by the supplied text:
- Epochs to convergence drop by a factor of 2.16–2.67 compared with random initialization, for every method except EWC.
- Schema initialization is faster than a single training epoch and scales better than model initialization. No absolute timings are in the passages.
- For TransH, the best model, Ωbase improves by 11%, 4% and 13% and Ωnew by 9%, 46% and 26% on S, M and L.
- For HolE, Ωnew more than doubles.
- The introduction says training can be up to nearly 3× faster with 40% better predictive performance.

Limitations and caveats:
- Tables 1–3 and A1–A4 are only captions in the passages, so no absolute MRR, Hits@3 or Ω values are available.
- The TransH gains are relative percentages, and the text does not say whether they are relative or absolute (percentage-point) gains.
- The method needs a KG schema with class memberships, and here those come from an external DBpedia mapping.
- Initialization of new relations is not handled.
- Evaluation uses only FB15K-237-derived data with small updates.
- Several models are named (RotatE, TransR, ProjE) without numbers.
- No hardware, power or FPGA metrics, so all hardware fields are n/r.

Benchmark rows: the rows cover the only explicit numeric model–dataset results in the passages: TransH with fine-tuning on FBinc-S, Schema vs Random initialization, as relative improvement percentages. Confidence is medium because the tables were not available.

note:
What it is: an empirical study of on-device inference on an Android phone with a Kryo CPU (8 cores), a GPU and an NPU, using LiteRT. It compares CPU single-thread (CPU-SC), CPU multithread (CPU-MC), GPU in FP32 and FP16 modes, and NPU, across these precision variants: FP32, FP16, INT8, FINT8, INT16, FINT16 and dynamic. Models tested: ResNet18/50 (classification) and YOLOv8/YOLO11 (detection). The reference for all speed-up and accuracy comparisons is FP32 on a single CPU thread.

Main claims from the passages:
1. INT16 variants have very high latency, so the authors drop them from further analysis.
2. The NPU is the fastest device, then the GPU, then the CPU. On ResNet50 with INT8, the NPU is more than 120x faster than CPU-SC.
3. Dynamic quantization is much slower on the NPU. The authors say this is because mixed precisions force casts on the CPU and data transfers between the NPU and CPU.
4. Multithreaded CPU tops out at 3.4x (INT8 on 8 cores), which the authors attribute to the asymmetric core design.
5. On the GPU, quantization barely changes speed. Switching to FP16 mode gives close to 2x.
6. ResNet18 Top-1 is about 69 for most variants, but FINT8 collapses to 0.08.

Critical points:
- The passages contain only captions for Tables I–XVI, not their values. No absolute latency in ms, FPS, power or mAP numbers can be extracted, and the rows below record the few values stated in the prose.
- The SoC and phone model are not named in the passages (only "Kryo CPU"), and the dataset is not stated (ImageNet/COCO are likely but unconfirmed).
- The FINT8 collapse to 0.08 looks like a conversion or calibration failure, not a real limit of 8-bit quantization. The authors exclude it instead of diagnosing it.
- The ">120x" figure combines two changes at once: the device (NPU vs CPU-SC) and the precision (INT8 vs the FP32 baseline).
- The metadata axis "yolo-fpga" looks wrong. There is no FPGA; this is mobile CPU/GPU/NPU work, so LUT, DSP and BRAM do not apply.
- Metadata is flagged as needing manual checking.

note: hls4ml is an open-source compiler-style toolflow. It parses models from front ends (Keras 2/3, QKeras, HGQ/HGQ2, PyTorch, ONNX/QONNX) into an internal representation, runs optimizer passes on it, and generates HLS code through back ends for Vitis/Vivado, oneAPI/Quartus and Catapult. Critical reading: (1) The reported FPGA results are out-of-context place-and-route results on AMD parts (XCVU9P, XCVU13P, XC7A35T). There are no on-board measurements and no power figures. The Evaluation section mentions Agilex7/oneAPI results, but no such numbers appear in the supplied passages. (2) Throughput is implied only by II = 1 at the achieved clock; FPS and GOPS are never reported. (3) The QKeras baselines are cited from earlier work (e.g. [31], [2]) and were not rerun under the same tool versions. The HGQ rows are Pareto points regularized with different beta values, and per-layer bit-widths are not given. (4) The table extraction is noisy. The block labeled Table 4 appears to merge Table 3 (5 ns clock, with II column) with the true Table 4 (1 GHz target, with Fmax column). I therefore took the extracted rows from the cleaner Table 5 and Table 9. (5) The DA strategy (da4ml) removes all DSP usage and often lowers latency. It does not support RF > 1, and its benefit may shrink when high precision is needed. (6) The ASIC results (Catapult, 28 nm: 0.81 mm2 for the 2D variant, 0.39 mm2 for the 1D variant, <1 uW/pixel) are estimates or come from prior work. (7) The authors acknowledge that HLS output can be up to 2x worse than hand-mapped Verilog, that feature support is uneven across back ends, and that HLS compilation of large models can fail. Example: the Latency-strategy model with the highest accuracy failed placement on the XC7A35T.

note: Critical reading: The paper adds a new hls4ml backend (released in hls4ml v1.3.0) that targets Microchip SmartHLS, so hls4ml can now generate designs for flash-based, radiation-hard PolarFire FPGAs. It demonstrates the backend with a 32→2 dense autoencoder encoder (ReLU) that compresses PicoCal calorimeter pulses into two 10-bit latent values. Quantization-aware training (QKeras) uses <16,9> inputs, <10,4> weights and biases, and <10,7> activations. The quantization scan shows reconstruction MSE levelling off at about 10 bits. The 10-bit multiplications map to 4-input LUTs, so no 18x18 math blocks are used. Timing: post-synthesis fmax is 200 MHz for the full model and 300 MHz for the nano model, against a 160 MHz target. II is 3–4 cycles, so a new input can be accepted every 25 ns, which meets the 40 MHz bunch-crossing rate. Latency is 25 ns (4 cycles) for the nano-FPGA model and 150 ns for the full model. These latencies are reported only in ns, so latency_ms is n/r to avoid converting units. Resources: about 1% of LUTs/FFs per channel. The nano model on the MPF100T uses 3.10% of 4-input LUTs, which scales to about 25% for 8 channels. That figure is a percentage, not a count, so the luts column is n/r. Physics results: CFD timestamp residual σ is 0.15 for the autoencoder versus 0.13 for direct regression. The CFD timestamp resolution is slightly better on the reconstructed pulses than on the original 32-sample pulses. Caveats: (1) Table 1's actual numbers are not in the supplied passages, so absolute LUT/FF/BRAM counts are unknown. (2) Most results are post-synthesis or co-simulation. Only the MPF300TS was run on hardware, and the paper says only that it 'agrees' with co-simulation, without giving separate numbers in these passages. (3) No power is reported. (4) The model is tiny (a single dense layer), so it shows the toolflow works rather than stress-testing it. (5) The data are Geant4 simulations with a hand-picked downsampling from 1024 to 32 samples, and timing validation covers front-pulse seed cells only. (6) The 'nano' model's lower internal precision is not fully specified in these passages. (7) There is no radiation testing; radiation tolerance is argued from the flash configuration memory alone.

note:
Critical reading note: Leftheriotis et al. present an open-source FPGA accelerator for LSTM autoencoders (LSTM-AEs) on a ZCU104 board (XCZU7EV). It uses a dataflow design in which each LSTM layer is its own module and the modules talk through FIFOs. This lets different layers work on different timesteps at the same time ("temporal parallelism"). The paper balances the pipeline by choosing reuse factors so every layer takes about the same time per timestep. It gives a closed-form latency model: T times the slowest stage's per-timestep latency, plus the pipeline fill time.

The authors compared four models (F32/F64 wide, D2/D6 deep) on sequences of 1 to 64 timesteps. Baselines were a Xeon Gold 5218R CPU and a V100 GPU, both running PyTorch JIT-compiled code, averaged over 1000 inferences. Reported gains: latency up to 79.6x faster than CPU and 18.2x faster than GPU; energy per timestep up to 1722x lower than CPU and 59.3x lower than GPU. Adding depth scales well: going from F64-D2 to F64-D6 at 64 timesteps raises FPGA latency about 1.4x, versus 2.9x on CPU and 2.2x on GPU.

Caveats:
1. The passages never state numeric precision, the quantization scheme, the clock frequency, or the toolflow. Neither is any HLS tool named.
2. Only the column headers of Table 1 (resource utilization) survived extraction. No LUT/FF/BRAM/DSP percentages are available. The only reuse-factor detail given is that F32 models use RHm=1 and F64 models use 4 or 8.
3. Tables 2 and 3 were flattened. The six rows per model presumably cover 1 to 64 timesteps, but only the first (1) and last (64) row labels can be inferred with confidence.
4. Several FPGA energy values are missing from the flattened Table 3.
5. FPGA power is given only as a range, 11-12 W, without saying whether it is board or chip power. It is therefore recorded as n/r in the rows.
6. No anomaly-detection accuracy or dataset is reported, so the paper's value for real-time anomaly detection is not shown.
7. The GPU baseline at 1 timestep is dominated by launch overhead, which inflates the small-sequence speedups.
8. The speedup comparison is between a single-board FPGA and PyTorch on server hardware, with no comparison to other FPGA LSTM accelerators such as SHARP.
9. Extraction warnings flag the metadata for manual checking.

MERS (Multiple Embedding Replay Selection; Yanowsky & Weinshall, arXiv 2604.08336) changes how replay-based class-incremental learning picks exemplars for its buffer. It combines a supervised embedding with a self-supervised one (SimCLR, VICReg or DINOv2) in one weighted multi-group maximum k-coverage objective. It comes in two variants, MERS ProbCover and MERS MaxHerding. Per-embedding RBF bandwidths use the median heuristic. Per-embedding weights come from a k-NN density ratio. Because the objective is monotone submodular, greedy selection keeps the (1-1/e) approximation guarantee. The paper tests MERS with ER, ER-ACE and ER-ACE-STAR on Split CIFAR-100 (buffer 100-1000) and Split TinyImageNet (buffer 200-6000). Baselines are Random, Herding, Rainbow Memory, TEAL, ProbCover and MaxHerding. Reported metrics are FAA (final average accuracy) and AAA (average accuracy across all tasks). The authors claim MERS is best across buffers, replay methods and datasets, with the largest gains at 1000 exemplars or fewer, where the gap narrows as the buffer grows. They also say stability is higher and forgetting lower. A theoretical argument (equal-volume Gaussian proxies with a KL gap, framed as domain adaptation) says self-supervised geometry should make selection more robust to new classes.

Critical points:
(1) The table extracts for Tables 1 and 2 (CIFAR-100, ER-ACE-STAR and ER-ACE) have lost their column headers. For example, the |M|=1000 row of Table 1 reads 60.03 / 64.17 / 63.92 / 65.54 / 61.50 / 64.05, with max 65.54, but no value can be tied to a method. The bold-face marking of the best result was also lost. So the headline claims cannot be checked from these passages.
(2) The main FAA results are only in figures (Figs. 2-4), and the full tables are in appendices that were not supplied.
(3) The self-supervised encoder is retrained from scratch every episode, or DINOv2 is used as a frozen, externally pretrained model. The claim of "no added model parameters" hides this compute and memory cost, and DINOv2 brings in outside pretraining data. No selection runtime is reported.
(4) The theory relies on stylized Gaussian proxies, not on measured embedding statistics.
(5) The text says "Herding (Welling, 2009...)" but also credits ProbCover to Bae et al. rather than Yehuda et al. This looks like a citation slip.

No hardware or FPGA measurements appear (no FPS, GOPS, latency, power or resource use). This is a pure algorithmic continual-learning paper and does not fit the hardware benchmark schema. No rows are given: the only numbers are accuracies that cannot be tied to a method, and turning them into rows would mean guessing which method each belongs to.

MF-CKGE (Qi et al., arXiv 2604.10947) is a continual knowledge graph embedding method for link prediction. It is not a hardware or accelerator paper. The passages report no FPGA, ASIC or GPU implementation and no platform, FPS, GOPS, power, LUT, DSP or BRAM figures, so I extracted no benchmark rows.

Method: during offline learning, each new snapshot gets its own frozen embedding space ("temporal decoupling"). Embeddings whose similarity to an earlier embedding is at or above a threshold θ are replaced by a pointer to that earlier embedding ("semantic decoupling"). During online inference, the score from each snapshot is weighted by a softmax over the mean of the top-k similarities between the query relation and the candidate relations. The base model is TransE with dimension 200 and the Adam optimizer. Learning rate, batch size, α and η are chosen from small grids.

Claims: across 8 datasets, MF-CKGE is on average (maximum) 1.7% (2.7%) better in MRR, 1.3% (3.0%) in Hits@1 and 1.4% (3.8%) in Hits@10 than the best baseline. The baselines are IncDE, LKGE, FastKGE, EWC, SI, PNN, CWR, GEM, EMR and DiCGRL, plus Retrain.

Critical points:
(1) Only relative gains appear in the passages. The absolute MRR and Hits values in Tables 2, 3 and 4–7 were lost in extraction; only the captions survive. It is also unclear whether "%" means absolute points or relative change.
(2) The gains over the strongest regularization baseline are small: as low as 0.8 MRR and 0.4 Hits@10. The passages mention no variance, seeds or significance tests.
(3) The paper says MF-CKGE "surpasses Retrain on certain metrics" only for FB-CKGE and GraphHigher, where it is 0.1 MRR and 0.4 Hits@1 higher. That margin is small.
(4) Efficiency claims: training on S5 of FB-CKGE takes 46 s versus 899 s for Retrain (19× faster). These are training times, not inference latency, and no hardware platform is given. Memory is reported in GB in a figure, but those values were not extracted.
(5) Storing one embedding space per snapshot grows memory with the number of snapshots. The redundancy pruning depends on θ, and the passages do not give the final memory cost.
(6) The per-entity knowledge-domain count rising from 2.7 to 5.4 comes from the HYBRID dataset only (Figure 1).

Metadata issues: the listed venue is "arXiv preprint", but the text says SIGIR '26 (Melbourne), DOI 10.1145/3805712.3809683. The extraction flagged "aucune section détectée" (no sections detected), so every passage except Abstract is labelled "(préambule)". The Table 1 dataset statistics are garbled.

Why no rows: none of the passages reports a measured hardware result. The only absolute numbers are training times, and filling latency_ms would need a unit conversion (s to ms), which the instructions forbid. Recommendation: find the original PDF to recover the Table 2/3 values before filling in the paper-fiche.

rows.platform: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Broadcom BCM2711, quad-core Cortex-A72 @ 1.8GHz, 8 GB LPDDR4), CPU-only

note: Critical reading: This is a systems/prototype paper, not an FPGA accelerator paper. The auto-assigned axis 'yolo-fpga' looks wrong: the platform is a CPU-only Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (BCM2711, quad-core Cortex-A72 @ 1.8 GHz, 8 GB LPDDR4), with no FPGA or NPU. The contribution is a lean multi-agent architecture. A deterministic event-driven core router links four agents: a vision agent (a YOLO 'n' detector plus a passive IoU-based tracker), a reporting agent (a local Ollama LLM), and communication and control agents (a Slack chatbot). The authors present this as a lightweight alternative to LLM-driven orchestration such as OpenClaw. The evaluation is mostly qualitative: live street and indoor scenes, no named dataset, no detection accuracy metric, no power figures, and CPU load shown only in a figure (Fig. 7). The only hardware number in the passages: the full configuration (yolov8n + llama3.2:1b, all agents local) ran at 'less then 3 fps' at 640x480. The fps cell holds 3, but it is an upper bound, not a point measurement. Tested models were yolo26n, yolo11n, yolo12n, yolov5nu, yolo5su and yolov8n. yolov8n was judged best for tracking reliability because larger models lowered the frame rate and forced tracker re-initialisations. LLMs tested were tinyllama (637 MB), llama3.2:1b (1.3 GB), gemma3 (3.3 GB) and kimi-k2.5:cloud. llama3.2:1b gave the best quality/speed trade-off locally, but notifications were delayed and some were lost to timeouts. The cloud LLM gave the best results. The authors conclude that fully centralized local operation works but is not suitable for latency-critical notification, and that OpenClaw-style orchestration needs an external LLM. The code is not yet released, and the metadata extraction was flagged for manual checking.

rows.accuracy_metric: relative MRR drop when accounting for entity interference (%)
rows.baseline: MRR under standard protocol without entity interference (MRR w/o)

note:
Pons et al. (arXiv 2604.19401, 2026) study continual knowledge graph embedding (CKGE). It is not a hardware or FPGA paper: none of the supplied passages report a platform, throughput, latency, power or resource figures.

Main claim: the usual CKGE evaluation ranks old test triples only against the entities that existed at that snapshot. This works like a task-incremental setup and ignores "entity interference", where newly added entities get ranked above the correct answer. The authors propose a corrected protocol that uses the current entity set for all test snapshots. They say the old protocol overestimates performance by up to 25%, mainly on datasets where the number of entities grows a lot (entity growth from first to last snapshot: GraphHigher 1516%, GraphEqual 400%, ENTITY 400%). The effect is small where growth is small (PS-CKGE 7%, RELATION 26%). On ENTITY, retraining loses 11% when interference is counted. It goes from being beaten by 5 of 7 CKGE methods to being the best method.

They also propose a forgetting metric with weighting over CL cycles and test-set size, normalised by θ_{i,i}. Their conclusions: entity interference is the main source of forgetting when entity growth is high, and representation drift dominates when growth is low. Translational KGE models are more stable; semantic models adapt better but forget more.

Setup: 8 benchmarks (ENTITY, RELATION, FACT, HYBRID, GraphEqual, GraphHigher, GraphLower, PS-CKGE). TransE is the base model for all CKGE methods, with embedding dimension fixed at 200 and the original authors' hyperparameters.

Critical points:
- The MRR tables (Tables 3–4, the forgetting-metric table and the KGE-model table) are garbled in the extraction and have no usable numbers. Absolute MRR values could not be recorded.
- The "25%" and "11%" figures are relative drops. They are not absolute accuracy.
- The equation for the forgetting metric is only partly extracted.
- Hyperparameters were reused from the original papers rather than retuned under the corrected protocol, which may favour some methods.
- Only TransE is used for the CKGE method comparison.
- Metadata extraction was flagged for manual check.

One row is included for the only clearly stated measured result (retraining on ENTITY). All hardware fields are n/r.

note: ImageHD (FCCM 2026) is an accelerator for unsupervised continual learning on a ZCU104 FPGA, built with Vitis HLS 2024.2 and clocked at 300 MHz. Its pipeline has four stages: an INT8 post-training-quantized MobileNetV2 feature extractor, HDC ID-level encoding with word-packed binary hypervectors, Hamming similarity search, and a single-tier bounded cluster memory. That memory is consolidated with Top-M kMeans++ in place of the spectral clustering used in [11]. Key results (Table VII, batch 1, end to end): on CORe50 the FPGA takes 0.48 ms per image (2097.05 img/s) at 3.7 W, or 1.76 mJ/img. That is 40× lower latency and 383× better energy efficiency than an EPYC 7763 CPU. It also beats an RTX A4000 GPU (2.31 ms, 184.80 mJ/img) and a Jetson AGX Orin (13.14 ms, 77.5 mJ/img). On CIFAR-10 it takes 0.27 ms (3703.70 img/s) at 3.6 W, or 0.97 mJ/img. Resources (Table II): 143,927 LUTs (62%), 126 DSPs (7%), 322 BRAM18K (52%) and 57 URAMs. Critical points: (1) FPGA latency and power come from the 'integrated analyzer' and tools in the Vitis Unified IDE, not board-level instruments. This suggests tool-estimated rather than measured power, while the CPU and GPU figures come from powertop and nvidia-smi, so the comparison is not like-for-like. (2) The comparisons with prior work in Table IV use different datasets. For example, the 19.7× gain over [11] divides [11]'s CIFAR-100 result on a Jetson TX2 by ImageHD's CORe50 result, and ILOC excludes feature extraction. The paper itself says accuracy comparisons are not applicable. (3) Absolute clustering quality is low: with INT8, ACC is about 0.19–0.27 and NMI about 0.06–0.13. 'Without sacrificing accuracy' holds on average but hides a real drop in CORe50 purity, from 0.2732 (FP32) to 0.1707 (INT8). (4) GOPS is not reported. (5) The paper does not say whether resource use differs by dataset; Table II gives only one design.

rows.toolflow: stand-alone VTA compiler (ONNX -> VTA IR -> binaries), Strategy 4 partitioning: 10.8M instructions, 9.1M UOPs
rows.baseline: ONNX Runtime (±1 differences on up to 35% of outputs); NumPy reference (bit-accurate)

note:
What it shows: the authors (Airbus/ONERA) extend their stand-alone VTA compiler, built with DO-178C certification in mind, so that it can compile a whole network. It now handles matrices larger than the SRAM by partitioning them, and it automates the data reshaping between layers. It is tested on a quantized YOLO-NAS with 146 ONNX operators. 108 of them (QLinearConv, QLinearMul, MaxPool) run on the VTA and 38 fall back to the CPU because they need floating point. Compiling with Strategy 4 takes about 2 minutes and produces about 10.8M instructions and 9.1M UOPs. A run in the functional C++ simulator takes about 3 minutes.

What it does not show: nothing runs on an FPGA, and there is no cycle-accurate measurement. There are no FPS, latency, throughput, power or resource-use numbers (LUT/DSP/BRAM), and no detection accuracy on a dataset. The only correctness check is a bit-by-bit comparison on random int8 inputs over 10 runs. Output matches a NumPy reference written to follow the ONNX maths exactly. Against ONNX Runtime, values are mostly off by ±1 on up to 35% of outputs, which the authors blame on ONNX Runtime's QLinearConv optimisations.

Critical points:
1. Table 2 shows Strategy 3 gives the fewest instructions (6,348,149) and Strategy 4 the most (10,765,279), yet the pipeline figures quoted use Strategy 4. The paper also admits that instruction count does not predict VTA latency, so no strategy is shown to be better in practice.
2. Memory cost is dominated by biases being expanded into full matrices: 297 MiB versus 33 KiB of ONNX biases for YOLO-NAS, plus 93 MiB of instructions. That is a serious problem for embedded use.
3. Most of the simulation time goes to CPU-side data shuffling, and floating-point rescaling limits what can be offloaded.
4. The text is inconsistent: the introduction says int32 inputs, weights and biases, while the experiments use int8 inputs.

Text-extraction problems:
- Exponents were flattened: "228" means 2^28, and "25×27" means 2^5×2^7.
- The strategy labels are missing from Tables 2 and 3. I assumed the rows are Strategies 1 to 4 in order.
- In Table 3 Case 3, the same value (32,845, +1406.0%) appears twice, which may be an extraction error.
- The "Compiled" label is missing from the bias row of Table 1.

About the single row: it records a functional-simulation result, not a measured hardware benchmark, so every hardware field is n/r.

note:
FastOmniTMAE changes how Omni TM-AE (a Tsetlin Machine autoencoder for static word embeddings) is trained. It removes the global class_sum/weight step, so clauses can be evaluated and updated in parallel and locally. It also adds a custom HDL IP accelerator (AXI-Lite control, AXI-MM DDR access, BRAM buffers, FSM) for Zynq-7000 (Zybo) and Zynq UltraScale+ (ZCU104).

**Results (Table 2):** on RG65 with 44 tokens, 8,000 examples per token, 32 clauses, T=20000 and s=1.0, the training times were:
- ZCU104 with 12 engines: 119.9±0.9 s, versus 848.7 s on its single ARM core (7.08×), with RG65 ρ=0.696.
- Zybo with 2 engines: 657.4±1.1 s, versus 3667.5 s on its ARM core (5.58×), with ρ=0.669.

**Limitations:**
1. Speedups are only measured against a single embedded ARM core. A single-threaded Core i9 CPU (57.7 s) and the H100 host CPU (87.3 s) are both faster than the ZCU104 FPGA.
2. No power, energy, clock frequency or LUT/DSP/BRAM figures appear in these passages; resource use is deferred to Appendix A.4, which was not supplied. Claims of a "small footprint" and "lower power" are therefore not quantified here.
3. The FPGA RG65 ρ values (0.696 and 0.669) are higher than the DGX CPU result in Table 1 (0.656), but the setups differ (8,000 vs 2,000 examples per token), so they cannot be compared directly.
4. Other claims:
   - The GPU slowdowns (CUDA 0.18×, OpenCL 0.22–0.29×) are explained as a mismatch between GPU architecture and the TM's logic operations. The passages do not include profiling to support this.
   - The DGX CPU speedup over Omni TM-AE is only 1.2× (242.9 s vs 293.1 s). The abstract's "up to 5×" figure is for classification and is not visible in these passages.

rows.task: Federated continual NER across domains under user-level DP (replay-release ε=4)
rows.baseline: CSLR-OptimalTransport 44.7; CSLR-Hungarian 44.1; FedCIL+DP 40.6; DP-SGD (no replay) 37.7; non-private FedTA 50.8

note:
CSLR (Canonicalized Stable-List Replay) is a way to release replay data under user-level DP in federated continual learning. Each client releases a small DP list of candidate replay distributions (Gaussians) over frozen sentence embeddings, such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with d=384 or BERT-base token embeddings for NER. The server uses log-density signatures at public anchor sentences to tell the unordered list elements apart. It then aggregates clipped sufficient statistics per canonical mode with secure aggregation and Gaussian noise. The theory claims that O(log(N/η)/p) anchors are enough under an anchor-signature margin. The non-identifiability result is scoped to an unordered-label oracle model, and the authors say coordinate-space Hungarian and OT baselines fall outside it. Results cover four benchmarks (Split-AG-News, Split-Amazon, OntoNotes-Domain NER, MultiWOZ-Intent) over five seeds. The authors state a gain of 3.9–5.6 average-accuracy points over the strongest non-CSLR DP baseline at ε=4, and 3.0–4.0 points over CSLR-OptimalTransport.

Critical points:
(1) The privacy guarantee covers only replay release. DP-SGD's ε is not budget-equivalent to it, and task-head updates are not privatized, so the setup is not end-to-end private.
(2) The Table 2 caption does not state ε. ε=4 comes from the main-text description.
(3) In the extracted tables, a second baseline row has no label (57.4/48.6/43.0/49.9 in Table 2). Given the baselines listed, it is probably DP-Stat-Share, but this should be checked against the PDF.
(4) Standard deviations are small (0.3–0.9) across five seeds. Effect-size CIs are deferred to Appendix H, which was not supplied.
(5) The frozen-encoder assumption limits scope, and anchors must be fixed before any private release.
(6) This is not a hardware paper: there are no FPGA, latency, throughput or power measurements, so every hardware field is n/r.
(7) Extraction metadata is flagged as unverified and no sections were detected. All passages except the Abstract are under '(préambule)'.

No platform is given for that measurement. Table 7 names its speed platforms (CPU ONNX on a Xeon @ 2.00 GHz, and T4 TensorRT10), but the passages contain none of its numbers. They also give no absolute latency, FPS, power or resource figures.

Accuracy claims:
- Removing DFL costs 0.6 AP (47.0 to 46.4). L1 loss, STAL and the backbone/neck refinement (+0.2 each) bring it back to the same accuracy. The 47.0 total is my own arithmetic from these steps; the text only says 'same accuracy'.

rows.model: ResNet-18 (final model after 10 tasks, frozen backbone + new linear head)
rows.baseline: Task 0 checkpoint accuracy 0.548; final model accuracy 0.000

note: Main claim: catastrophic forgetting is mostly a loss of access to task knowledge (the output pathway), not erasure of what the network stored. Setup: ResNet-18 trained from random initialization on Split CIFAR-100 (10 tasks of 10 classes), plain SGD with cross-entropy, no replay or regularization, with a checkpoint saved after each task. Task 0 results: accuracy drops from 0.548 to 0.000. The linear probe on Layer 4 drops from 0.616 to 0.468, which is 76% retention. The Accessibility Gap (probe accuracy minus task accuracy in the final model) is 0.468 − 0.000 = 0.468. Freezing the backbone and training a new linear head on Task 0 data gives 0.415, which is 75.7% of 0.548. Probes on Layers 1–3 keep 100–104% of their checkpoint accuracy, so the loss sits in Layer 4 and the classifier. Projection energy keeps rising as K grows, and the paper reports strong subspace rotation. Critical points: (1) There is no control such as a probe or head reset on a randomly initialized or untrained frozen ResNet-18. Random convolutional features alone can reach well above chance on 10-way CIFAR, so 'recovery' is not separated from relearning, because the new head is trained on Task 0 data. (2) There is only one run, with no seeds or variance reported, and only Task 0 is analysed in depth. (3) The checkpoint 'persistence' result in Table II holds by construction: stored weights keep their accuracy, which says nothing about the final model. (4) The starting accuracy of 0.548 is low. (5) Most table cells were lost in extraction; the numbers above come from the prose. The extraction metadata also flags the paper details for manual checking. None of these passages report hardware results (no platform, throughput, power or resource figures), so all hardware fields are n/r. The two rows record the paper's main accuracy measurements.

note:
What the paper does: it packs several arbitrary-bitwidth signed or unsigned operands into one DSP multiplier input. The packing uses the DSP pre-adder: sign bits are subtracted as D − A, so no fabric adders are needed. It builds two FINN-integrated architectures on this. SDV packs one multiplier input for matrix-vector multiplication (MVM). It tracks lane spill-over with a modulo-4 reference computed in fractured LUTs, and needs lane size L ≥ wa + wb − 1. BSEG packs both inputs for convolutions and biases each lane with 2^(L−1) guard offsets.

Evaluation setup: out-of-context Vivado 2025.2 synthesis targeting a ZCU104 (DSP48E2). The target clock was 250 MHz. Table IV compares maximum frequency: 580 MHz for the FINN baseline vs 590 MHz for BSEG.

Headline claims:
- For UltraNet INT4 at 416×416, BSEG uses 21% fewer LUTs and gets 36% more FPS/DSP than FINN, where the FINN baseline already uses SDV.
- On convolution layers only, BSEG uses 27% fewer LUTs than HiKonv, 29% more DSPs, and gets 25% more FPS/DSP.
- On the base convolution layer, BSEG uses 63% fewer LUTs and 25% fewer DSPs.

Caveats:
1. All results are post-synthesis only. There are no on-board measurements of throughput or power, and no accuracy is reported.
2. Table II is garbled in the extraction. The LUT row (43k/48k/63k/50k–46k/35k–31k) and the FPS/DSP row (0.7/1.2/1.1/1.5/1.5) were matched to designs by cross-checking against the percentages in the text. Absolute FPS and DSP counts are not recoverable.
3. The comparison with HiKonv and Base [21] is not like-for-like. Those works targeted the Ultra96 at 160×320 input, while this paper uses ZCU104 at 416×416.
4. BSEG only pays off in the first three UltraNet layers; SDV is better for the others. This is because FINN's input generator becomes costly when there are many input channels.
5. The frequency passage also contains a stray 17761. It is not tied to any metric, so it was not used.

**Reported results:**
- **Detection:** 93.6 AP and 92.2 recall at IoU ≥ 0.5 on SL-LPR, with 9.9 ms per frame on the FPGA.
- **Character recognition:** 97.42 character-level accuracy and 87.88 plate-level accuracy on SL-LPR, with 4.0 ms per plate on the FPGA.

- The passages do not give LUT, DSP or BRAM use, bitwidths, clock frequency or GOPS.
- The 4.2 W figure has no stated measurement scope (chip or board), so it is marked unspecified.
- 11.5 FPS is derived from a worst-case 87 ms at 10 plates. It is not a measured average, and the paper says it holds "in most urban road scenarios."
- The abstract says "93.6% mAP," but the results section calls it AP.
- Speed comparisons with other work use latencies copied from the original papers, on different hardware (CPU, GPU, FPGA). They are not reproduced under the same conditions.
- The Table V and VI accuracy values for PKU, UFPR-ALPR, AOLP and Arg-plate did not survive text extraction, so they are omitted here.
- The only same-platform comparison is Li et al.: 50 ms per plate on the KV260, which the authors say is about 12× slower but more accurate.
- Table VII gives the per-step latencies for the Xeon and Cortex-A53 CPU-only runs, but their values did not survive extraction. Only the KV260 column is available.

**Row choices:** I recorded two rows, the end-to-end system and the detection model. The character recognition numbers are in the note only.

They also approximate C2PSA spatial attention: parallel 1x1 Q/K/V convolutions, a scaled element-wise q⊙k product, and hard-sigmoid in place of softmax. The models are quantized to INT8 with post-training quantization and tested on six datasets and all eight DPU sizes (B512–B4096).

Main results (IV. RESULTS): YOLOv26n and YOLOv26n-OBB have the best end-to-end performance on B4096: 34.05 and 29.55 FPS, with 29.37 and 33.85 ms latency. These were measured on one DPU core using the PETS2009-S2L1 video (768×576), not on the accuracy datasets.

(2) The accuracy loss figures disagree. The abstract and conclusion say about 5% absolute loss from quantization, but the results section says about 7% on average across datasets for the attention-based variants. Some cases are much worse, for example YOLOv8n on KITTI: 0.64 to 0.34.
(3) Tables I and II disagree slightly (YOLOv8n KITTI modified: 0.63 vs 0.64 on CPU).
(4) The DPU-only FPS and latency are shown only in Figs. 6–8, which were not supplied. The large gap between DPU and end-to-end speed is blamed on Python post-processing and NMS on the ARM, so end-to-end FPS mostly reflects software, not the accelerator.
(5) The B1152 resource row looks odd: 38 BRAM, compared with 76 for B1024.
(6) GOPS is not reported, and accuracy is given only as mAP@0.5:0.95.

The rows below pair each model's FPGA mAP (COCO for the standard model, DOTA for the OBB model) with the throughput measured on PETS2009. They also use the design-level B4096 resources and power. These mixed pairings are why confidence is medium.

The second is a fully quantum QAE with 23 parameters, scored from trash-wire z-scores. Both were synthesized for an Alveo U200 with a 5.5 ns target clock, using ap_fixed formats listed in Table 1. The reported latencies are 6.1 µs for the hybrid VAE and 0.47 µs for the QAE, and both fit in one SLR. I left latency_ms as n/r because the paper reports these values in µs and the instructions do not allow unit conversion. The authors therefore argue that TPR@1e-5 is the more reliable metric. (4) The design was tuned by an agentic AI loop (Claude Code) that minimized latency under a one-SLR resource limit. (5) To keep emulation manageable, the 10 jets are split into two 5-qubit registers of 32 amplitudes each. This limits entanglement, and correlator measurements are used to partly recover the lost information. SAT-Edge-Agent (He & Xu, arXiv 2608.03728, 2026) is a systems paper about hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) orchestration. It is not a detector or FPGA paper. A FastAPI agent runs on a COTS ARM heterogeneous edge SoC (8x Cortex-A55 up to 2304 MHz, 31 GiB memory, Debian 11 on aarch64) with an NPU. The agent coordinates a local OpenAI-compatible LLM and a project-internal YOLO-style oriented-bounding-box (OBB) detector labelled "YOLO26". The paper says this label is not a public detector family. The detector runs at image size 1024 with object threshold 0.25 and NMS threshold 0.45.

Critical points:
- The authors say explicitly that there is no accuracy benchmark, no validated geolocation error, no calibrated energy result and no flight readiness.
- n=20 on two fixed images is too few to describe the latency distribution for FAIR1M as a whole.
- The detector weights, exact board vendor and exact LLM are private.
- A factor-of-two aggregation bug meant the substage fields had to be excluded.
- The Table 10 plug-meter power values are not in the supplied passages, so power is n/r.

Survey (arXiv 2608.21657, 2026) of 25 FPGA compression–hardware co-design case studies from 2015–2026. The authors sort them into a five-category taxonomy based on which FPGA resource each technique mainly changes: (A) removes DSPs, (B) repurposes DSPs or uses mixed precision, (C) exploits sparsity, (D) targets the memory hierarchy, (E) works at the toolchain or deployment level. Table I puts every study into the same columns: compression ratio, accuracy change, throughput, energy efficiency, DSP/LUT/BRAM usage and baseline. The main finding is that only 1 of 25 works reports compression ratio and accuracy change against one common baseline. Only 2 report energy efficiency against a common GPU baseline. - The FPGA-only, resource-level focus goes deeper than the cross-platform survey by Deng et al.
- Missing values are marked explicitly: N/R for not reported, N/A for not applicable, and a dash for ASIC studies.
- The authors say plainly that the literature search was targeted and not systematic (not PRISMA), so the meta-analytic counts describe these 25 studies, not the whole field.

Weaknesses and caveats:
- The survey produces no new measurements. Every hardware number is taken from the cited primary papers and should be checked against them.
- ASIC studies (NullHop, Eyeriss, the HLS4ML 65 nm energy figure) sit in the same table as FPGA studies, which makes comparisons harder.
- Studies were placed in categories by the authors' judgement, and some span two categories (for example FlightLLM).
- The extracted text of Table I is garbled: columns run together, and the DSP cell for the FINN row is broken.

note:
This is not a hardware paper. It is about continual knowledge graph embedding (KGE) and reports no FPS, GOPS, latency, power or FPGA resource figures, so every hardware field is n/r. The two rows below are accuracy results only.

Claim: when new entities are added, they compete with the known answers to old queries. The paper calls this candidate-set interference and says it is a source of rank loss separate from catastrophic forgetting. It proposes Meor, a one-sided squared-hinge regularizer. Meor compares a smoothed measure of how strongly new entities score above the answer against old entities that are matched on structure without looking at model scores.

Main evidence (ENTITY–ComplEx, 8 paired runs):
- Absolute historical current-universe MRR (H_cur) is 0.0887, the highest in Table 2.
- The gain over replay is 0.0057 (one-sided 95% lower bound 0.0052). Almost all of it comes from a 0.0055 drop in interference (D_MCI); old-universe MRR changes by only 0.0002.
- Gains over persistent calibration, the matched-maximum control (MMR) and the unmatched-reference control (UOR) are 0.0071, 0.0051 and 0.0045.
- In the transfer study, all 10 FBInc-S/L host and backbone settings improve, with gains of about 0.0020–0.0032 and every CI excluding zero.

Critical points:
1. The effects are small in absolute terms. 0.0057 MRR is about 6% relative on a base of about 0.089. The overall MRR level is low.
2. During refinement, old embeddings are frozen and only new parameters are updated. That setup favours the interference framing and limits how far the result generalises to hosts that update all parameters.
3. Newcomer acquisition (A_TN) goes slightly down in every transfer setting (−0.0001 to −0.0015). It stays within the paper's own −0.005 preservation margin, but that margin was chosen by the authors.
4. The CIs are unadjusted per-cell intervals, not family-wise.
5. Persistent calibration beats Meor on A_TN by 0.0038. H_old and D_MCI were not recorded for calibration.
6. The authors say the intervention is inactive on WN-CKGE, so claims are limited to ENTITY and FBInc.
7. Most numbers in Tables 2–5 did not survive PDF extraction. The absolute H_old, D_MCI and A_TN values are missing and need checking against the PDF.
8. The metadata and axes are flagged for manual verification.

note:
What the paper is: a proton-irradiation reliability study, not a performance paper. The device is a Tensil TCU (16×16 systolic array, 100 MHz, 16-bit fixed-point FP16BP8) running ResNet-20 for CIFAR-10 on an Avnet Ultra96-V2 (XCZU3EG Zynq UltraScale+). It runs under PYNQ Linux v2.7. The beam came from the AIC-144 cyclotron at IFJ PAN at nominal 20, 40 and 58 MeV, using a small (~2-cm) and a wide (~4-cm) field.

Main results:
- Total fluence was 6.19×10^10 p/cm2. 92 blocks were launched and 83 completed (8300 inferences). Class records were kept for only 62 blocks (6200 inferences).
- There were nine primary onsets: seven Linux-SEFIs and two output events.
- The pooled wide-field Linux-SEFI cross section is 3.6×10^-10 cm2/system [1.5×10^-10, 7.5×10^-10]. The small-field conditions give only upper limits.
- The key finding is one silent-corruption event in run 5, block 10. The first 61 predictions were correct, then 39 in a row read "bird", a class absent from the input pool. Every availability monitor stayed nominal: process alive, 23–24 ms cadence, silent kernel log, memory test passed, power rails in range. A watchdog using only those signals would have missed it.

Weaknesses:
1. Output verification is uneven and thinnest where the output events happened: 42 of 43 blocks kept their records at 20 MeV, but only 11 of 28 at 40 MeV and 9 of 21 at 58 MeV. The authors admit the loss may be correlated with abnormal blocks, which would bias the output cross sections low.
2. The input pool is tiny: 10 CIFAR-10 test images covering 6 classes. No random seed was used, and only the top-1 class was kept, so numerical errors that leave the winning class unchanged cannot be seen.
3. Counts are very small (each nonzero energy-specific output estimate rests on one event). The field-comparison p-values are exploratory: not preregistered and not adjusted for multiple tests.
4. The run 4 event count is ambiguous and depends on the clustering rule.
5. Linux-SEFI is defined by symptoms and may include interruptions not caused by radiation, so the cross sections are upper bounds.
6. Other setup gaps: LPDDR4 has no ECC, device lot and date codes were not recorded, only nominal (not component-specific) energy is reported, and a continuous current trace exists only for run 1.

Benchmark data: the supplied passages give no LUT, DSP, BRAM, GOPS or power values. Power rails were sampled but no values are reported. The only timing figures are an inter-record cadence of 23–24 ms and about 2.34 s per 100 inferences. The cadence includes PYNQ and logging overhead, so it is not a pure accelerator latency. Before irradiation, all 10 pool images were classified correctly (10/10); this is not a standard accuracy benchmark, so the accuracy field is left as n/r. The paper metadata carries extraction warnings (metadata needs manual checking; axes were inferred automatically).

note:
Critical reading: the paper deploys FINN streaming YOLO-style detectors (LP-YOLO w4a4 320×320, LP-YOLO Slim w2a4 256×256, and a custom YOLOv3-tiny w4a4 reference) on a PYNQ-Z1 (Zynq XC7Z020). The flow is Brevitas QAT → QONNX → FINN → Vivado. Four requirements must all pass at once: more than 30 FPS, more than 7 FPS/W, PL latency under 50 ms, and VOC mAP@0.5 above 0.55. Only LP-YOLO Slim at 142.86 MHz meets all four: 35.66 FPS, 2.91 W, 12.25 FPS/W, 45.11 ms PL latency, 49.77 ms end-to-end latency, and 0.594 VOC mAP.

Strengths: the numbers are measured on the board (batch 100, power at the 12 V input rail, so it is board-level). The paper keeps FINN estimates separate from measurements; for example, FINN estimated 38 FPS but the board measured about 22 FPS. It also reports PL and end-to-end latency separately, and the end-to-end overhead is about 4.65 ms.

Caveats:
(1) The 0.594 mAP for the 142.86 MHz design was not re-measured. It is carried over from the 125 MHz run because 'the model is unchanged'.
(2) Accuracy is the tightest requirement, only 0.044 above the 0.55 threshold.
(3) The Table I text is garbled. The CLK/Batch column and the 125 MHz Slim row are missing, and the YOLOv3-tiny clock is not given.
(4) No LUT/DSP/BRAM use or GOPS figures are reported, even though the paper discusses resource limits.
(5) The two best hardware results (200 MHz and manual-FIFO LP-YOLO) have no mAP.
(6) The QAT claim (within 0.006 mAP of floating point) was shown on YOLOv3-tiny, not on the deployed w2a4 Slim model.
(7) The COCO numbers use a 'filtered' board-test protocol re-measured in Aug. 2026, so their provenance differs.
(8) The paper cites Section VII-D, and the extraction flags Section VI as undetected, so some content may be missing.
(9) Wording such as 'supplied table' suggests the text was derived from a project report.

For the rows: latency_ms is the HW-PL latency (end-to-end latency is 49.77 ms at 142.86 MHz and 56.13 ms at 125 MHz). FPS is sustained throughput at batch 100.

FINN-Tro (Ahmed, Karki, Jungeblut, arXiv 2609.26824, 2026) is a hardware-security paper, not an accelerator design paper. It adds a counter-triggered Trojan to the HLS C++ of the last MVAU layer during FINN (v0.10.1) layer specialisation and PrepareIP code generation. The quantised model and weights are not changed. There are 2 trigger modes (Periodic, Persistent; N=5) and 3 payloads (Bias Addition, Logit Swap, Bias Subtraction; b=255), giving 6 configurations. The authors say FINN's functional simulation cannot catch it because it checks a single input and resets design state each time.

Evaluation: a binarised 4-layer MLP on MNIST (784-256-256-10) and a binarised 12-layer CNN on CIFAR-10. Both run on a PYNQ-Z1 (xc7z020) at 100 MHz with batch size 1000, use 0 DSPs and share identical folding.

- **Clean baselines:** MNIST reaches 92.96 accuracy at 737,655 images/s with a 1.356 ms runtime. CIFAR-10 reaches 84.19 accuracy at 1,995 images/s with a 501.205 ms runtime.
- **Worst attack:** persistent Bias Addition (A1-T1) drops accuracy to 10.12 on MNIST and 10.00 on CIFAR-10. Across all configurations, degradation ranges from 0.90 to 82.84.
- **Overhead:** LUT increases are at most 6.71% (MNIST) and 2.50% (CIFAR-10); FF increases at most 7.49% and 3.98%. Power stays within 9 mW of baseline.

Critical points:
1. **Runtime is for the whole batch, not per image.** The runtime is for 1000 images (1000 / 1.356 ms ≈ 737k/s), so latency_ms is n/r in the rows.
2. **Resources are only given as percentages.** LUT and BRAM figures are percentages of the device (MNIST 25.83% LUT, 10.36% BRAM; CIFAR-10 47.87% LUT, 71.07% BRAM), not absolute counts, so luts and bram are n/r. The overhead figures may be relative changes or percentage-point changes; the paper does not say which.
3. **Power is an estimate, not a measurement.** Power is post-implementation on-chip power (1.642 W and 2.085 W), which reads as a Vivado estimate rather than a board measurement. power_scope is set to estimated.
4. **The MNIST baseline is weak.** 92.96 is low for this kind of binarised MLP, so absolute accuracy drops should be read against that weak baseline.
5. **Per-configuration numbers are mostly missing.** Only the baseline and A1-T1 values appear in the supplied text; the rest of Tables IV and V was not supplied.
6. **The fixed trigger is easy to detect.** With N=5 and b=255 the Trojan is quite visible; the stealth claim relies on untested choices of larger N or smaller b.
7. **No defence is tested.** Countermeasures are left to future work.
8. **The source metadata is unreliable.** It is flagged extraction ok:false, so it should be checked by hand.

note:
COPE (arXiv 2609.26853) is an LLM continual-personalization method, not a hardware paper. None of the supplied passages reports a measured hardware result: no FPS, GOPS, latency, power, or FPGA resource figures. So all hardware fields are n/r, and the two rows only record task-quality scores.

**Method:** Each user gets a learnable personalized embedding (l=10 virtual tokens, about 1.2e-5 of Qwen3-1.7B's parameters per user). A single on-policy PPO update step combines three objectives:
- L_SFT: textual feedback trains the embedding only (model weights frozen).
- J_eval: self-evaluation calibration; updates both the embedding and the model weights.
- J_policy: a reward equal to completeness × personalization; updates the model weights only.
When users give no feedback, the self-evaluated score serves as a proxy reward.

**Setup:** PersonaLens benchmark, 256 users with 17 domains each. The model is updated after each of the first 51 interactions (3 tasks × 17 domains), and a fourth traversal is held out for testing. The metric is personalization score × binary completeness, out of 10, reported as mean±std over 3 runs.

**Results:** At p=0.75, COPE scores 4.74 vs 3.69 for PAP (the best training-free baseline). COPE+SR is best in every setting, peaking at 5.36; T-PAP+SR reaches 4.98. The ablations show that removing J_eval hurts most (3.36 vs 4.69). The score rises with model size (Qwen3 1.7B → 8B: 4.69 → 5.49), and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reaches 5.16.

**Critical points:**
1. Users, feedback, and completeness judgments are all simulated by LLMs (the Qwen-Flash simulator and evaluator). This creates a risk of closed-loop or same-family bias. The authors check this by swapping in a DeepSeek-V3 simulator and running a blinded comparison with one human annotator on 204 response pairs, but a single annotator is weak evidence.
2. The self-evaluation proxy agrees with the user on only 72.63% of the pairs where both give a directional judgment. The population-level correlation is r=0.81 during training and 0.71 on held-out runs.
3. Table 1's row labels are lost in the extracted text. Only T-PAP+SR and COPE+SR can be identified directly; the COPE and PAP values come from the prose.
4. No training cost, latency, or compute overhead is reported. The prose mentions PAP's extra latency qualitatively but gives no numbers.
5. Evaluation covers a short horizon (51 updates), and the general-capability results are deferred to Appendix K, which was not supplied.
